title: DCI releases PHOTO of armed and dangerous robbery suspect on the run, appeals to Kenyans to help track him down (LOOK)
description: Wednesday, November 04, 2026 - The Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) has launched a manhunt for a wanted robbery suspect believed to be behind several violent criminal incidents in Nairobi and neighbouring areas. In a public notice issued on Wednesday, November 4, the investigative agency identified the suspect as John Masila Nzioka and appealed to members of the public to provide information that could lead to his arrest. "The Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI) is appealing to members of the public for any information that may lead to the arrest of John Masila Nzioka, who is wanted in connection with multiple cases of robbery with violence," the notice read. The agency described Nzioka as armed and dangerous, warning that he could pose a serious security threat. According to the DCI, the suspect has previously engaged police officers in a shootout during an operation, leaving some officers injured before he managed to escape. "The suspect is considered armed and dangerous. He is believed to have used a firearm during robberies committed within Nairobi Region and its environs. “In a recent shootout, police officers were injured before the suspect escaped the police dragnet," the statement added. The DCI also provided details of his reported home area, identifying him as a resident of Machakos County, specifically Kangundo Sub-County, Kanzalu Division, Kanzalu Location and Kikambuani Sub-Location. The agency urged anyone with information regarding his whereabouts to report to the authorities through its established channels, assuring the public that information could be shared anonymously. Members of the public can contact the DCI through its toll-free hotline 0800 722 203 or WhatsApp number 0709 570 000. Alternatively, information can be reported at the nearest police station or through the national emergency numbers 999, 911 and 112. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Pharmacists warn Kenyan women against using cetirizine tablets to allegedly tighten ‘Kasusu’ as demand for the allergy medicine increases.
description: Thursday, November 05, 2026 - The Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) has warned Kenyan women against misusing cetirizine tablets in an alleged attempt to tighten their private parts, cautioning that the bizarre practice could expose them to serious health complications. The warning follows the circulation of social media claims encouraging women to insert the commonly used allergy medication into their intimate areas to achieve a tightening effect. In a statement issued on Thursday, November 5, PSK expressed concern over the growing misinformation, clarifying that cetirizine was never designed or approved for such purposes. "The Pharmaceutical Society of Kenya (PSK) has noted with concern recent discussions circulating on social media promoting the use of cetirizine, a commonly used antihistamine, for purported v@g!n@l tightening, including claims encouraging the insertion of cetirizine tablets into the birth canal," the statement read. The professional body explained that cetirizine is an antihistamine intended to be swallowed to manage allergic reactions such as sneezing, runny noses, itchy eyes and skin conditions, including hives. Pharmacists further dismissed claims that the medication could tighten women's intimate areas by causing dryness. According to PSK, although antihistamines may cause dryness as a side effect, reduced lubrication does not strengthen pelvic muscles or alter the natural anatomy of the female reproductive system. Instead, inserting the tablets could cause irritation, increased friction, discomfort, and possible tissue injuries. The society also warned that oral cetirizine tablets contain ingredients that have not been tested for application to delicate intimate tissues. Women who may have already experimented with the practice were urged to stop immediately and seek medical attention if they experienced pain, bleeding, burning sensations, itching, unusual discharge or fever. Beyond the health risks, PSK revealed that the viral claims had triggered increased demand for cetirizine, resulting in reports of price hikes and shortages in some pharmacies. The society warned that the situation could disadvantage patients who genuinely depend on the medication to manage allergies. It urged Kenyans to purchase medicines only from Pharmacy and Poisons Board (PPB)-licensed premises where registered pharmacists are available. PSK also warned the public against relying on unverified social media health advice, emphasizing the importance of seeking guidance from qualified medical professionals before attempting unfamiliar health practices. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

In an emotional social media post, the grieving mother questioned why Lexie had to leave her and repeatedly pleaded with her daughter to come back. “My daughter, why, why, why? Why, Alexier, did you have to leave me like this? It hurts, mama, it hurts so bad. I don't even know how to understand all this. My baby, please come back. Let all this be a dream,” she wrote. She also expressed concern about Lexie's two brothers, wondering how they would grow up without the love and care their sister gave them. The mother said she did not know how to find the strength to accept the loss or even remain strong for her other children. She recalled that Lexie was full of life and said receiving the news of her death on October 31, 2026, was the worst moment of her life. “You mean my baby is sleeping forever? title: Ogopa Single Mothers! Kenyan man cries out as he narrates his marital woes! Marry a single mother at your own risk
description: Tuesday, November 10, 2026 - A Kenyan man has opened up about his troubled marriage to a woman he met in Kitengela when she was pregnant with another man's child. In an emotional post, the man narrated how he met the woman after she lost her job at an EPZ company while pregnant with a young man she was dating at the time. He claims that he fell in love with her, married her while she was still pregnant, and took responsibility for the child, whom he says he even gave a name from his family. According to the man, things were initially smooth in their marriage, and they lived happily together until his wife secured a new job at Kitengela Mall about two months ago. He now claims that her attitude towards him has completely changed, accusing her of disrespecting him and treating him like a housemaid in their own home. The man alleges that his wife sometimes arrives home as late as midnight and no longer bothers to cook, leaving him feeling neglected and frustrated. He also claims that she speaks to him disrespectfully and treats him differently since getting the new job. "Ogopa single mothers. I don't know what to do, man," he lamented while seeking advice from other social media users. Check out the post. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: ‘It is well with my soul’: The extraordinary story behind a hymn born out of tragedy
description: Horatio Spafford’s 1873 hymn, written after losing four daughters at sea, remains Christianity’s most powerful declaration of faith amid devastating loss By Ashford Kimani Horatio Gates Spafford, a successful Chicago lawyer and committed Christian, wrote one of the most enduring hymns in the history of Christian worship not from a place of comfort, but from the depths of unbearable loss. Composed in 1873 after a series of tragedies that would have broken most people, It Is Well with My Soul continues to be sung in churches, at funerals and during moments of private crisis across the world — its message of faith transcending generations and denominations. Spafford was born in 1828 and built a prosperous legal career in Chicago, Illinois, maintaining close relationships with prominent religious figures, including the celebrated evangelist Dwight L. Moody. He had a wife, Anna, and five children. By the early 1870s, his life bore all the hallmarks of stability and professional achievement. Yet that stability concealed the fragility that comes with anchoring one’s security in family, property and professional success. The first blow came in October 1871, when the Great Chicago Fire tore through the city. Spafford had invested heavily in property, and the disaster inflicted serious financial losses. Around the same period, the family suffered the death of a young son. Grief and uncertainty entered a household that had previously known relative comfort. Even so, the worst was still ahead. In November 1873, Spafford planned a European trip with Anna and their four daughters — Annie, Margaret Lee, Bessie and Tanetta. Business commitments forced him to remain behind in Chicago while his family sailed ahead aboard the French steamship Ville du Havre, intending to join them later. On 22 November 1873, the Ville du Havre collided with another vessel in the Atlantic Ocean and sank. More than 200 people perished. All four of Spafford’s daughters were among the dead. Anna survived and was pulled from the water. The woman who had boarded the ship with her four children was now returning to shore without them. She sent her husband a telegram. The message is traditionally remembered for its devastating brevity: “Saved alone. What shall I do?” Those four words communicated a loss almost beyond comprehension. Spafford had already buried a son and endured significant financial ruin. Now, in a single maritime disaster, he had lost all four daughters. The tragedy posed a question that cuts to the heart of faith: what happens when the God in whom we trust does not prevent the suffering we most desperately wish to avoid? For Spafford, this was no abstract theological problem. It was immediate, personal and shattering. His daughters were gone, his wife was grieving, and the future they had imagined together had been destroyed. According to the widely recorded history of the hymn, Spafford later sailed across the Atlantic to reunite with Anna. The ship’s captain reportedly told him when they were passing near the area where the Ville du Havre had gone down. It was in the wake of this crossing — over the waters that had taken his children — that Spafford wrote the words of It Is Well with My Soul. Though popular accounts differ on the precise moment of composition, the connection between the hymn and the loss of his daughters is well established. The opening verse captures the remarkable tension between suffering and faith: “When peace, like a river, attendeth my way, when sorrows like sea billows roll; whatever my lot, Thou hast taught me to say, it is well, it is well with my soul.” These are not the words of a man whose grief had passed. They are the words of a man choosing, consciously and painfully, to anchor his soul in something beyond his circumstances. The distinction matters. The hymn does not ask Christians to deny grief, suppress emotion or pretend that tragedy does not hurt. It presents faith as a source of hope that can survive even when circumstances remain painful and incomprehensible. To declare that all is well with one’s soul is not to claim that all is well with one’s life. The music that gave the hymn its familiar form was composed by Philip Paul Bliss, an American gospel singer and composer who set Spafford’s words to a melody he titled Ville du Havre, in direct reference to the ship and the tragedy. The hymn was published in 1876 in Gospel Hymns No. 2, a collection associated with Bliss and the evangelist Ira D. Sankey. What began as an intensely private expression of faith gradually became a treasured fixture of Christian worship worldwide. Spafford’s later years brought further change. In 1881, he and Anna moved to Jerusalem with family and associates, establishing a Christian community known as the American Colony, which devoted itself to charitable and humanitarian work. Spafford died in Jerusalem in 1888. Anna continued the work of the colony until her own death in 1923. Today, It Is Well with My Soul continues to speak to those facing bereavement, illness, financial hardship and unanswered questions. Its enduring power lies in its refusal to equate faith with a trouble-free life. Like Job, who acknowledged God through devastating loss, or Habakkuk, who resolved to rejoice even when the fields produced nothing, Spafford’s words carry a hope that does not depend on favourable circumstances. More than 150 years after its composition, the hymn remains what it always was: a declaration that faith can coexist with grief, that hope can outlast uncertainty, and that even when life is not well, the soul can be. title: Lecturers return to class — but warn of fresh strike
description: Kenya’s public universities resumed yesterday after a month-long shutdown, yet lecturers are already threatening to walk out again over unresolved pay disputes By Ruth Omaiko Kenya’s public universities reopened yesterday after a month of empty lecture halls, with students returning to class on Monday following the end of a nationwide lecturers’ strike that paralysed teaching, examinations, research and graduation ceremonies across the country. The strike, called on 2nd October by three unions — the Universities Academic Staff Union (UASU), the Kenya Universities Staff Union (KUSU) and the Kenya Union of Domestic, Hotels, Educational Institutions, Hospitals and Allied Workers (KUDHEIHA) — was triggered by the government’s failure to implement the 2025–2029 Collective Bargaining Agreement (CBA). It ended on 30th October after the government committed KSh 20 billion to fund the CBA, to be disbursed in three annual phases, alongside a 3.5 per cent basic salary increase backdated to July 2025. “We have achieved the objectives of our strike. Prepare to go to class,” UASU Secretary-General Constantine Wesonga announced. The relief, however, may be short-lived. Appearing before the National Assembly committees on education and labour on Wednesday, Wesonga flagged two unresolved issues — plans to fund lecturers’ salaries from student fees, and KSh 100 billion in outstanding pension and salary remittances. “The storm might have subsided, but there are two issues that will make us rise again,” he told parliament. Labour Committee chairperson Ken Chonga warned the deal remains vulnerable without Treasury backing. Education Committee chairperson Julius Melly assured unions parliament would secure the first KSh 6.7 billion tranche through the supplementary budget. Students have returned — but with one eye on December examinations and the other on a government whose promises have a habit of arriving late. author: the mt kenya times
title: Court steps in as FKF leadership war threatens Kenya’s AFCON 2027 dream
description: A Murang’a High Court petition seeking conservatory orders against rival FKF factions has thrown Kenya’s football governance crisis into the judicial arena, with the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations co-hosting at stake By Martin Weche The Football Kenya Federation’s protracted leadership crisis landed before the High Court at Murang’a last week after a sports stakeholder filed an urgent constitutional petition seeking court intervention to halt what he described as a dangerous dual power structure threatening to destroy the institutional integrity of Kenyan football. The petition challenges the current FKF disputes, and a subsequent application has also been filed challenging the Special General Meeting resolutions of 7 November 2026. Patrick Kinyua filed Petition No. E028 of 2026 on 3 November at the Murang’a Law Courts Constitutional and Human Rights Division, naming the Football Kenya Federation, its Congress, its National Executive Committee, the Cabinet Secretary for Youth Affairs, Creative Economy and Sports, and the Sports Registrar as respondents. The petition was certified urgent and placed before Justice Dorah Chepkwony, with case activities recorded on both 4 and 9 November. The crisis at the heart of the petition has been simmering since April. Hussein Mohammed was elected FKF President on 7 December 2024, with McDonald Mariga elected as his Vice-President in a process recognised by both FIFA and the Confederation of African Football. Within months, however, the leadership had descended into open warfare. On 24 April 2026, nine of the fourteen National Executive Committee members passed a resolution directing Mohammed to step aside over alleged financial impropriety linked to a KSh 42.4 million insurance tender connected to the 2024 African Nations Championship, simultaneously installing Mariga as acting president. FIFA moved swiftly to reject the resolution, declaring it null and void for failing to comply with the procedural requirements of the FKF Constitution, particularly Article 41, which governs the suspension or removal of elected officials. FIFA was explicit: the steps required — proper agenda communication, quorum, voting thresholds and the right to be heard — had not been followed. “Actions taken outside the clearly defined statutory framework cannot produce valid legal effects within the association,” FIFA stated, warning that members acting in breach of the FKF Constitution risked disciplinary consequences. Despite the global body’s categorical position, the Mariga-aligned faction refused to stand down, repeatedly preventing the committee from achieving the quorum required under Article 40 of the FKF Constitution. The human cost has been considerable. Mohammed made repeated attempts through June, July, August, September and October to convene NEC meetings to address the 2026/2027 budget, national team coaching appointments, league structures, refereeing policy and AFCON 2027 preparations. Each meeting collapsed for want of quorum. By October, Mohammed had publicly declared he had given up trying to work with the seven dissenting members and warned they would face disciplinary action. A pre-consultative NEC Kamukunji held on 13 October offered a rare moment of engagement when both factions attended, but it unravelled quickly. The Mariga side presented thirteen governance concerns; only four were addressed before the meeting was adjourned. When a formal NEC meeting was called the following day, the Mariga faction stayed away, citing a lapsed seven-day notice period under Article 38(3) of the FKF Constitution. “We cannot punish millions of Kenyans because of seven people,” Mohammed told journalists afterwards. By late October the situation had deteriorated into competing disciplinary processes. General Assembly representatives issued proposals seeking the expulsion of seven NEC members aligned with Mariga — including Mariga himself, Robert Kenneth Macharia and Bernard Korir Lagat — for alleged breaches of the FKF Constitution and FIFA Statutes. Four days later, separate General Assembly representatives issued a Summons to Show Cause against Mohammed, citing six charges including financial irregularities and alleged manipulation of NEC minutes. The petition asks the court to declare the dual power structure a threat to the rule of law, restrain all parallel disciplinary processes, direct the Cabinet Secretary and Sports Registrar to exercise their supervisory powers under the Sports Act No. 25 of 2013, and compel the entire dispute into a constitutionally compliant resolution process. Former Harambee Stars coach Jacob Mulee captured the wider despair. “Kenya is the only country right now where the league has not started. Even in Ukraine, where there is war, the league is ongoing,” he said. With Kenya co-hosting the 2027 Africa Cup of Nations, CAF President Patrice Motsepe has already warned: “We have never needed unity in Kenyan football as we need it now.” The court, it seems, may now have to deliver what the boardroom could not. title: Who will carry the students’ voice? Laikipia University prepares for November 18 elections
description: With LUSA polls days away, students face a defining choice about the kind of leadership that will represent their interests and hold the administration to account By Jonothan Muchiri Laikipia University is gearing up for one of the most significant moments in its student governance calendar, with the Laikipia University Students Association (LUSA) elections set for Tuesday. The polls will give thousands of students the opportunity to choose representatives who will speak on their behalf, champion their interests and engage the university administration on issues that shape daily campus life. Student leadership matters more than many appreciate. Through LUSA, students have a recognised platform to raise concerns, participate in institutional governance and push back when things go wrong. Tuesday’s election is therefore not merely a procedural exercise — it is a chance for the student body to decide, with intention, what kind of representation it wants for the term ahead. As the date closes in, attention shifts to the candidates, their messages and the concrete proposals they put before voters. The issues that define student elections at Laikipia are rarely abstract — accommodation, welfare, transport, academic support, financial hardship, mental health and the quality of communication between student leaders and university management. Candidates will be expected to address these with specifics, not slogans. The university has an established record of credible student elections. The 2024/2025 LUSA Electoral College election was held on 12th March 2025, followed by the Student Executive Council election two days later, with the newly elected leadership sworn in on 20th March. Emmanuel Kibet Koech was elected Chairperson of the Executive Council in a process that Dean of Students Beatrice Yogo described as the smoothest and best-attended in the university’s history. That transition set a standard — not just for organisation, but for the spirit in which student democracy ought to be conducted. Its lessons remain relevant. A successful poll should not be measured by turnout alone. Students will expect those elected on Tuesday to remain accessible long after the celebrations, communicate regularly and honour commitments made during the campaign. Leadership that disappears between terms serves no one. The Directorate of Student Affairs carries responsibility for ensuring Tuesday’s election proceeds in an orderly manner — with clear communication, strict adherence to electoral rules and cooperation among candidates, voters and university officials. The environment surrounding the election matters as much as the outcome. Beyond campaign activity, the coming days offer students a moment of genuine reflection. What does effective representation look like? Who, among those presenting themselves for election, has demonstrated the seriousness, empathy and commitment the role demands? Those chosen will be expected to represent the entire student community — not just their supporters — and to engage the administration constructively even when the conversation is difficult. Ultimately, Tuesday’s election will determine more than who occupies student leadership positions. It will offer a clear measure of students’ confidence in those who seek to serve them. As Laikipia University prepares for the polls, one question remains: who will earn that trust — and carry the students’ voice? The post Who will carry the students’ voice? title: Samsung tops Africa smartphone market for first time in three decades
description: Flexible daily and weekly payment plans have unlocked premium device sales across the continent, handing the South Korean giant a commanding lead over its rivals By Jane Njeri Samsung Electronics has topped Africa’s smartphone market in both revenue and unit sales for the first time in thirty years, driven by a customised installment payment model that has fundamentally reshaped how consumers across the continent access and purchase mobile devices. According to market research firm TechInsights, Samsung’s unit sales surged 34.8 per cent in the second quarter of 2026, even as total smartphone sales across the African market fell 16.6 per cent year on year over the same period. The divergence is striking: while the broader market contracted, Samsung moved decisively in the opposite direction, capturing ground that its rivals lost. The catalyst, TechInsights says, was not a product breakthrough but a commercial innovation tailored to African economic realities. Rather than requiring a single upfront payment or a conventional monthly instalment plan, Samsung introduced a model that allows customers to pay for devices in daily or weekly amounts — a structure that mirrors the income patterns of millions of African workers who are paid irregularly or in cash. “The introduction of a customised installment model that lets customers pay for devices in daily or weekly amounts, reflecting local income structures where monthly salaries are not common, appears to have been a key factor,” TechInsights said in a statement. The results have been commercially significant. The installment payment model accounted for 46 per cent of Samsung’s smartphone revenue in Africa, underscoring how central the financing innovation has become to the company’s continental strategy. Crucially, the scheme has not merely driven sales of entry-level handsets. As the upfront cost barrier has lowered, consumers have demonstrated a willingness to trade up. “As the initial purchase burden has decreased, sales of premium products are also increasing. Samsung’s sales of Galaxy S and Z series devices in Africa rose 20 per cent year on year this year,” the research firm noted. The broader market share trajectory reinforces the scale of Samsung’s advance. The company’s share of smartphone unit sales in Africa grew from 22.4 per cent in 2024 to 26.5 per cent last year. On an annual basis for 2026, Samsung is projected to hold a 34.5 per cent share of sales value and a 38.7 per cent share of unit volume — figures that would represent an increase of more than 16 percentage points in unit market share over just two years. No other manufacturer in the African market is currently on a comparable growth trajectory. The significance of the achievement extends beyond the commercial. Africa’s smartphone market remains one of the most underpenetrated in the world relative to population size, meaning the continent represents a long-term growth prize that every major consumer electronics manufacturer is competing to claim. The fact that Samsung has cracked the market not through price-cutting alone but through a financing model built around local income behaviour suggests a strategic maturity that its competitors will find difficult to replicate quickly. Building the partnerships, digital infrastructure and consumer trust required to operate a daily payment system at scale across diverse African markets is not something a rival can copy overnight. For African consumers, particularly those in lower-income brackets who have historically been priced out of premium technology, the implications are tangible. Access to higher-specification devices — with better cameras, longer battery life, more processing power and improved security — has direct consequences for productivity, digital financial inclusion and participation in the growing digital economy. A smallholder farmer in rural Kenya who can now afford a Galaxy device through daily micropayments is not simply buying a smartphone; they are gaining access to mobile banking, agricultural information platforms, e-commerce and digital government services that were previously beyond reach. Samsung’s performance in Africa also carries a broader lesson for multinational corporations operating on the continent. The conventional assumption — that African consumers will always gravitate towards the cheapest available option — is being quietly dismantled. What African consumers consistently demonstrate is a preference for value and reliability, provided that the financing structures exist to make that value accessible. Samsung identified that gap and built a product around it. The results speak for themselves. With a projected 38.7 per cent share of unit volume by year end, Samsung’s dominance of Africa’s smartphone market looks set to deepen further still. author: the mt kenya times
title: Ruto and Gachagua trade blows as Kenya’s 2027 election battle turns brutal
description: With thirteen months to the general election, Kenya’s two most powerful political rivals have unleashed their sharpest attacks yet — and the temperature is only going up By David Kimani President William Ruto and former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua on Tuesday traded their most ferocious public exchanges to date, with Ruto accusing Gachagua of suppressing young political talent and Gachagua responding with a searing indictment of the President over the deaths of young Kenyans during the 2024 and 2025 protests — an escalation that signals the 2027 general election campaign has entered its most combative phase. The confrontation began in Kisii County, where Ruto was on the third day of a development tour of the Gusii region. Speaking before a crowd that included Kisii Governor Simba Arati and several Members of Parliament, the President invoked a biblical reference with unmistakable political intent, likening Gachagua to King Herod — the ruler who, in scripture, ordered the killing of infants perceived as threats to his power. “Those who have served in government and politics for long should be ready to retire with me in 2032 and pave way for young leaders to take over,” Ruto said, in remarks directed squarely at his estranged former running mate. He challenged the broader opposition to present a coherent development agenda rather than what he called “endless insults and political slogans,” insisting that Kenya had moved beyond the era of tribal politics and discrimination. Gachagua’s response was immediate, unsparing and aimed directly at the President’s most sensitive political wounds. “Mr. Taxes, think of and address the 55 million Kenyans you neglected and squandered their hard-earned taxes over the last four years,” Gachagua wrote in a public statement. He challenged Ruto’s invocation of youth by naming specific individuals — Rex Masai, Kennedy Onyango, Albert Ojwang, Erick Mutisia, Ibrahim Kamau and Boniface Kariuki — alongside more than 200 young people he said were killed during the Gen Z protests of 2024 and the Saba Saba demonstrations of 2025. “Are they still the leaders of 2032?” he asked. “Didn’t you know that Gen Zs were young when you ordered their macabre abductions and brutal killings?” Gachagua went further, raising the spectre of the 2007-2008 post-election violence, referencing the Kiambaa Church burning and Ruto’s alleged role in the ethnic mobilisation of that period. He compared the President to a list of Africa’s most reviled post-independence dictators — Idi Amin, Mobutu Sese Seko, Siad Barre, Jean-Bédel Bokassa, Sani Abacha, Robert Mugabe and Omar al-Bashir — in language designed to wound as much as to persuade. The exchange is not merely a clash of personalities. It is an early but revealing preview of the political warfare that will define Kenya’s path to the August 2027 general election — a contest that is shaping up to be one of the most consequential and potentially volatile in the country’s post-independence history. The fissures exposed by the Ruto-Gachagua rupture — which culminated in Gachagua’s parliamentary impeachment last year — have not healed. If anything, they have deepened into what analysts now describe as a defining fault line in Kenyan politics, one that cuts across ethnicity, class and generation in ways that older political templates struggle to explain. Ruto’s strategic positioning in Gusii is deliberate and telling. The region delivered a significant vote share to the Kenya Kwanza alliance in 2022, and the President’s allies in the area have been at pains to consolidate that support ahead of next year. Governor Arati, whose political journey from opposition firebrand to Ruto ally has itself been a subject of considerable commentary, told the crowd that Gachagua’s tribal politics had no place in modern Kenya. “Gachagua recently said if things go wrong in Kenya after the next election, he will flee Kenya and settle on his farm in Texas,” Arati warned. “Kenyans should therefore be wary of this evil man.” South Mugirango MP Silvanus Osoro went further, claiming that Gachagua’s impeachment had actually accelerated development in the region. “Gachagua was the stumbling block to the development of our community because of his philosophy of shares,” Osoro said. The reference to Gachagua’s “shares” philosophy — his public position that communities that had supported Kenya Kwanza deserved proportional returns from government — has become a central line of attack from the Ruto camp. The President has countered it with the concept he calls “Usawa ni Sawa,” broadly translated as equity or equal treatment, arguing that his administration distributes development resources without discrimination. Gachagua, in his statement yesterday, dismissed this as an “obnoxious fallacy.” Ruto also addressed the growing opposition alliance-building exercise with a tone of studied indifference that his allies will hope projects confidence rather than concealment. “Their political arrangement is an internal matter that should not take priority over national issues affecting Kenyans,” he said. “They should keep it to themselves.” The opposition’s efforts to coalesce around a single presidential candidate have proceeded in public fits and starts, with various leaders announcing unity while the structural disagreements underneath remain unresolved. What is becoming clear, however, is that the 2027 election will not be decided in the way that previous Kenyan elections have been. The Gen Z protests fundamentally altered the political landscape, introducing a generation of voters and activists who are openly contemptuous of the political class across the spectrum — including, it must be noted, those in the opposition. The deaths that occurred during those protests have not been forgotten, and Gachagua’s decision to name the dead by name in a political statement directed at the President reflects an understanding that this constituency cannot be won with ordinary campaign promises. For Ruto, the challenge is to convert his development record — real in some respects, contested in others — into a re-election mandate in an environment of acute economic hardship and deep public distrust. For Gachagua and the opposition, the challenge is to translate public anger into political organisation disciplined enough to win, not merely to protest. Thirteen months remain. Sony and Microsoft are urging fans to preload the game before its launch on November 19th, as network services will likely be bottlenecked by the sheer demand for this game. description: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 - A bar attendant from Meru has been accused of stealing more than KSh100,000 from a man identified as Murangiri after getting him intoxicated and luring him into her house. According to a social media post exposing the alleged theft, the woman first made sure Murangiri was heavily intoxicated before locking him inside her house. She is then accused of withdrawing KSh40,000 from his account in Meru town at around 1 am. A person exposing the theft has shared what is said to be an M-Pesa statement showing the transactions, claiming that the woman stole over KSh100,000 from the victim. Murangiri was previously an ambulance driver at Githongo Hospital, and the woman resorted to withdrawing the money in Meru town at night after realising that he was a well-known person in Githongo. Check out the posts. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Kenyan man found dead in US home days after celebrating birthday as family appeals for help to bring body home (PHOTOs)
description: Wednesday, November 11, 2026 - A Kenyan family is mourning the sudden death of their loved one, Dickson Gitonga Mbatau, who was found dead inside his home in Phoenix, Arizona, on October 28, 2026, just four days after celebrating his 54th birthday. Dickson had marked his birthday on October 24, sharing photographs from a dinner with his family. The pictures captured what appeared to be a joyful occasion, making his sudden demise even more heartbreaking for those who knew and loved him. According to the family, concern began mounting after they went about 48 hours without hearing from him. Worried about his whereabouts and unable to establish contact, the family requested a welfare check from the Phoenix Police Department. It was during the police visit that they received the devastating news that Dickson had been found deceased inside his residence. His death has left relatives and friends grappling with grief as they try to come to terms with losing him so unexpectedly. Beyond the emotional pain, the family is now faced with the challenge of bringing his remains back to Kenya for burial. May Dickson's family and loved ones find strength, comfort and peace during these difficult times. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Authenticity over algorithms: World Media Summit explores trust in AI era
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia BEIJING, Nov. 9 (Xinhua) — An international dialogue at the 7th World Media Summit (WMS) explored some of the most pressing questions: who really shapes the news agenda? Why do people trust one source over another, and what impact will artificial intelligence (AI) have on journalism? “Newsrooms are no longer the only players deciding which stories reach the audience,” Guo Wei, the event’s moderator, said in her opening remarks for the event focusing on “influence, AI and trust” here Saturday. “Content creators have built their own audiences, social media platforms influence what people see, and AI is changing almost every stage of news production,” Guo said. DIVERSIFIED MEDIA ECOSYSTEM Speakers at the dialogue described a shift in which the gatekeepers of news dissemination have expanded from traditional media outlets to platforms, algorithms and individual creators. Panelists said the more diversified ecosystem had not diminished the importance of professional standards, and several argued that authenticity, judgment and trust had become more, not less, valuable in public-interest journalism. The panel included Vsevolod Pulya, head of RT China and editor-in-chief of Gateway to Russia; Diego Ruzzarin, a Mexican content creator with more than 10 million followers across platforms and also a partner director of MPV Management; and Zephyr, host of the Boston Round Face Channel known for current-affairs commentary. Their backgrounds spanned traditional media, the global creator economy and younger audiences. WHO SETS THE AGENDA The discussion opened with a fundamental question about influence: From the perspective of a major international media organization, do newsrooms still shape the news agenda, or do they depend more on social media platforms to reach audiences? Pulya described the change from inside the industry. “Traditional news agencies were the gatekeepers who decided for the audience what and when to know about the outside world. But now big tech companies have become the gatekeepers.” He described how the previous top-down structure of news dissemination is giving way to a different model. Influencers, he said, communicate horizontally, much like talking to a friend. “Real emotional attachment is something that any media should learn to develop.” That shift is evident even in the composition of global media gatherings. The WMS has invited not only mainstream media representatives, but also a growing number of internationally known content creators, noted Guo, also a Xinhua News Agency journalist. “This is both a footnote to the changing media landscape and a source of more diverse perspectives and voices for global news communication,” the moderator said. The panel also examined why younger audiences increasingly turn to individual creators for news rather than established news organizations. For Ruzzarin, the answer lies beyond institutional brands, in lived experience and cultural connection. “Every time I come to China, I bring at least four to five different influencers from different countries in the Global South for them to experience firsthand. Nothing is more powerful than coming here, having tea and talking to local people,” he said. He added that his two most-watched videos on YouTube over four consecutive years were a review of Sun Tzu’s The Art of War and an analysis of Dragon Ball Z, the Japanese anime drawing inspiration from the Monkey King, Sun Wukong, from classic Chinese novel Journey to the West. Neither is conventional hard news, yet both use shared cultural motifs to connect with young audiences across borders. For traditional media, Pulya said the lesson was clear. “You have to jump on the pop culture train. Pop culture is a separate world worth exploring and worth reflecting on.” AI, DEEPFAKES AND TRUST Guo noted that AI can help journalists write, translate, edit, summarize and analyze information, leading to faster production and lower costs, and asked whether the industry risks becoming too dependent on it, with young journalists in particular missing the chance to practice basic skills. Zephyr approached the issue from the perspective of an individual creator. “I don’t believe that AI will one day replace me.” In his view, the difference between humans and AI lies precisely in an authentic personality and irreplaceable individual judgment. Guo said knowing how to use AI may become a basic requirement, but professional judgment, critical thinking and the ability to earn people’s trust may become even more important. Panelists noted that AI-generated videos, voices and images are making it harder to distinguish authentic content from fabricated material, especially with deepfakes, and that a single error can damage credibility built over years or even decades. Zephyr described a dilemma facing serious content creators. “Often we find that content we put a lot of money and energy into doesn’t perform as well as amusing false content.” Yet he stressed maintaining credibility remained central to their work. Ruzzarin emphasized face-to-face contact as a means of building trust, something that neither algorithms nor virtual content could replace. The panel also raised a question of responsibility when it comes to misleading content being produced with the help of AI. Who should be held accountable — the person who creates it, the media organization that publishes it, the platform that distributes it, or the technology company that builds and provides the AI tool? The discussion did not offer a simple answer, with participants noting that, given the multiple actors within the information space, responsibility can no longer be placed at the door of a single gatekeeper. Participants suggested that in the age of deepfakes, professional judgment, critical thinking and the ability to earn trust serve as human filters against misinformation. Under the theme “Media in the Intelligent Age: From Consensus to Action,” this year’s WMS, jointly organized by Xinhua News Agency and the Beijing municipal government from Nov. 5 to 9, drew nearly 500 representatives from nearly 330 mainstream media outlets, think tanks, government bodies, the United Nations and other international organizations across 112 countries and regions. ■ The post Authenticity over algorithms: World Media Summit explores trust in AI era appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Blow to Trump as Kenya rules out hosting Ebola quarantine for foreign nationals
description: Nairobi rejects demands to hold foreign travellers as it enters a 42-day countdown to being declared Ebola-free By Yvonne Wambui Kenya’s Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale yesterday ruled out plans to make the country a quarantine centre for foreign nationals suspected of Ebola exposure, dealing a direct blow to the United States and other governments that had sought to use Kenyan health facilities as holding points for travellers required to isolate before returning home. Speaking at a press briefing at Afya House in Nairobi, Duale was unequivocal: Kenya would not allow foreign governments to use its facilities as transit quarantine centres, nor would it issue Ebola-free certificates or quarantine documentation to foreign travellers for international travel purposes. He argued that such certificates have no basis under the International Health Regulations — the globally agreed framework governing cross-border public health measures — and that Kenya had no obligation to absorb the quarantine requirements of other countries. The announcement carries particular significance given the controversy surrounding the 50-bed Ebola isolation facility at Laikipia Air Base in Nanyuki, built through a partnership between Kenya and the United States. The facility had drawn fierce public opposition and legal challenge, with critics warning it could turn Kenya into a quarantine destination for foreign nationals exposed to the virus in neighbouring countries. Asked about the facility’s future, Duale declined to comment, saying the matter was before the courts. His statements came as Kenya recorded a milestone in its response to the outbreak. The Ministry of Health confirmed yesterday that the last patient receiving treatment for Ebola had been discharged after making a full recovery — a development that now triggers the start of a critical 42-day monitoring period beginning today. If no new infections are reported during that window, Kenya is expected to be formally declared Ebola-free on 23 December 2026. The outbreak, which gripped the country and prompted an international response, recorded nine confirmed cases in total, among them four healthcare workers who contracted the virus while treating patients. Seven people recovered; two died. The final 11 individuals who had been held under quarantine completed their monitoring period and were released to rejoin their families. Yet Duale was careful to caution that the discharge of the last patient did not signal the end of the government’s response. Surveillance will continue, traveller screening at points of entry will be maintained, and all suspected cases will be investigated. The Ministry of Health is also preparing additional measures for Kenyans returning from Ebola-affected areas, particularly the Democratic Republic of Congo, which has experienced repeated outbreaks. Those measures are expected to include mandatory health declarations, arrival screening and 21 days of medical monitoring. Duale used the briefing to sharpen his criticism of foreign governments that had imposed blanket travel and visa restrictions on Kenyan citizens since the outbreak began. He argued that Kenya had honoured every obligation under international health law — reporting infections promptly, sharing surveillance data and cooperating fully with international health organisations — and that it deserved recognition rather than punishment for doing so. “Transparency must be rewarded, not punished,” he said, calling on affected countries to review and lift their restrictions without further delay. The position represents a significant hardening of Kenya’s stance on international Ebola quarantine arrangements. Rather than accommodating external demands, the government appears determined to defend national interests while continuing to co-operate with other countries on public health matters through established frameworks. The balance is a delicate one: Kenya needs to reassure trading partners, tourists and international investors that the country remains open and safe, while resisting arrangements it regards as an imposition on its sovereignty and health infrastructure. Duale’s message on that front was direct. Kenya, he insisted, remains open for business, tourism, trade and international travel. He urged citizens to remain vigilant as the country works towards an official end to the outbreak — a declaration that, if everything holds, will come just before Christmas. The 42-day clock now running is not merely a public health formality. It represents Kenya’s best opportunity in months to close a difficult chapter, restore full confidence in its borders, and demonstrate that a country can manage a serious outbreak transparently and competently without being made to shoulder the quarantine burdens of wealthier nations. Whether those nations accept that argument — or quietly maintain their restrictions regardless — remains to be seen. author: ayesha talib
title: Three decades in the classroom: The teacher who believes the future belongs to those who never stop learning
description: North Macedonia’s Suzana Kelesoska has spent 33 years shaping young minds — and she is not done yet By Ayesha Talib Suzana Kelesoska has devoted more than three decades of her life to teaching children aged six to ten in North Macedonia, building a career defined by quiet dedication, professional rigour and an unshakeable belief that every child deserves an education tailored to who they are, not who the system expects them to be. Her story begins in Bitola, where she graduated from the Faculty of Pedagogy “St. Kliment Ohridski” in 1988, earning the foundation she would spend the next three and a half decades building upon. She entered the classroom in 1993, and what followed was not simply a career but a calling. For the better part of those years, she taught at the primary school “Murat Labunishti” in Labunishta, in the municipality of Struga — a community she served with consistency and care through changing governments, shifting curricula and the relentless evolution of what it means to educate a child in the modern world. There is something worth pausing on in that kind of commitment. Teaching in a single community for decades is not the glamorous arc that headlines tend to celebrate. It does not come with the visibility of a ministerial appointment or the recognition of a national prize. What it offers instead is something rarer: the lived experience of watching children grow into adults, of seeing the values and habits instilled in a first-grade classroom carry a person through secondary school, university and beyond. Kelesoska has had that experience many times over. She has, in the truest sense, raised generations. In March 2026, she began a new chapter, moving to the primary school “Brakja Miladinovci” in Struga, where she continues the work that has defined her professional life. The move did not represent a retreat or a winding down. For Kelesoska, it was simply the next room in a house she has spent her entire adult life building — the house of primary education in her country. What sets her apart from many educators of comparable experience is her refusal to let expertise curdle into complacency. It is a professional hazard that affects teachers and doctors and lawyers alike: the longer you do something, the easier it becomes to rely on what has worked before and stop asking whether something better might exist. Kelesoska has consistently resisted that temptation. Throughout her career, she has participated actively in national and international seminars, webinars, conferences and symposiums — not as a box-ticking exercise, but out of genuine intellectual curiosity about the craft she has chosen. Her approach in the classroom reflects a deep and practical understanding of child psychology. She does not apply a single template to thirty different children and expect uniform results. Instead, she plans her teaching materials with care and adjusts them continuously — individualising content, pacing and method according to the capabilities and potential of each child in front of her. It sounds straightforward when stated plainly, but any teacher will tell you that it is one of the most demanding disciplines in education, requiring constant observation, reflection and the willingness to change course when a child is not reaching their potential through the method being used. She is guided, too, by a clear sense of what she is ultimately responsible for. Her priority, she says, has always been the proper upbringing, education and progress of her students — not test scores alone, not administrative compliance, not the performance metrics that have come to dominate educational discourse in many countries, but the whole child. High personal integrity and dignity mark her conduct, and she sets goals for her pupils that are clear, achievable and genuinely motivating — goals designed not to intimidate but to stretch. It is against this backdrop that her enthusiasm for the future of education becomes both credible and compelling. Kelesoska is not a technologist by training, but she has watched the classroom change across three decades and she understands, perhaps better than most, that another significant shift is under way. She believes firmly that now is the right moment for primary education to embrace the possibilities offered by artificial intelligence and modern digital tools — not to replace the teacher, but to lift the administrative burden that consumes so much of a teacher’s time and energy, and to elevate the quality of the teaching process itself. It is a vision that carries weight precisely because it comes from someone who has earned the right to hold it. Kelesoska is not a theorist speaking from a conference platform about classrooms she has not visited in years. She is a practitioner, still teaching, still refining, still present in the daily reality of primary education. Her conviction that technology should serve pedagogy rather than the other way around is grounded in that experience — in knowing what a teacher actually needs and what a child actually responds to. After 33 years, Suzana Kelesoska is still learning. That, more than any qualification or commendation, is what makes her worth listening to. title: The rot in Sakaja’s boda boda compliance sector
description: Johnson Sakaja promised Nairobi order on two wheels — instead, his enforcement officers are running a roadside extortion racket By Bernard Mithia Johnson Arthur Sakaja arrived at City Hall in 2022 with one of the most decisive mandates Nairobi had produced in years — nearly 700,000 votes, a margin of more than 160,000 over his nearest challenger — and residents expected him to bring long-overdue order to a city that boda boda riders had, by any honest measure, turned into a daily hazard. The chaos was real and well-documented. Riders terrorised motorists, used pavements as shortcuts, rode against traffic and, in the ugliest incidents, torched vehicles involved in accidents rather than allowing the law to take its course. Street justice had replaced traffic law. Something had to change. Sakaja acted. Under Kenya Gazette Supplement No. 26, dated 11 December 2025, his administration introduced a boda boda compliance framework with teeth: annual parking fees of KSh10,000, mandatory branding requirements for delivery riders and an enforcement unit tasked with bringing the sector to heel. On paper, it was exactly what Nairobi needed. In practice, it has become something else entirely. On any busy day in Nairobi today, boda boda riders can be observed speeding along pedestrian walkways, making illegal turns and riding on the wrong side of the road — in full view of the very enforcement officers deployed to stop them. The compliance unit has not tamed the sector. It has monetised it. The pattern is consistent and brazen. County enforcement officers — the kanjo — impound motorcycles for genuine offences: wrong parking, pavement riding, failure to comply with branding requirements. But those motorcycles rarely reach county offices for formal fine processing. Instead, they are held in parking lots while negotiations take place. The going rate runs from KSh500 to KSh3,000, varying by offence, the seniority of the officer involved and, reportedly, the number of officials sharing the proceeds. What is particularly striking is how sophisticated the operation has become. To avoid cash trails, some officers have reportedly set up till numbers and pay bill accounts for mobile payments, with transactions occasionally routed through street vendors operating informal M-Pesa points. This is not opportunistic corruption. It is organised. There is a further layer that traps newer riders especially. Many of the motorcycles openly defying compliance regulations are, according to those familiar with the sector, owned by county officers, police officials or veteran riders who have cultivated working relationships with enforcement personnel. These motorcycles move through the city untouched. The result is a deliberately engineered environment where naive or newly arrived riders, unaware of these arrangements, follow what appears to be normal practice — only to find themselves targeted. The enforcement officer has been watching, waiting, the way a leopard waits in cover before it moves. The financial cost to Nairobi County is significant. If the compliance framework were functioning as designed, the annual KSh10,000 parking fee alone — applied consistently across a sector that numbers in the tens of thousands — would generate substantial revenue for the county. Add branding fees and penalty collections and the figures become considerable. Instead, that money is being diverted into private pockets before it reaches a single county account. The damage is not only fiscal. The boda boda sector remains dangerous, undisciplined and contemptuous of traffic law — not despite enforcement, but in some respects because of it. When the people tasked with upholding a framework are the primary beneficiaries of its failure, the framework cannot work. Riders who might otherwise comply have little incentive to do so when the alternative is a negotiated payment on the roadside. Sakaja inherited a city with enormous expectations riding on his administration. Nairobi had watched the turbulence of the Mike Sonko years, endured the instability of an impeachment and a prolonged period of uncertain governance, and placed considerable faith in a governor who projected competence and vision. The boda boda compliance sector was an early test of whether that faith was warranted. The compliance unit still has time to demonstrate its purpose. But that will require the governor to look beyond the gazette notice and confront what is actually happening on Nairobi’s streets — where his enforcement officers are not enforcing the law, but profiting from its absence. Bernard Mithia Senior advisor, Strategic partnerships Exponential international. The post The rot in Sakaja’s boda boda compliance sector appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: The roots we ignore: Childhood mental health in rural Kenya and why early wounds become adult illness
description: Kenya’s rural children are carrying grief, fear and trauma into adulthood — and the system designed to catch them is barely there By Wanjohi P. Mugambi Wanjiru was nine when her teacher stopped calling her by name — not out of cruelty, but because Wanjiru had stopped answering. She had once been the girl who raised her hand first. Then her mother left for work in Nairobi and her grandmother fell ill, and something in her quietly changed. She began arriving late, forgot her books and cried whenever asked to read aloud. The school record, in its neat handwriting, used one word: rude. That word followed her for a full term, until a new guidance teacher asked a different question. Not “why are you rude?” but “what happened at home?” Because the question was gentle, Wanjiru finally told the truth. She was not rude. She was afraid, exhausted and carrying a grief that no nine-year-old should carry alone. Wanjiru is not a real name, but her story is real — pieced together from listening circles held in Nyeri, Murang’a and Embu between 2023 and 2025. In each circle, teachers told variations of the same account, though the names and villages changed. A child who had lost a parent. A child beaten for failing. A child who had listened to shouting every night. The behaviour changed; the wound underneath was almost always the same. To understand Wanjiru, we must understand what early childhood does to the developing brain. The World Health Organisation estimates that one in seven children aged 10 to 19 lives with a mental disorder, while UNICEF puts the proportion of those receiving no treatment in sub-Saharan Africa at more than 70 per cent. The first five years are especially critical: the brain is learning, during that window, whether the world is safe or dangerous. John Bowlby’s Attachment Theory explains the mechanism clearly. A child with a consistent, caring adult develops a secure internal model — learning to regulate emotions, trust others and engage with learning. When that attachment is broken by neglect, harsh punishment, parental absence or chronic conflict, the child develops an insecure model and begins to anticipate danger even in safe environments. Wanjiru did not stop learning because she was dull. She stopped because her nervous system was preoccupied with surviving. Felitti and colleagues, in their landmark research on Adverse Childhood Experiences, identified a dose-response relationship: the more adversities a child accumulates, the higher the risk of adult anxiety, depression, addiction and chronic illness. By the time Wanjiru’s story reached a listening circle, she had already accumulated three — separation, loss and shame. She was not heading toward illness because she was weak. She was heading there because no one had yet interrupted the accumulation. What interrupted it was not a hospital, a psychiatrist or a large government programme. It was one teacher, one room and one hour a week. That teacher created what psychologists call a therapeutic space, though in that rural school it had no formal name. It was simply a listening circle, held every Wednesday after lunch, where children could speak without being corrected or laughed at. In that circle, Wanjiru learned, slowly, to name what she felt — that grief is not rudeness, and that fear is not disobedience. Through storytelling and drawing, adapted forms of expressive and play therapy, she communicated what she could not yet articulate in words. Through child-adapted cognitive behavioural techniques, she learned to notice the thought “I am stupid” and replace it, gently, with something truer: “I found this difficult today because I was worried about home.” The teacher also changed her language. Instead of “you are a mistake,” she said “you made a mistake.” Instead of “why did you score 60 and not 90?” she asked “I see you tried — what was difficult?” These were not merely polite adjustments. They were therapeutic, because they separated Wanjiru’s identity from her behaviour and allowed her to try again without shame. By the end of one term, Wanjiru was not suddenly healed — but she was different. She arrived earlier, answered questions and no longer wept when asked to read aloud. The change did not come from punishment. It came from being heard by one stable adult. Psychologist Ann Masten has identified this as the single most powerful protective factor in childhood: one consistent, supportive relationship. In Wanjiru’s case, that relationship was a teacher who chose curiosity over correction. This is the lesson rural Kenya must absorb. The Kenya Basic Education Curriculum Framework recognises guidance and counselling as a core support, yet in most rural schools counselling is either absent or reduced to discipline. The Mental Health Act of 2022 promises community-based care, and the Kenya Mental Health Policy 2015–2030 calls for integration into primary healthcare — yet most rural dispensaries still have no screening tools for children, and most county hospitals across the Mt Kenya region have no dedicated child mental health unit. The answer is not to wait for Nairobi to send specialists. It is to train teachers as first responders, equip community health promoters to screen during home visits, and support parent groups through churches, chiefs’ barazas and school meetings. When therapy is localised, it becomes accessible. When it is accessible, it becomes healing. Wanjiru is now in Grade 8. She still misses her mother and still worries about her grandmother — but she no longer believes she is a problem. She believes she is a child who faced problems. That shift has changed how she learns, how she speaks and how she imagines her future. If we protect the roots, we protect the whole tree. title: Drug abuse and Kenya’s youth: A threat to lives and the economy
description: Substance abuse is quietly dismantling Kenya’s most valuable resource — and the response remains dangerously inadequate By Esther Wambui Kenya’s young people are the country’s most valuable asset — and drug and substance abuse is steadily destroying them. What begins as experimentation, peer pressure or an attempt to cope with stress can rapidly harden into dependence, derailing education, damaging health, fracturing relationships and stripping young people of the productive futures they were promised. The National Authority for the Campaign Against Alcohol and Drug Abuse has identified youth as among the most vulnerable groups in Kenya, confirming that this is not a private struggle but a national emergency with serious economic consequences. The scale of the problem demands an urgent, coordinated response. Schools and universities must strengthen drug education, expand counselling services and develop early-identification systems for students at risk. Parents and communities must create environments where young people can speak openly about stress, peer pressure and addiction without fear of stigma — because silence is where dependence takes root. Government agencies and health professionals must make treatment and rehabilitation services genuinely accessible, not merely available on paper to those with the means to reach them. Kenya cannot afford to treat this as a marginal concern. A generation lost to addiction is a generation of businesses not built, families not stabilised and national development stalled. Every young person who slips through the gaps in prevention and recovery represents not only a personal tragedy but a measurable economic cost the country will carry for years. Protecting Kenya’s youth from drug abuse is not charity. It is the most practical investment this country can make in its own future. title: Kenya’s Ebola battle: Is the country finally winning the fight against the deadly virus?
description: With its last patient discharged and a 42-day countdown begun, Kenya is closer than ever to an Ebola-free declaration — but the threat is far from over By Collins Kibet Kenya reached a landmark moment in its fight against Ebola yesterday when the country’s last patient undergoing treatment for the disease was discharged, triggering a critical 42-day monitoring period that, if passed without incident, will see the country officially declared Ebola-free on 23 December 2026. Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale made the announcement at Afya House in Nairobi, bringing cautious relief to millions of Kenyans who have watched the outbreak unfold since the country confirmed its first case of Bundibugyo virus disease on 6 October 2026. That initial case involved a Kenyan national who had travelled from the Democratic Republic of Congo through Uganda before developing symptoms — a reminder of how quickly infectious disease can cross borders in an interconnected region. The outbreak, which the World Health Organisation has been monitoring closely, eventually recorded nine confirmed cases. The initial patient infected four family members and four healthcare workers who had attended to him before Ebola was suspected. Two people died; seven recovered. All secondary infections were identified among individuals already in quarantine, a containment achievement that prevented the virus from reaching the wider community. Health authorities successfully traced and monitored 135 contacts linked to the initial case — a logistical undertaking that underscored the seriousness with which Kenya’s public health system responded. Yesterday’s discharge of the final patient also saw the last 11 contacts complete their monitoring period and return home in good health. Kenya today has no Ebola patients under treatment and no identified contacts in quarantine. The 42-day countdown, based on twice the longest recognised incubation period of the virus, began this morning and must run without a new infection before the declaration can be made. The WHO has praised Kenya’s response, recognising healthcare workers, government institutions and communities for containing an outbreak that, in less prepared circumstances, could have spiralled into a national crisis. Officials highlighted early detection, transparency, coordinated emergency operations and rigorous contact tracing as the pillars of an effective response. The outbreak demonstrated what is possible when public health institutions and ordinary citizens work in the same direction — a lesson worth recording for future reference. That future reference may come sooner than anyone would like. The situation in the DRC, the source of Kenya’s initial case, remains deeply alarming. The DRC has recorded more than 11,000 infections and over 5,000 deaths in its ongoing outbreak, according to the latest regional figures. Cross-border movement, commerce and international travel create continuous opportunities for the virus to migrate. Kenya’s last patient may have recovered, but the regional environment that produced this outbreak has not changed. The government has consequently maintained heightened surveillance, including screening at points of entry, community monitoring and rapid response capacity. The Ministry of Health has reminded the public to remain alert for symptoms — fever, weakness, muscle pain, vomiting, diarrhoea and unexplained bleeding — and to contact the toll-free number 719 at the first sign of concern. These measures are not precautionary theatre. They are essential disciplines that must hold for 42 more days and well beyond. The infection of four healthcare workers during the outbreak deserves particular attention. Medical professionals on the frontline of any infectious disease response face risks that the public rarely fully appreciates. Their exposure in this instance highlights the ongoing need for adequate protective equipment, rigorous infection prevention protocols, continuous training and sufficient medical resources at every level of the health system. Protecting healthcare workers is not merely an institutional obligation — it is a prerequisite for protecting everyone else. The outbreak has also exposed structural questions about Kenya’s broader preparedness for public health emergencies. The country managed to contain infections within a single transmission cluster, which is a genuine achievement. But the experience has revealed the importance of modern laboratory facilities in counties beyond Nairobi, trained emergency response personnel across regions and disease surveillance systems that do not depend on a centralised response from the capital. County governments must absorb this lesson and invest accordingly, particularly in areas where access to quality medical services remains limited. Public awareness must remain a central pillar of the strategy. Misinformation, fear and stigma are as dangerous in a health emergency as the pathogen itself. They discourage people from seeking care, undermine contact tracing and punish survivors who deserve support rather than discrimination. The government must continue providing accurate, accessible information through health facilities, schools, community leaders and credible media. Recovered patients must be welcomed back into their communities without reservation. Accountability matters too. The resources deployed during this emergency response — medical supplies, personnel, logistics and emergency funds — must be accounted for transparently. Public confidence in the health system is a long-term asset, and it is built or eroded by how institutions behave under pressure. The lessons from this outbreak should translate into lasting structural improvements, not temporary measures that fade once the emergency passes. Kenya has demonstrated something important during these weeks: that a coordinated, transparent and community-rooted response can contain a dangerous pathogen even in a country with real healthcare constraints. That is not a small achievement, and it should be recognised as such. But the celebration must wait. The coming 42 days will determine whether Kenya completes this chapter cleanly. Kenyans must remain vigilant, healthcare workers must continue receiving the support they have earned, and the government must sustain the discipline that brought the country to this point. The finish line is 23 December 2026. Kenya has come too far to stumble now. title: Education is the key to a brighter future
description: Kenya is sitting on its most powerful development tool — and consistently underfunding it By Pamela Aoko Education remains the most reliable path out of poverty, the foundation of economic growth and the engine of social progress — yet Kenya continues to treat it as a budget line rather than a national priority. The evidence for education’s transformative power is not in dispute. When individuals acquire knowledge, practical skills and professional qualifications, their employment prospects improve, their earning potential rises and their communities benefit. Multiply that across millions of young Kenyans and the national dividend is enormous. The question is not whether education matters — it is why the system designed to deliver it remains so chronically under-resourced. The challenges are well known and persistently unresolved: inadequate learning facilities, prohibitive costs for low-income families, insufficient teaching materials and deeply unequal access between urban and rural communities. These are not new problems. They are structural failures that successive governments have acknowledged and inadequately addressed. The remedies are equally well understood. Increased public funding for education, improved school infrastructure, the recruitment of qualified teachers in underserved areas and targeted scholarships for students from disadvantaged backgrounds would collectively transform outcomes. Parents must remain active partners in their children’s learning, and teachers must continue adopting methods that reach every student — not only the most prepared. None of this is complicated in principle. What it requires is political will and sustained financial commitment — both of which have too often fallen short. The future of every nation begins in a classroom. The quality of what happens inside that classroom determines everything that follows. title: Laikipia University: A centre of learning, opportunity and growth
description: Nestled in the highlands of Laikipia County, a quietly ambitious public university is producing graduates ready to compete By Naomi Andhamo Laikipia University, situated along the Nyahururu–Nakuru Highway in the heart of Laikipia County, is doing something that too few Kenyan institutions manage quietly well: preparing ordinary students for an increasingly competitive world. The university’s academic offer spans education, communication, science, technology, business and criminology — a breadth that lecturer Angeline Kwamboka says gives students genuine flexibility in shaping their career paths. She credits assignments, group discussions and research projects with building the independent thinking employers now demand. “Quality teaching and active student participation,” she says, “are essential in preparing learners for what lies ahead.” Students appear to agree. Charlotte Pearl describes her lecturers as approachable and genuinely invested in student success. She singles out group discussions and library facilities as particularly valuable — spaces where ideas are tested and knowledge deepened. The university’s cool highland climate, she adds with a smile, does not hurt concentration either. Student leader Michael Njoroge, who represents the School of Education, describes his role as a bridge between student concerns and university management — one that demands patience, empathy and the ability to hold competing opinions without losing sight of practical solutions. He notes that students facing financial pressure can access work opportunities within the institution, a small but meaningful safety net. Laikipia University will need to keep pace with the accelerating demands of digital skills and practical training. The foundations, however, are solid. For the students who walk through its gates each semester, the opportunity to learn, grow and move closer to their ambitions remains very much alive.
