title: Kalonzo takes Kenya’s opposition campaign to Washington ahead of 2027 election
description: The Wiper Patriotic Front leader will lobby United States Congress members and rally diaspora communities across six American cities as the opposition race to build a credible challenge to President Ruto. By David Kimani Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka, leader of the Wiper Patriotic Front and head of The Ukombozi Alliance, will lead a nine-member delegation to the United States from Wednesday, 18 November, to Tuesday, 24 November 2026, presenting the Kenyan opposition’s alternative governance agenda on Capitol Hill and mobilising diaspora voters ahead of the August 2027 general election. The seven-day working visit marks a decisive international phase in the opposition’s campaign to unseat President William Ruto — and it arrives at a moment when the domestic political landscape is shifting faster than any single alliance can comfortably manage. According to a media advisory issued by the Office of the 10th Vice President in Nairobi, the itinerary blends formal legislative consultations in Washington, D.C., with academic forums, religious gatherings, and community town halls across Boston, Massachusetts; Germantown and Baltimore, Maryland; Minneapolis, Minnesota; and Cleveland, Ohio. The delegation departs Nairobi on Monday, 16 November, arriving in the American capital ahead of Wednesday’s flagship engagements inside the Capitol Hill complex, which conclude with a formal evening dinner alongside Washington leadership. On Thursday, 19 November, Musyoka travels to Boston for an institutional forum at the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, meeting alumni, faculty, and members of the technology and investment community — an audience whose interest in East African economic governance and democratic resilience makes them natural interlocutors for an opposition leader positioning himself as a credible, institution-minded alternative. The tour returns to the capital region on Friday, 20 November, for a town hall with the Washington, Maryland, and Virginia diaspora and an East Coast dinner, before moving to Baltimore on Saturday morning for a Sabbath service at Living Springs Seventh Day Adventist Church. That evening, Musyoka flies to Minneapolis to join Ambassador Mohamed Abdi Afey at the Somali Hero Awards and Somali Book Fair — a deliberately symbolic appearance. The tour concludes with a two-day finale in Cleveland: a diaspora Thanksgiving dinner on Sunday and the Building Bridges: Cleveland-Kenya-Africa Reception on Monday before the return flight to Nairobi. Beyond the choreography of a transatlantic tour, the trip reflects the intensifying strategic calculations that now define Kenyan politics nine months before polling day. At home, the political landscape has entered a fluid and fiercely contested pre-election period. The passing of former Prime Minister Raila Odinga removed the singular gravitational force that had anchored opposition politics for more than two decades, fracturing traditional voting blocs and opening space for new configurations — and new ambitions. President Ruto has worked aggressively to consolidate his United Democratic Alliance base while leveraging his broad-based governing arrangement to make inroads into areas that once reliably returned opposition majorities. Against that pressure, opposition figures have rallied under The Ukombozi Alliance — co-chaired by Siaya Governor James Orengo and former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i — in an effort to construct a unified front capable of mounting a credible electoral challenge. The architecture of that front, however, remains contested. Musyoka has repeatedly made clear that his own presidential ambitions must carry genuine weight in coalition negotiations, signalling that he is unwilling to step aside after four decades at the heart of Kenyan statecraft without a serious conversation about the top of the ticket. Speaking during recent grassroots rallies in South Nyanza — where his convoy encountered disruptions in Migori County before moving on to Homa Bay — Musyoka urged voters to embrace a platform of national transformation while invoking Odinga’s legacy as both inspiration and political inheritance. His office reinforced that posture in a statement issued earlier this month: “Our party leader has always maintained that his presidential ambitions must be taken seriously, and we remain confident that the ongoing discussions within the opposition will give due consideration to this position.” Internal friction has complicated efforts to settle on a single flagbearer. Tensions involving former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua and emerging generational voices such as Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna have exposed competing regional interests and tactical disagreements over how best to confront the incumbent. Polling data released this week by TIFA Research sharpens the stakes: President Ruto’s ruling party has regained ground at 25 per cent national support even as opposition voters remain fragmented across multiple personalities and movements. The numbers make the cost of continued division legible and urgent in equal measure. It is against that backdrop that Musyoka’s Washington mission carries its dual purpose. Externally, it projects statesmanship to international observers — American policymakers, academic institutions, and diaspora communities — who represent both diplomatic legitimacy and financial resources. Internally, it signals to domestic rivals that he commands a level of diplomatic stature and organisational reach that no other opposition figure can currently match. In crafting his pitch to Capitol Hill lawmakers and MIT audiences, Musyoka is drawing on a career that spans four decades in law, diplomacy, and governance. Having served as Kenya’s tenth Vice-President between 2008 and 2013, and previously as Minister for Foreign Affairs, Education, Tourism, and Environment, the Senior Counsel occupies a rare position among Kenyan politicians: he has negotiated on the world stage, not merely observed it. His advisory highlights his central role in the negotiations that produced the Comprehensive Peace Agreement and the birth of South Sudan, alongside his mediation during Kenya’s 2007–2008 post-election crisis. For American policymakers focused on regional stability across the Horn of Africa and democratic governance in East Africa’s largest economy, Musyoka’s team is presenting The Ukombozi Alliance as a predictable, experienced alternative to the current administration. Equally central to the tour’s strategic logic is the Kenyan diaspora in North America, whose financial remittances constitute one of Kenya’s largest sources of foreign exchange and whose political influence reaches directly into rural homesteads and urban constituencies back home. Town halls in Maryland, Minnesota, and Ohio offer the opposition a fundraising avenue at a moment when state resources heavily favour the incumbent. title: Catholic bishops warn Parliament against electoral bills that could undermine 2027 vote
description: The Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops singles out a proposed ban on livestreaming presidential tallies as legislation likely to heighten tensions and erode public confidence in the polls. By Agnes Kilonzo The Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops yesterday cautioned Parliament against advancing electoral amendment bills that could compromise the credibility of the 2027 General Election, specifically warning that a proposed ban on the livestreaming of presidential vote tallies would generate unnecessary tension and undermine public trust in the electoral process. The statement, signed by KCCB Chairman Archbishop Maurice Muhatia Makumba, was issued following a gathering of Catholic bishops at the John Cardinal Njue Pastoral Centre in Embu on Wednesday, 11 November. “We are concerned that the introduction of bills — such as the banning of livestreaming of the presidential vote tally — raises unnecessary tensions in the country,” the bishops stated, urging the Speakers of both Houses of Parliament to ensure that divisive legislation does not advance. The Church’s intervention places one of Kenya’s most influential institutional voices squarely against a proposal that critics argue would restrict public access to real-time electoral information at the most sensitive moment of any election cycle — the presidential count. The bishops framed transparency not as a preference but as a democratic imperative. “Parliament has yet one more chance to redeem itself by totally rejecting such an attempt to muzzle free access to information,” they said. “There should be full transparency in the elections where Kenyans have access to all information.” The language is pointed — “redeem itself” is not the phrasing of a body offering gentle counsel, but of one that has watched previous parliamentary conduct on electoral matters and found it wanting. Their statement arrives at a moment of acute sensitivity in Kenya’s electoral calendar. With the August 2027 General Election nine months away and political competition already intensifying across coalition formations and presidential polling, any legislative change to the electoral framework carries disproportionate weight. The proposed livestreaming ban, if enacted, would remove a mechanism that has become central to how Kenyan voters and observers independently verify tallying in real time — a safeguard whose value is precisely its public, unmediated nature. Beyond the livestreaming proposal, the bishops directed separate calls at three institutions. They challenged the Independent Electoral and Boundaries Commission to strengthen its operational preparations — voter registration, logistics, official training, results verification, and complaints resolution — while resisting any attempts by politicians or external interests to compromise its independence. They called on the Judiciary to handle electoral disputes diligently and without partiality, warning against a repetition of past electoral violence that claimed lives and destroyed property. And they urged political leaders to conduct campaigns peacefully and responsibly, insisting that electoral reforms must build public confidence rather than deepen division. Kenya’s Catholic bishops speak to a congregation that spans every region, ethnic community, and political affiliation in the country. When they address Parliament in terms this direct — nine months before a consequential election — the message carries weight that extends well beyond the Church’s own membership. Parliament now has its answer from the pews. What it does next will be watched accordingly. title: Crystal Asige takes on KRA over disability tax rules she says undermine hard-won rights
description: The nominated senator warns that proposed exemption regulations introduce a hierarchy of disability, impose unlawful fees, and require the permanently disabled to prove their condition every five years. By Agnes Kilonzo Nominated Senator Crystal Asige yesterday publicly challenged the Kenya Revenue Authority over draft tax exemption regulations for persons with disabilities, warning that the proposed rules could erode constitutional rights and increase the financial burden on some of Kenya’s most vulnerable families. Asige, who is blind and has consistently used her Senate platform to advocate for disability inclusion, posted her objections on her X account on Thursday, 12 November 2026, targeting specific provisions in the Draft Income Tax (Persons with Disabilities, Parents or Guardians Tax Exemptions) Regulations, 2026, which KRA has opened for public comment until 24 November. “Nothing about us, without us — yet here we go again,” Asige wrote, framing the regulations not as a technical oversight but as a retreat from gains that Kenya’s disability community has fought to secure over many years. Her criticism was precise, directed at three specific provisions rather than the regulations as a whole — a legislative approach that reflects both her legal literacy and the seriousness with which she intends to pursue formal interventions. Her primary objection concerns Regulation 10(2), which she says introduces graduated exemption levels based on the severity of a person’s disability. Under the proposed framework, individuals classified with milder disabilities would qualify for partial tax relief while those classified with severe disabilities would receive full exemptions. Asige argued that this approach creates what she described as a hierarchy of human suffering — a scale on which one person’s access to rights is measured against another’s degree of impairment. “Equity isn’t a ladder,” she said, calling for a framework that treats the needs of persons with disabilities as a matter of right rather than degree. The concern is not merely philosophical. In practice, disability classifications are determined by medical assessors whose criteria, processes, and consistency vary. A system that ties tax relief to classification outcomes creates a gatekeeping mechanism that could disadvantage individuals whose conditions, though genuinely disabling, fall below the threshold required for full exemption. Asige’s objection is that the threshold itself should not exist — that access to relief should not depend on where a person sits on an administrative spectrum of disability severity. Her second objection targets a proposed KSh1,000 processing fee for parents or guardians applying for tax exemptions related to caring for a person with a certified severe disability. Asige argued that this fee directly contradicts the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025, which she says repealed assessment fees. If that legal reading is correct, KRA has drafted a provision that is inconsistent with the statute it is meant to implement — a significant drafting error that would need to be corrected before the regulations are finalised. The senator said she intends to submit formal interventions on this point, suggesting the challenge may extend beyond public comment into legal proceedings if the fee is retained. The draft regulations provide for a separate tax exemption for a parent or guardian caring for a person with a certified severe disability who cannot meet their own basic needs. However, the application is restricted to one parent or guardian per person with a disability. Asige questioned whether this adequately accounts for families in which both parents share caregiving responsibilities, or households in which more than one child has a disability. The practical implications are considerable: a family with two children who have severe disabilities would, under the proposed rules, be entitled to only two single-parent exemptions rather than a recognition of the compounded caregiving burden that both parents carry. Her third objection addresses a proposed requirement for people with permanent disabilities to undergo reassessment every five years to maintain their tax exemption status. The requirement draws a sharp and direct response: “Permanent means permanent,” Asige said. She argued that compelling people with permanent disabilities to periodically prove their condition — at personal cost and inconvenience — treats disability rights as provisional rather than settled. The reassessment requirement also raises practical questions about accessibility: for many persons with disabilities, particularly those in rural areas or with limited mobility, travelling to assessment centres every five years represents a significant and recurring barrier. KRA has described the proposed regulations as procedural rules designed to implement the tax exemptions established under the Persons with Disabilities Act, 2025, and has invited submissions from the public, professionals, and stakeholders by 24 November. The consultation window is standard practice for draft regulations, but Asige’s intervention raises the stakes considerably. A nominated senator with direct lived experience of disability, a detailed knowledge of the relevant legislation, and a public platform has identified specific provisions she considers constitutionally problematic. That combination — legal precision, personal authority, and public visibility — is difficult for a regulatory body to dismiss as uninformed criticism. Kenya’s disability community has long argued that policy affecting their lives is too often made without meaningful participation from those it directly impacts. Asige’s opening line — “Nothing about us, without us” — is a phrase with a history that stretches back decades through disability rights movements worldwide. That she felt compelled to use it in response to regulations drafted in 2026 says something about how far the principle has yet to travel from statement to practice. The November 24 deadline is ten days away. What follows it will determine whether the regulations are refined to meet constitutional standards or challenged in a forum where Asige has already signalled she is prepared to go. title: Linda Mwananchi tops Nairobi as TIFA poll reshapes Kenya’s 2027 political map
description: Edwin Sifuna’s movement leads the capital with 26 per cent support while nationally UDA reclaims first place — but a presidential race tied at 31 per cent signals the most competitive election Kenya has seen in a decade. By Anita Njeri The Linda Mwananchi Movement has emerged as Nairobi’s most popular political party at 26 per cent, ahead of Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party at 11 per cent, ODM at nine per cent, and President William Ruto’s UDA at eight per cent, according to a TIFA Research survey released yesterday covering 2,036 adults interviewed face-to-face across all 47 counties between 26 October and 5 November 2026. The findings land at a pivotal moment in Kenya’s pre-election calendar, reshaping assumptions about where political power is consolidating and where it is haemorrhaging — with consequences that will drive coalition negotiations for months to come. The Nairobi numbers are the poll’s most striking single finding. That Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s movement — formally launched only on 30 October and holding its National Delegates Conference behind closed doors today — already commands more than a quarter of the capital’s party allegiance speaks to the speed at which the post-Raila Odinga political landscape is being reorganised. Wiper and Jubilee each register seven per cent in Nairobi, while 31 per cent of the capital’s respondents say they identify with no party at all — a bloc of unattached voters whose eventual alignment may determine not just Nairobi’s parliamentary seats but the presidential result itself. Nationally, the picture is more nuanced. UDA has reclaimed its position as Kenya’s most popular party, rising from 17 per cent in June to 25 per cent in November — a recovery that reflects both the stabilising effect of incumbency and the resources available to a governing party in an election year. Linda Mwananchi sits second at 17 per cent nationally, overtaking ODM, whose support has been halved since TIFA’s June survey, falling from 20 per cent to ten per cent. That collapse is the poll’s most consequential structural finding. ODM retains its strongest regional foothold in Nyanza at 33 per cent, but beyond that base the party that defined Kenyan opposition politics for two decades is losing voters at a rate that suggests organisational erosion rather than a temporary dip. The regional breakdown of Linda Mwananchi’s support reveals both the movement’s strength and its current limits. Western Kenya delivers its highest regional figure at 40 per cent — a number that confirms Sifuna has successfully extended his political network beyond Luo Nyanza into a region that carries substantial parliamentary weight and that has historically been fought over rather than owned by any single political force. Nairobi follows at 26 per cent, Nyanza at 18 per cent, and the Coast at 16 per cent. The movement’s relative weakness in Mount Kenya, the Central Rift, and Northern Kenya — where UDA commands 56 per cent and 60 per cent respectively — defines the geographic challenge that any Sifuna presidential campaign must address before August 2027. UDA’s regional dominance outside the opposition’s core zones underlines why the presidential race remains genuinely open despite the headline tie. Ruto’s support is structurally embedded across Northern Kenya, the Central Rift, and the Coast in ways that reflect both political organisation and infrastructure spending targeted at those regions during his administration. Sifuna’s path to 50-per-cent-plus-one runs through consolidating the existing opposition vote — currently spread across Kalonzo Musyoka at nine per cent, Fred Matiang’i at five per cent, and Gachagua at four per cent — while simultaneously making inroads into the 21 per cent of Mount Kenya voters and 17 per cent of Nairobi voters who remain undecided. Neither task is straightforward, but the arithmetic is real. In Nairobi’s presidential preference numbers, Sifuna leads at 39 per cent against Ruto’s 13 per cent, with Kalonzo at 11 per cent and Matiang’i at ten per cent. That 26-point lead in the capital — Kenya’s largest single constituency — is a figure that will accelerate coalition conversations, as other opposition principals calculate whether their interests are better served by negotiating terms with Sifuna now or waiting to see whether his national numbers hold through the first quarter of 2027. The poll also captures a finding with significant implications for the broad-based government arrangement between UDA and ODM: 43 per cent of Kenyans oppose it, against 32 per cent who support it. In Nairobi, opposition runs at 57 per cent, with only 13 per cent in favour. Those numbers are a direct challenge to the political logic that brought ODM into government — and they help explain the speed of ODM’s national decline. Voters who backed Odinga’s movement as an opposition force appear unwilling to extend that loyalty to a junior partner in a Ruto administration, and many are evidently finding their new home in Linda Mwananchi. Kenya’s 2027 presidential election is shaping into something the country has not seen in a decade: a race with no predetermined outcome, no dominant incumbent, and no guaranteed coalition. The TIFA poll does not predict a winner — nine months of political realignment, coalition negotiations, and campaign dynamics separate these numbers from a ballot paper. What it does confirm is that Sifuna has transformed from a prominent opposition voice into a credible presidential contender in the space of months, that ODM’s post-Odinga decline is structural rather than temporary, and that the broad-based government arrangement has generated more public resistance than its architects appear to have anticipated. title: Oburu Oginga returns to Senate after two months of illness
description: The Siaya Senator received a standing ovation from colleagues as he made his first appearance in the House since travelling to the United Kingdom for medical treatment in September. By James Mwangi Siaya Senator Oburu Oginga returned to Parliament yesterday after nearly two months of absence due to illness, receiving a standing ovation from fellow senators as he took his seat in the chamber for the first time since departing for medical treatment in the United Kingdom in September. Oginga, who appeared visibly upbeat during Thursday’s sitting, used his return to deliver a message of political tolerance — urging Kenyans to maintain cordial relationships across political divides even as the country moves into an increasingly competitive pre-election period. “We can hold opposing political views and still treat one another with respect,” Oginga told the Senate. “Political differences should never be allowed to tear us apart as a people.” The appeal, delivered by one of Kenya’s most experienced legislators to a chamber that received him warmly, carried particular resonance coming from a senator whose own absence had been exploited to spread disinformation about his health and, in some quarters, his survival. Oginga departed for the United Kingdom on 10 September for what the Orange Democratic Movement described at the time as a routine medical check-up. As weeks passed without a public update, speculation filled the vacuum. Social media accounts circulated claims that the senator had died — a campaign of misinformation that his office and the ODM moved swiftly to counter. In a statement issued on 6 October, the Office of the ODM Party Leader described the claims as “malicious, unfounded fake news and propaganda” and urged the public to rely exclusively on official communication channels. “We wish to assure the general public, members of the Orange Democratic Movement, the people of Siaya County, and the entire nation that Dr Oburu Oginga is well, safe, and in good spirits,” the statement said. Oginga himself subsequently dismissed the rumours directly, saying reports of his death were entirely without foundation. Yesterday’s return gave the senator an opportunity to address not only his colleagues but the wider public that had followed his absence with concern. He spoke of the period of illness with candour, acknowledging the difficulty of being bedridden while away from the political arena he has inhabited for decades. What sustained him, he said, were the messages of goodwill that poured in from Kenyans across the country — across party lines, across regional boundaries, across the very political divides he was now urging the nation to bridge. That detail is not incidental. It speaks to something about Oginga’s standing in Kenyan public life that transcends his party affiliation. As the son of Jaramogi Oginga Odinga, the founding father of Kenyan opposition politics, and a veteran legislator whose career spans multiple political eras, Oburu Oginga occupies a place in the national consciousness that is partly personal, partly historical, and partly symbolic. His illness attracted concern from people who may have little in common politically with ODM or with Siaya County. His recovery, and the warmth of his Senate reception yesterday, reflected that breadth. His call for political tolerance, however, arrives at a moment when Kenya’s political temperature is rising rather than falling. With the August 2027 General Election now less than nine months away, the country’s political class is engaged in an increasingly intense process of coalition-building, candidate positioning, and strategic realignment. The TIFA Research poll released this week, which showed President William Ruto and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna tied at 31 per cent each as preferred presidential candidates, underscored how competitive and consequential the coming months will be. ODM itself, the party Oginga serves as a senior figure, has seen its national support rating halved since June — from 20 per cent to ten per cent — as voters redistribute across the reconfigured opposition landscape following the departure of former party leader Raila Odinga from domestic electoral politics. It is into that landscape that Oginga has returned — a landscape that is simultaneously more fluid and more fraught than the one he left in September. The opposition is attempting to consolidate around multiple candidates, each with their own regional base and strategic calculus. The question of who leads that consolidated front, and on what terms, remains unresolved. Coalition negotiations are active, often fractious, and operating under the pressure of a ticking electoral clock. Oginga’s voice in those negotiations — measured, historically grounded, and now carrying the particular authority of someone who has faced mortality and chosen to speak about unity — may carry more weight than the transactional calculations of politicians jockeying for position. Whether that voice will be heard above the noise of a presidential race that is already generating considerable heat is another matter. For now, the Senate stood and applauded. In Kenyan politics, that moment of bipartisan warmth is rarer than it should be — and perhaps more necessary than the participants fully realise. title: Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement holds closed NDC as 2027 platform takes shape
description: The movement bars media from its National Delegates Conference today as it formalises its transition from The Equitable Party and ratifies a leadership structure built around Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna. By James Mwangi The Linda Mwananchi Movement today holds its National Delegates Conference behind closed doors, with journalists barred from proceedings as the political outfit formalises its transition from The Equitable Party and ratifies a leadership structure intended to anchor its 2027 General Election campaign. The conference, whose venue has not been made public, is restricted to delegates drawn from members registered under The Equitable Party at the time the NDC notice was published, with each county allocated a fixed number of seats based on registered membership. “Kindly note that today’s NDC will be a closed-door meeting, with no media coverage,” said Pauline Njoroge, the movement’s Head of Communication, confirming the decision yesterday. The movement described the gathering as a statutory requirement under the Political Parties Act, necessary to approve the party’s name change and ratify the resolutions needed to complete its transition. “We ask for your understanding and cooperation as we undertake this important process,” its official notice stated. The decision to exclude the media is unusual for a political movement seeking national visibility ahead of a general election, and it has drawn attention precisely because of what the conference is being asked to approve. At the movement’s public launch on 30 October, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna was unveiled as the proposed party leader — a role that, once ratified today, would give him a formal institutional platform from which to prosecute his 2027 ambitions. Former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, former Law Society of Kenya president Faith Odhiambo, and Mavoko MP Patrick Makau were named as proposed deputies. Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi was proposed as chairperson, Suba South MP Caroli Omondi as secretary-general, and Njoroge as deputy secretary-general. Trans Nzoia Governor George Natembeya was unveiled as head of the movement’s presidential campaign — a signal that the Linda Mwananchi Movement intends to field a presidential candidate rather than serve as a junior coalition partner. The path to today’s conference has not been straightforward. The movement faced legal challenges at the Political Parties Disputes Tribunal, where party member Emmanuel Willyngtone Khamala filed a petition seeking to block the NDC over alleged irregularities in leadership appointments, delegate selection, and internal decision-making. Khamala argued that officials had been appointed without elections or adequate member involvement, and that the party had not conducted grassroots elections to establish the branch and county structures from which legitimate delegates could be drawn. He also challenged the process through which Sifuna and other officials had been positioned for party roles, questioning whether it complied with the party’s constitution and the Political Parties Act. The tribunal dismissed the petition, clearing the way for the conference to proceed — but the complaints it raised about procedural regularity did not disappear with the ruling. They remain live questions about the legitimacy of the structure delegates are today being asked to endorse. That tension sits at the centre of a broader story about how Kenyan opposition politics is being remade in the nine months remaining before the August 2027 ballot. The Linda Mwananchi Movement is one of several vehicles being assembled or reconfigured by politicians who sense that the post-Raila Odinga landscape has created an opening that did not exist before. Odinga’s departure from domestic electoral politics removed the singular force that had organised opposition energies for more than two decades, leaving a vacuum that multiple figures are now racing to fill with varying degrees of institutional credibility and popular support. Sifuna’s calculation is distinctive. Where others have sought to inherit Odinga’s mantle by positioning themselves as continuity candidates within the Orange Democratic Movement’s structures, Sifuna has chosen to build a separate vehicle — one that he controls from the top, that bears no inherited obligations to rival factions, and that can be deployed as either an independent presidential platform or a negotiating asset in coalition talks. The Linda Mwananchi Movement, if today’s conference proceeds as planned, gives him that instrument. The question of whether it also gives him a credible path to State House is considerably harder to answer. His networks span both Luo Nyanza and Western Kenya, and his profile as a combative, media-savvy senator has made him one of the opposition’s most recognisable voices. But recognition and organisation are different currencies in Kenyan electoral politics, and the movement’s decision to operate today’s conference without public scrutiny — undisclosed venue, no media, restricted delegate lists — sits awkwardly alongside any claim to represent a new, transparent political culture. Movements that begin by closing their doors invite the question of what they are protecting. The wider opposition landscape into which the Linda Mwananchi Movement is launching remains unsettled. The Ukombozi Alliance, co-chaired by Siaya Governor James Orengo and former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i, is attempting to construct a unified front, while Stephen Kalonzo Musyoka’s Wiper Patriotic Front insists that his presidential ambitions must carry genuine weight in any coalition arithmetic. Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party is simultaneously building its own national structures, with this week’s fresh questions over his formal registration status at the Registrar of Political Parties adding a new complication to his consolidation efforts. TIFA Research polling released this week shows President Ruto’s UDA recovering ground at 25 per cent national support — a figure that underscores how much the opposition’s fragmentation is currently benefiting the incumbent. Against all of that, today’s closed-door conference in an undisclosed location is either a disciplined operational decision by a movement that knows exactly what it is building, or an early warning about the transparency deficits that could limit its appeal when the campaign reaches full intensity. title: Ruto unveils education gains at Mombasa school heads conference
description: The President tells school administrators that 100,000 teachers have been recruited and 23,000 classrooms built as the government accelerates its overhaul of Kenya’s education system. By Jane Njambi President William Ruto yesterday told the Kenya Comprehensive Schools Heads Association Annual General Meeting in Nyali, Mombasa, that his administration has recruited 100,000 teachers, built 23,000 classrooms, and restructured primary and junior schools under single comprehensive management as part of a broad effort to modernise Kenya’s education system. Speaking at the Sheikh Zayed Children Welfare Centre, Ruto announced that a further 20,000 teachers would be hired next month. “We are building an education system that prepares our children for the world they will inherit, equipping them with the knowledge, skills and competence to think creatively, solve problems and turn ideas into practical solutions,” Ruto said. He added that school funding had been increased and was now being disbursed on time — a long-standing complaint among school administrators that his administration says it has resolved through the unified management structure. The address comes nine months before the August 2027 General Election, with education investment forming a central pillar of the government’s public record. Ruto framed the reforms as an investment in human capital, pledging that every teacher would receive the support needed to deliver quality education and every child the opportunity to succeed. The classrooms are built. Whether the learning follows is the measure that matters. title: Six dead, five rescued as building collapses along Mombasa Road
description: At least six people were killed and five others rescued alive on Friday when an eight-storey building under construction collapsed along Mombasa Road in Nairobi. The building, near the Standard Gauge Railway (SGR) terminus, caved in at about 9.52am while construction workers were on site, with the top slab giving way, according to preliminary reports from Nairobi City County emergency teams. Nairobi County Chief Officer for Disaster Management Bramwell Simiyu confirmed the six deaths as rescuers continued to search the rubble for possible survivors. "Three bodies were retrieved during the initial morning operations, while three more were recovered later from the debris. All six victims were middle-aged men," he said. The five survivors have been pulled out alive and are receiving emergency medical attention. It is not yet clear how many workers were at the site when the building collapsed. The county fire team and the Urban Search and Rescue (USAR) team were deployed to the scene and continue to comb through the debris for anyone who may still be trapped. Authorities have urged motorists and other members of the public using Mombasa Road near the SGR terminus to keep away from the area to allow emergency teams to carry out rescue operations. The collapse again raises concerns about building safety and compliance with construction regulations in Nairobi, where structural failures have repeatedly raised questions about the enforcement and supervision of construction projects.

title: Blow to President RUTO as vocal Mt. Kenya MP dumps UDA for GACHAGUA’s DCP ahead of 2027 elections.
description: Friday, November 13, 2026 - President William Ruto’s United Democratic Alliance (UDA) has suffered another political setback after Runyenjes Member of Parliament Eric Muchangi Karemba defected to former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP). Karemba’s move comes barely weeks after announcing his decision not to seek re-election on the UDA ticket, marking another significant shift in the political landscape of the Mt Kenya region. On Friday, November 13, Gachagua confirmed that he had officially welcomed the Runyenjes legislator into DCP following a meeting at his Wamunyoro residence. “This morning at my Wamunyoro residence, I have welcomed the Member of Parliament for Runyenjes, Hon. Eric Muchangi Karemba, to the DCP Party after Decamping from UDA,” Gachagua announced. The DCP leader further revealed that Karemba would team up with Manyatta MP Gitonga Mukunji to strengthen the party's presence across Embu County. Gachagua also announced plans to visit Runyenjes next week, where he intends to formally introduce the legislator to residents under his new political outfit. He said DCP was targeting the Embu governorship, parliamentary seats, and all 20 ward positions. On October 26, Karemba announced that he would not defend his parliamentary seat on a UDA ticket, saying he wanted to consult constituents and other leaders before deciding his political future. His defection adds to a growing list of Mt Kenya politicians abandoning Ruto's ruling party for Gachagua’s DCP. On October 9, Nakuru Senator Tabitha Karanja also ditched UDA, declaring that she would pursue the Nakuru gubernatorial seat on a DCP ticket. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Suspect behind Ksh 172.3 million gold scam arrested after landing at JKIA - See how he executed the scam
description: Friday, November 13, 2026 - Detectives have arrested an Indian national accused of orchestrating a massive gold investment scam involving USD 1,325,970 (approximately KSh 172.3 million). The suspect, identified as Maheshbhai Rameshbhai Bhadra, was intercepted and arrested at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport (JKIA) moments after landing from Dubai, United Arab Emirates. According to the Directorate of Criminal Investigations (DCI), the arrest followed investigations into a complaint by an investor who claimed he had been defrauded of the colossal amount through an informal Hawala money-transfer arrangement involving agents in Dubai and Kenya. At the centre of the alleged scam was a lucrative promise of 210 kilograms of gold. Investigators established that the complainant was allegedly induced to part with the money on the promise of securing the precious metal. However, the anticipated gold transaction never materialised, leaving the investor counting massive losses. The suspect's arrest was carried out pursuant to a stop order issued by the Milimani Law Courts, paving the way for further legal proceedings. Bhadra is currently in police custody, undergoing processing ahead of his arraignment in court. The DCI has reaffirmed its commitment to pursuing financial fraudsters, tracing suspicious transactions and bringing individuals accused of exploiting unsuspecting investors to justice The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Leadership is about improving what exists, not just creating what’s new
description: From golf club governance to campus elections, real leadership demands vision, accountability and the courage to build on others’ ideas By Lewis Murangiri Eric Nderitu, chairman at Nakuru Golf Club, offers a leadership philosophy that cuts against the grain of conventional thinking: innovation rarely means inventing from scratch. More often, it means seeing what exists and making it better. Nderitu illustrates the point with a simple example — a metallic round bin. The original designer may not have perfected it, but that imperfection is not a failure. It is an opening. Change the shape, vary the materials, improve the function. The lesson is transferable well beyond product design: a leader’s first instinct should not be to dismiss an idea but to ask how it can be strengthened. That principle applies with equal force to student governance. Bresdone, a Communication and Media student at Laikipia University, has taken it into the arena of campus elections. His campaign is built not on spectacle but on engagement — listening to fellow students, articulating their concerns and committing to represent them with accountability rather than ambition. Student leadership is too often mistaken for a title. In practice, it is a responsibility. Students expect leaders who will carry their challenges into the right rooms, defend their interests without fear and create an environment where every voice is taken seriously. A student representative who treats the role as a personal achievement has already failed the people who elected him. Whether in a golf club boardroom or a university senate, the standard is the same: lead with vision, build on what exists, and never confuse the office with the purpose. title: Artificial Intelligence and Language Learning: A New opportunity for students around the world
description: Artificial Intelligence and Language Learning: A New opportunity for students around the world By Dilfuza Ahmadjonova Narimonjon Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly influencing education, particularly foreign language learning. AI-powered tools allow students to practise speaking, improve writing, expand vocabulary and receive personalised feedback. These technologies can provide additional learning opportunities for students who have limited access to language-learning resources. However, AI also presents challenges related to accuracy, privacy and independent thinking. This article explores the opportunities and limitations of artificial intelligence in language education, with particular attention to students in Uzbekistan. It argues that AI should support teachers and learners rather than replace human communication and independent learning. Keywords: Artificial intelligence, language learning, foreign language education, English language teaching, digital learning, Uzbekistan. Introduction In today’s rapidly changing world, artificial intelligence (AI) is becoming an important part of education. From online classrooms to digital learning applications, technology is changing the way students acquire knowledge and develop new skills. One area that has particularly benefited from these developments is foreign language learning. For millions of students around the world, learning English is an important step towards accessing international education, career opportunities and global communication. Artificial intelligence offers new possibilities to make this process more accessible, flexible and effective. However, an important question remains: can technology really help students become better language learners? This article examines how artificial intelligence is transforming language education, the opportunities it creates for students and the challenges that must be considered. How Artificial Intelligence Is Transforming Language Learning Traditional language learning often depends on textbooks, classroom activities and communication with teachers. Although these methods remain valuable, students sometimes need additional opportunities to practise outside the classroom. Artificial intelligence can help fill this gap. AI-powered applications allow learners to practise grammar, improve vocabulary, check their writing and participate in simulated conversations. One of the most valuable features of AI is personalised learning. Students have different learning styles and face different challenges. Some struggle with grammar, while others find speaking or pronunciation difficult. AI tools can provide explanations and exercises according to individual learning needs. For example, a student who is afraid of speaking English in front of others can begin by practising conversations with an AI chatbot. This can help build confidence before communicating with real people. Opportunities for Students in Uzbekistan In countries such as Uzbekistan, foreign language education plays an important role in preparing young people for an increasingly interconnected world. Many students want to improve their English but may not always have access to international learning environments or regular conversations with fluent speakers. Artificial intelligence can provide additional learning opportunities in such situations. Students can practise English, explore unfamiliar subjects and receive explanations outside traditional classroom hours. More importantly, these tools can encourage independent learning. Students no longer need to wait for every lesson to ask a question or review a difficult topic. They can take greater responsibility for their educational development. For students studying foreign languages and literature, AI can also support reading comprehension, vocabulary development and writing practice. Nevertheless, technology should complement existing educational opportunities rather than replace qualified teachers and meaningful communication. The Challenges of Using AI in Education Despite its advantages, artificial intelligence is not a perfect solution. First, AI-generated information is not always accurate. Students may receive incorrect grammar explanations, unnatural expressions or misleading answers. Therefore, checking information through reliable educational sources remains essential. Second, excessive dependence on AI can reduce independent thinking. If learners ask artificial intelligence to complete every assignment, they may miss valuable opportunities to develop their own writing and problem-solving abilities. Third, privacy is an important issue. Students should be careful about sharing personal information or confidential documents with digital platforms. Another challenge is unequal access to technology. Not everyone has reliable internet connections, digital devices or access to advanced educational applications. This can create differences in learning opportunities between students. UNESCO’s 2023 guidance on generative AI in education highlights the importance of human-centred, safe and responsible technology use. Why Teachers Still Matter Artificial intelligence may provide explanations and learning exercises, but education is about much more than receiving information. Teachers motivate students, recognise individual difficulties and encourage creativity. They also create opportunities for discussions, teamwork and meaningful communication. An AI application may correct a grammatical mistake, but a teacher can explain the context, purpose and appropriate use of a particular expression. The most effective approach is therefore to combine technological innovation with traditional teaching methods. AI can support teachers by providing additional learning materials, while teachers can help students evaluate information, develop critical thinking and use technology responsibly. Responsible Use of Artificial Intelligence To benefit from AI, students should learn how to use it responsibly. There are several important principles: * Use AI to understand difficult topics rather than simply copy answers. * Check important information using reliable educational sources. * Practise writing independently before requesting feedback. * Protect personal information when using digital platforms. * Combine AI practice with real conversations and classroom activities. Following these principles can help students improve their language skills while maintaining independence and critical thinking. Looking Towards the Future The future of language learning will not depend entirely on artificial intelligence. Instead, it will depend on how effectively students, teachers and educational institutions use technological opportunities. For young people in Uzbekistan and other developing countries, AI can become a valuable educational resource. It can help learners explore international knowledge, practise foreign languages and prepare for future opportunities. However, learning a language still requires dedication, patience and consistent effort. Technology can make the journey easier, but it cannot replace the learner’s personal commitment. Further research is also needed to understand the long-term effects of AI on language development, motivation and independent communication. Conclusion Artificial intelligence is creating new opportunities in foreign language education. title: San Siro redemption: Italy end 64-year wait to hand Zidane first defeat
description: The Azzurri overturned an early deficit to beat France 3–1 and go top of Nations League Group A1 with one round remaining By Andalo Christine Ingutia Italy produced a memorable night at the San Siro on Thursday, overturning an early deficit to beat France 3–1 in the UEFA Nations League and record their first home victory over Les Bleus in 64 years — while handing Zinedine Zidane his first defeat as France head coach in the process. The Azzurri move top of Group A1 on ten points, level with France but ahead on the head-to-head tiebreaker, with Belgium one point behind and the race for the quarter-finals still very much alive. France needed just ten minutes to silence the home crowd when Michael Olise capitalised on a costly error by goalkeeper Gianluigi Donnarumma to put the visitors ahead. Italy, however, responded with composure rather than panic. In the 26th minute, Nicolò Cambiaghi drove down the left and delivered a perfectly weighted ball into the box for Pio Esposito, who finished calmly to level. The San Siro roared back to life and Italy grew visibly in confidence as the half progressed. The second period was intense from the outset. France threatened to regain the lead, only for Rayan Cherki’s effort to strike the woodwork. Italy were then given the chance to take control in the 60th minute when Malo Gusto brought down Cambiaghi in the penalty area, but Sebastiano Esposito stepped up and sent his spot-kick wide, squandering the opportunity. The miss proved only a temporary frustration. Three minutes later, Davide Frattesi found space inside the box and unleashed a first-time finish to put Italy ahead for the first time, turning the contest decisively in the hosts’ favour. With momentum firmly on their side, Italy pressed for the kill — and found it in the 75th minute. Dayot Upamecano brought down substitute Antonio Vergara in the area, and this time Pio Esposito was ice-cool from the spot, converting to complete his brace and put the result beyond any doubt. The final whistle triggered jubilant celebrations among the Italian supporters, who had waited since 1962 for a home win over their neighbours across the Alps. For Zidane, it was a sobering evening. His side had arrived in Milan unbeaten under his management and carrying genuine momentum. The second half exposed their vulnerability to sustained pressure and direct attacking play — lessons he will need to absorb quickly ahead of Sunday’s final group fixture against Türkiye. Italy travel to Brussels to face Belgium on Sunday in a fixture that carries quarter-final implications for all three sides. With only the top two from Group A1 advancing, neither Italy nor France can afford the luxury of a slip. Belgium, sitting one point off the pace, will be equally motivated to ensure the drama goes to the final whistle. What is already certain is that Thursday’s result at the San Siro will be remembered well beyond this tournament — the night Italy finally broke a six-decade hoodoo, and the night Zidane’s unbeaten record as France manager came to an emphatic end. title: Three arrested as detectives uncover explosives cache in Tassia
description: Intelligence-led operation in Embakasi yields grenades and ammunition from residential house By John Kinyua Detectives on Friday arrested three suspects and recovered a significant cache of explosive devices and ammunition from a residential property in Tassia, Embakasi, in an intelligence-led operation that underscores the Directorate of Criminal Investigations’ growing capacity to act on credible public tip-offs. Embakasi detectives trailed and arrested Kelvin Oluoch Obunaka and his brother Benjamin Obunaka, known locally as Obunaka the DJ, at a residence near Tassia Stage. Under interrogation, the brothers led investigators to a second house belonging to Kennedy Nzau, situated near Triple M Supermarket in Tassia, where a search yielded the concealed arsenal — packed inside a brown leather bag. The haul included six CS smoke hand-thrown grenades, four Model 2020 tear gas grenades, one 64mm CS smoke grenade, three 37/38mm rifle-launched tear gas grenades, one 37/38mm flash-bang grenade and sixteen rounds of 7.62mm blank ammunition. Crime Scene Investigation detectives documented and secured all recovered items as exhibits pending further forensic examination. All three suspects remain in custody awaiting arraignment as detectives work to establish the intended use of the materials and determine whether the accused have links to wider criminal networks. The DCI credited members of the public with providing the intelligence that made the operation possible — a reminder that in Kenya’s fight against urban crime, community vigilance remains as important as any detective work. title: Teacher assistants: The unsung force multipliers in Kenya’s classrooms
description: As CBC demands more personalised teaching, the case for properly integrating teacher assistants has never been stronger By Ashford Kimani Teacher assistants occupy one of the most strategically important yet persistently undervalued positions in Kenya’s education system. In an era of curriculum reform, rising learner diversity and growing pressure to deliver measurable outcomes, the model of a single teacher managing all instructional, administrative and pastoral responsibilities is no longer sustainable. Teacher assistants are not support staff in the marginal sense — they are force multipliers who extend the reach, precision and effectiveness of teaching itself. At the instructional level, their role is decisive. Modern classrooms are heterogeneous by design. Learners differ in ability, pace, language proficiency, motivation and socio-emotional readiness. A teacher may construct a well-structured lesson, but its success depends on how effectively it is differentiated in real time. Teacher assistants make that differentiation possible. They facilitate small-group instruction, provide targeted remediation and reinforce key concepts for learners who need additional support — ensuring that the lesson reaches the full spectrum of abilities, not merely the median student. This matters most in foundational learning. Early-grade literacy and numeracy demand constant engagement, immediate feedback and repetitive practice — conditions that are difficult to sustain in overcrowded classrooms. A teacher assistant who sits with a struggling reader, guides phonemic awareness and corrects errors in the moment delivers interventions that accumulate significantly over time, narrowing long-term academic gaps before they become permanent. Beyond instruction, teacher assistants are central to classroom management. Disruptions — however minor — erode instructional time and dilute focus. Teacher assistants help maintain order by managing transitions, reinforcing behavioural expectations and addressing minor incidents before they escalate. Their presence keeps the teacher anchored in instruction rather than pulled repeatedly into discipline. The result is a more efficient use of time and a more conducive learning environment for everyone. In inclusive education settings, their value is even more pronounced. Integration of learners with disabilities into mainstream classrooms demands individualised support, adaptive strategies and continuous monitoring — not merely physical placement. Teacher assistants frequently provide this layer, assisting with mobility, adapting materials and delivering one-on-one guidance aligned with individualised education plans. Without them, inclusion risks remaining aspirational rather than operational. Their contribution to learners’ socio-emotional well-being is equally significant and often overlooked. Teacher assistants tend to occupy an accessible position within the classroom hierarchy. Learners who hesitate to engage directly with the teacher often find it easier to open up to an assistant. That relational proximity enables early identification of anxiety, bullying or disengagement — factors that are not peripheral to learning but foundational to it. A learner who feels seen and secure is far more likely to engage meaningfully with academic content. From an institutional standpoint, teacher assistants enhance overall system efficiency. When teachers are overburdened with administrative and logistical tasks — organising materials, tracking assignments, managing records — instructional quality suffers. Teacher assistants absorb many of these responsibilities, freeing teachers to concentrate on lesson design, differentiated instruction and assessment feedback. In systems increasingly driven by data and outcomes, this division of labour is essential rather than optional. The impact of teacher assistants is not, however, automatic. It is contingent on how they are integrated. In too many contexts, they are treated as informal aides with ambiguous roles and no meaningful professional development. Clear role definitions, structured collaboration with lead teachers and access to ongoing training are preconditions for effectiveness. Teacher assistants should participate in lesson planning, assessment reviews and professional learning communities. Positioned as co-educators rather than peripheral helpers, their contribution becomes transformative. There is also a broader workforce implication. Teacher assistants represent a strategic pipeline into the profession. With proper mentoring and structured certification pathways, they can transition into fully qualified teachers — bringing with them practical classroom experience that formal training alone cannot replicate. It is a model that strengthens both the quality and sustainability of the education workforce. In the Kenyan context, this argument is especially urgent. The Competency-Based Curriculum demands personalised, skills-oriented teaching, continuous assessment and learner-centred pedagogy. These goals require time, attention and individualised support — resources that are chronically stretched in public school settings. Teacher assistants offer a pragmatic solution, expanding instructional capacity without requiring an immediate structural overhaul. The question is no longer whether teacher assistants are useful. Evidence from classrooms consistently shows they are integral to bridging the gap between policy intent and classroom reality. They extend the teacher’s reach, deepen learner engagement and make inclusion genuinely operational. Investing in teacher assistants is not an optional enhancement. It is a strategic imperative. Education systems that continue to treat them as peripheral will struggle to meet the demands of modern learning. Those that integrate them effectively will unlock one of the most powerful and underused levers available for improving both equity and excellence in Kenyan education. title: High Court gives state six-month window to finalise AI Law, dismisses bid to halt public sector algorithms
description: By David Kimani The High Court in Kerugoya has handed the State a critical six-month window to complete its ongoing formulation of a national artificial intelligence policy and legislative framework, while simultaneously dismissing a wide-ranging constitutional petition that sought to immediately halt the deployment of automated algorithmic systems across key public agencies. In a landmark judgment delivered on November 12, 2026, Justice Edward M. Muriithi declined to issue prohibitory orders against state bodies—including the Social Health Authority (SHA), the Kenya National Examinations Council (KNEC), the Public Service Commission (PSC), and the National Transport and Safety Authority (NTSA)—ruling that the petitioners had failed to provide concrete proof that existing automated systems had violated constitutional rights. However, in a measured nod to the urgency of digital governance, the court held in abeyance the question of whether the Executive and Parliament have unreasonably delayed in enacting an AI statute, setting a mention date for May 13, 2027, to assess legislative progress. The constitutional petition, filed by John Wangai, Peter Agoro, and Dr. Antony Manyara, sought to compel the Cabinet Secretary for Information, Communications and the Digital Economy and the Principal Secretary for ICT to publish a draft national AI policy and table comprehensive governance legislation within 90 days. The trio argued that the State’s failure to establish a dedicated legal framework left Kenyans exposed to algorithmic discrimination, surveillance overreach, election interference, deepfakes, and unfair exclusions from essential public services. Specifically, the petitioners targeted six high-stakes public sector applications. They asked the court to bar the SHA from using its Proxy Means Testing algorithm to determine household insurance premiums under the Social Health Insurance Fund; restrain KNEC from deploying automated AI marking or grading tools in national examinations; stop the PSC from using algorithmic shortlisting and interviewing tools; halt NTSA’s use of smart cameras and AI-linked biometric trackers for instant fines; prohibit the Inspector General of Police and the Ministry of Interior from operating real-time facial recognition CCTV and predictive policing algorithms; and block the Ministry of Education from applying AI-based poverty-scoring models to allocate bursaries, scholarships, school capitation, and Higher Education Loans Board (HELB) funding. Opposing the suit, the State maintained that Kenya is neither operating in a legal vacuum nor dragging its feet on digital regulation. Through a replying affidavit sworn by ICT Principal Secretary John Tanui, the government outlined a structured, phased roadmap that began with the launch of the Kenya Artificial Intelligence Strategy (2025–2030) in March 2025. This was followed by multi-stakeholder consultation roundtables with academia, civil society, the private sector, and county governments in February 2026, culminating in the publication of the draft National AI and Other Emerging Technologies Policy for public participation on July 21, 2026. The State argued that the draft policy was slated for Cabinet approval before informing an AI and Other Emerging Technologies Bill, rendering the petitioners’ demand for a 90-day ultimatum overtaken by events and an intrusion into the constitutional doctrine of separation of powers. Existing Safeguards and Evidentiary Gaps In his analysis, Justice Muriithi dismantled the petitioners’ foundational premise that Kenyan law is entirely silent on automated decision-making. The court pointed directly to Sections 31, 35, and 41 of the Data Protection Act, which explicitly grant individuals the right not to be subjected to decisions based solely on automated processing that produce legal or significant effects. Under the Act, data controllers must conduct mandatory data protection impact assessments for high-risk operations, notify citizens in writing when automated decisions are made, and provide avenues for human reconsideration. Coupled with Article 47 of the Constitution on fair administrative action, the judge noted that robust statutory guardrails already exist, meaning any litigant challenging a specific state algorithm must plead and prove precise violations of those existing laws rather than relying on generalized fears. The court found stark evidentiary gaps across the petitioners’ claims against individual agencies. Regarding the Public Service Commission, CEO Paul Famba swore that all recruitment, shortlisting, and interviewing processes remain strictly manual and human-led—an assertion the petitioners failed to rebut. Similarly, the court noted there was zero evidence that KNEC had deployed or was about to deploy AI marking systems for national exams, nor was any proof presented showing how alleged poverty-scoring models in the Ministry of Education had infringed upon the rights of specific learners or institutions. The closest scrutiny fell on the Social Health Authority’s Proxy Means Testing system, which SHA CEO Dr. Mercy Mwangangi acknowledged is actively used to assess household contributions based on Kenya National Bureau of Statistics household survey datasets. While the petitioners argued the algorithm lacked transparency and human oversight, the court observed that the system is anchored in Section 27 of the Social Health Insurance Act and its accompanying regulations. Notably, internal SHA audit records placed before the court revealed that 20,282 members had appealed their initial algorithmic assessments via the *147# USSD code or the Afya Yangu portal, resulting in downward contribution revisions from a combined Sh58.51 million to Sh54.56 million—a reduction of nearly Sh3.95 million. Justice Muriithi observed that while the successful appeals highlighted initial inaccuracies in the model’s assessments, they simultaneously proved that an accessible, functioning human review mechanism exists to correct errors, making a total shutdown of the system disproportionate. Respecting the Separation of Powers On the broader constitutional question of whether the State had breached its positive obligations under Article 21(2) to enact protective legislation, Justice Muriithi drew on comparative global timelines and constitutional principles. Observing that modern AI governance only gained global momentum over the past five years—citing the European Union’s AI Act, which was proposed in 2021, enacted in 2024, and only began taking full effect in August 2026—the judge ruled that Kenya’s trajectory from a 2025 strategy to a July 2026 draft policy did not constitute undue delay. title: MPs and Nyeri assembly defect to DCP as Gachagua tightens grip on Mount Kenya ahead of 2027
description: The former Deputy President’s Wamunyoro residence is fast becoming the nerve centre of Kenya’s most consequential pre-election realignment By James Mwangi Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, on Friday received Runyenjes Member of Parliament Eric Muchangi Karemba and Subukia MP Samuel Gachobe at his Wamunyoro residence, formally welcoming both lawmakers into the Democracy for the Citizens Party following their departures from the ruling United Democratic Alliance — defections that deepen DCP’s parliamentary footprint and signal accelerating erosion of President William Ruto’s Mount Kenya base ahead of the August 2027 general election. Manyatta MP Gitonga Mukunji, already a DCP member, accompanied Karemba to the ceremony, reflecting the party’s growing confidence in presenting collective arrivals as a demonstration of momentum rather than isolated crossings. The occasion carried the unmistakable atmosphere of a party in ascent. Supporters wearing green caps and carrying “I Wamunyoro” placards packed the residence, providing the visual language of a movement that has travelled well beyond its origins as a vehicle of personal grievance into something with genuine structural ambition. Gachagua was direct about what he expects from his new recruits. Welcoming Gachobe, he said he had assured him that DCP’s nominations would be free and fair, and urged him to move swiftly to build his grassroots network ahead of the primaries scheduled for March. “Gachobe joins a growing number of leaders who have found a new home in the party of the present and the future,” Gachagua said. On Karemba, he announced that he would travel to Runyenjes Constituency next week to present the MP formally to his constituents, adding that both Karemba and Mukunji would lead DCP’s drive to win the Embu County governorship, all parliamentary seats and all 20 wards. The Wamunyoro gathering was not, however, the only significant political movement of the day. Gachagua also received the entire Nyeri County Assembly, led by Speaker James Gichuhi — an institutional body, not merely individual politicians, crossing to DCP in a single movement. Gachagua responded with a direct challenge to UDA: DCP will contest every elective seat across Nyeri, from governor to ward representative, with open primaries in March. The Nyeri assembly’s defection carries weight beyond the numbers it adds to DCP’s ranks. Nyeri is historically one of the most politically consequential counties in Mount Kenya, and its assembly’s public alignment with Gachagua is a reputational blow to UDA’s claim that it retains legitimate roots in the region. Combined with the arrival of two sitting MPs in a single day, it suggests that the political geography of central Kenya is shifting faster than the governing party’s public response has so far acknowledged. Gachagua’s position in Kenya’s pre-election landscape has evolved considerably since his impeachment. What began as a question of whether he could survive politically has become a question of whether anyone running for president in 2027 can afford to run against him. DCP commands substantial support across Mount Kenya and Maasailand, and Gachagua is widely regarded as the most consequential kingmaker the cycle will produce. The March primaries commitment is a calculated signal. Open, competitive nominations serve two purposes simultaneously: they project democratic credibility at a moment when UDA is associated in public discourse with imposed candidacies, and they provide a transparent mechanism for absorbing defectors from multiple parties without appearing to reward loyalty over merit. With nine months remaining before Kenya goes to the polls, Wamunyoro has become the most watched political address in the country. On Friday’s gatherings suggest the queue of arrivals is far from over. The future, as Gachagua’s supporters are increasingly fond of saying, is green. author: the mt kenya times
title: Who is the best artist? The question misses the point entirely
description: In writing and poetry, the only honest competition is with yourself — and showing up is already a victory By Grace Wanja There is no hierarchy in art. No artist is inherently better than another — each simply tells a different story, in a different voice, for a different reason. To ask who the best artist is assumes a kind of competition that art was never designed to host. How does a children’s book author compete with a folklore writer or a physics author? The question answers itself: they cannot, and they should not have to. Each is telling their own story, sharing their own truth, and the world is richer for every version. Awards, in this light, deserve to be understood for what they truly are — a warm tap on the shoulder, an acknowledgment that says well done for showing up, for being present, for doing the work consistently. They are not a verdict on superiority. When someone wins a prize, they have not been declared better than their peers. They have simply been seen, at that moment, by that particular audience. In writing and poetry, the only meaningful competition is internal. A writer competes with the version of themselves from last year — refining, deepening, growing. Like a diamond being shaped beneath the earth, each piece of work and each practice session brings greater clarity and brilliance. That is the real journey. If you have attended a literary event and left without an award, resist the temptation to measure your presence by what you did not receive. The fact that you are there, that you found the courage to write, to recite, to put your ideas into the world — that alone sets you apart. Many people who can speak fluently and tell stories beautifully never do so, because fear holds them back. You are doing it. That is not nothing. That is everything. Writing for awards alone narrows the purpose of a craft that was built for far greater things. Let recognition be a bonus, not the destination. Write to tell a story. Recite to move people. Create to leave something behind that did not exist before you made it. A book, when examined honestly, is never the work of one person alone. It begins as an idea in an author’s mind, takes shape through a designer’s eye, is refined by an editor’s hand, carried to readers by a marketing team, and ultimately belongs to the people who read it. Writing is a collective act. That is not a diminishment of the author — it is an affirmation of what literature is for. When asked what it meant to be recognised among the best authors in Africa at the 2022 Zikomo Zambia Awards, that understanding shaped the response. The recognition was meaningful, but it did not make the work better than anyone else’s. It meant visibility. It meant showing up consistently and presenting the craft with commitment. Visibility is not superiority — it is simply presence. Art is not a race. It is an interpretation of the world, offered from every conceivable angle, in every conceivable form. Copy no one. Find your own voice, your own rhythm, your own way of seeing. When you bring something genuinely new to your audience, you give them a gift they cannot get anywhere else. In Africa, writing may not fill pots or pay every bill, but it has rescued countless souls from paths that would have led them astray. It enlightens. It heals. It transforms grief into meaning. So create — boldly, honestly, and entirely on your own terms. The post Who is the best artist? The question misses the point entirely appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.
