author: elizabeth angira
title: Koskei, Muoria Challenge TVET Institutions to turn research into practical solutions
description: By Elizabeth Angira Technical and vocational education and training (TVET) institutions have been challenged to translate research and innovations into practical solutions that address societal challenges, create jobs and boost economic development. Speaking during the 3rd International Multidisciplinary Research Conference at Kisii National Polytechnic, Principal Secretary for TVET Dr Esther Muoria said research should go beyond academic publications and presentations to deliver solutions that can be implemented and commercialised. Muoria said the conferences provide an important platform for learners, researchers, academicians and technical institutions to exchange ideas, identify challenges and develop innovations that respond to the country’s needs. She emphasised the need for stronger collaboration between research institutions, policymakers, Parliament, county governments and industry players to ensure research findings reach the communities and people who need them most. “Research should not continue to remain on the shelves. We must translate our findings into practical solutions and involve everybody, from policymakers and parliamentarians to industries and communities, so that we can have end-to-end solutions for this country,” she said. Muoria cited agriculture as one of the sectors where research can make a significant contribution to food security, noting that findings from universities and technical institutions should be translated into practical knowledge that farmers can apply to improve production She also highlighted innovations emerging from TVET institutions, including the development of a cooking stove that uses waste oil, demonstrating how learners can transform locally available materials into practical solutions. According to Muoria, such innovations demonstrate the importance of linking research with practical skills, production and entrepreneurship. She further called on institutions to work closely with the Kenya Industrial Property Institute (KIPI) to patent their innovations and protect young innovators from having their ideas copied or exploited without recognition. The PS urged researchers to make their conferences more inclusive by bringing together scientists, young innovators, farmers, manufacturers, small and medium-sized enterprises and other industry players. She said research findings should be communicated in language that ordinary people can understand and apply, rather than being confined to complicated academic presentations. Chief of Staff and Head of Public Service Felix Koskei also challenged researchers and technical institutions to make their conferences more inclusive by involving decision-makers, politicians, consumers, industry players and other stakeholders. Koskei said researchers should move beyond presenting findings to fellow academics and deliberately engage people responsible for making policies, allocating resources and implementing proposed solutions. He urged institutions to make their research discussions relevant to ordinary citizens, noting that involving policymakers and Parliament could help secure the support and resources needed to implement promising innovations. Koskei also emphasised the importance of succession management in research and innovation, urging senior researchers and professors to mentor young innovators instead of limiting their opportunities. In her remarks, Muoria linked the conference theme, Science, Technology, Innovation and Future Green Jobs, to the objectives of Competency-Based Education and Training (CBET), which seeks to equip learners with practical skills to solve problems, develop innovations and create economic opportunities. She said TVET institutions must ensure that research produces solutions that benefit society while creating opportunities for commercialisation. Muoria noted that the Government’s green TVET agenda was already delivering results, with 91 TVET institutions having adopted solar energy solutions, reducing electricity costs by approximately 50 per cent. She said institutions were also embracing renewable energy, waste management and resource efficiency as part of efforts to integrate green competencies into training programmes. Muoria commended Kisii National Polytechnic, researchers, innovators and trainees for participating in the conference, urging them to ensure that its outcomes translate into practical projects, enterprises, employment opportunities and economic value. She challenged institutional leaders to ensure that investments in training, research and technology deliver measurable results and contribute to the country’s development agenda. The post Koskei, Muoria Challenge TVET Institutions to turn research into practical solutions appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Khaminwa to receive Kenya’s historic first honorary degree from Kaimosi Friends University
description: The veteran advocate’s six decades of constitutional battles earn him an honour that marks a milestone for both the man and the institution By Joyce Nekesa Kaimosi Friends University will confer its first-ever honorary degree on veteran Kenyan lawyer Dr John Mugalasinga Khaminwa during its fifth graduation ceremony on Friday, 20 November 2026, recognising more than six decades of distinguished service to constitutional law, justice and the rule of law in Kenya and beyond. The Honorary Degree of Doctor of Humane Letters, Honoris Causa, will be awarded at the university’s Graduation Square in a ceremony the institution has described as a historic milestone — one that elevates this year’s graduation beyond the conferment of academic qualifications into a moment of institutional and national significance. “This prestigious recognition celebrates Dr Khaminwa’s remarkable legal career spanning over six decades and his enduring contribution to the advancement of constitutional accountability, justice and the rule of law in Kenya and beyond,” the university said in a statement issued on Friday, 13 November. It invited both the Kenyan public and the international community to attend, calling Khaminwa “a remarkable legal luminary.” Khaminwa’s career is, by any measure, extraordinary. Admitted to the bar in an era when Kenya’s legal and political landscape was being shaped by the upheavals of early independence and later by the consolidation of one-party rule, he emerged as one of the most persistent and consequential advocates of constitutional accountability the country has produced. Across six decades, he appeared in landmark cases touching on governance, individual rights and the limits of state power — often at personal and professional cost, during periods when such advocacy carried genuine risk. His association with high-profile public interest litigation placed him repeatedly at the intersection of law and politics, defending constitutional principles at moments when those principles were under direct pressure. That record — built not over a few celebrated cases but over a continuous professional lifetime — forms the foundation of the recognition Kaimosi Friends University now bestows. The timing of the award carries additional resonance. Kenya is approaching a general election in August 2027, a period in which questions of constitutional integrity, judicial independence and the rule of law will once again move to the centre of national debate. Honouring a lawyer whose career has been defined by precisely those concerns sends a signal about the values an institution of higher learning chooses to elevate at a consequential moment. For Kaimosi Friends University, the award represents its own milestone. Conferring an honorary degree for the first time in its history is an institutional coming-of-age — a declaration that the university sees itself not merely as a provider of qualifications but as a participant in the broader life of the society it serves. When Khaminwa takes to the Graduation Square on Friday, he will carry with him the weight of a legal career that few in Kenya’s history can match — and an honour that, for both recipient and institution, signals that some contributions to justice are too significant to go formally unremarked. The post Khaminwa to receive Kenya’s historic first honorary degree from Kaimosi Friends University appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Sifuna’s party rebrands to Linda Mwananchi
description: The Nairobi senator’s National Delegates Conference transforms The Equitable Party root and branch — name, colours, symbol and constitution — as Kenya’s 2027 political realignment accelerates By David Kimani National delegates of The Equitable Party on Friday voted to rename the outfit the Linda Mwananchi Movement, approving a sweeping transformation of the party’s identity, internal governance and electoral strategy at a closed-door National Delegates Conference in Nairobi that marked the most significant structural step yet in Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna’s bid to build a credible presidential vehicle ahead of the August 2027 general election. The resolutions adopted at Friday’s NDC went considerably further than a simple name change. Delegates ratified amendments to the party’s constitution, revised its nomination and election rules, changed its official colours and symbol, relocated its registered headquarters, and — in a move with potentially far-reaching consequences for Kenya’s pre-election landscape — authorised the party leadership to pursue coalition-building engagements with like-minded political formations. In a single afternoon, The Equitable Party ceased to exist in any meaningful sense, and the Linda Mwananchi Movement stepped into its place. “We take this opportunity to thank the NDC for taking this key step in formalising the party’s transition to Linda Mwananchi Movement and strengthening its organisational structure,” the party said in a statement issued after the conference. The language was measured, but the ambition behind it was not. A party that renames itself, recolours itself, rewrites its constitution and restructures its nominations process in one sitting is not making administrative adjustments. It is preparing for war. The choice of name is itself a political statement of intent. Linda Mwananchi — Swahili for “protect the citizen” — plants the party’s flag squarely in the terrain of economic grievance and popular welfare, the very ground on which Kenya’s 2027 election is most likely to be contested. After years of rising taxation, a cost-of-living crisis that has squeezed households across the income spectrum, and the Gen Z protests of 2024 that shook the political establishment, the electorate that goes to the polls next August will be asking a pointed question of every candidate: what have you done for ordinary Kenyans, and what will you do next? The Linda Mwananchi Movement has chosen a name that attempts to answer that question before the campaign has formally begun. Sifuna himself is a figure who has built his public profile on combative, plain-spoken politics. As Nairobi Senator, he has been among the most vocal critics of the Ruto administration, deploying a rhetorical style that blends policy argument with populist directness. His base is urban, young and digitally connected — precisely the demographic that drove the finance bill protests and that will be a decisive force in 2027. Whether that base is large enough, and whether it can be extended beyond Nairobi into the counties that determine presidential elections, is the central question his new party must answer. The authorisation to pursue coalition-building is therefore the most consequential resolution the NDC passed. No single party in Kenya’s current fragmented political environment can reach State House alone. The arithmetic of Kenyan elections demands alliances, and the alliances that hold from announcement through polling day are those built on complementary regional bases, agreed candidate hierarchies and shared resources. Sifuna’s team has signalled that it understands this — the question is who will sit across the table. Kenya’s pre-election landscape in November 2026 is defined by simultaneous consolidation and volatility. On one side, President William Ruto’s administration is using the machinery of incumbency and the broad-based government arrangement with ODM to project stability and development delivery, most recently through the Nairobi infrastructure commitments announced at State House on the same day as the LMM conference. On the other, former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua is building the Democracy for the Citizens Party into a formidable Mount Kenya and Maasailand force, absorbing MPs and county assembly delegations at a pace that is visibly unsettling UDA’s regional calculations. Into this environment, the Linda Mwananchi Movement enters as a third force with an urban stronghold, a senator with national name recognition, and a brand built on economic justice. The structural parallels with previous election cycles are instructive. Kenya’s political history is littered with formations that rebranded, restructured and announced coalitions, only to fracture under the pressure of nomination disputes and resource shortages. The LMM’s decision to revise its nomination rules at the same NDC that approved the rebrand suggests the leadership is aware of this pattern and is attempting to pre-empt it — establishing agreed internal processes before the scramble for positions begins in earnest. What the party has not yet made public is a detailed policy platform, a confirmed coalition strategy, or a formal declaration of Sifuna’s presidential candidacy. These will come, almost certainly, in the months ahead. But the sequence matters. By establishing the institutional framework first — name, constitution, nomination rules, coalition mandate — the LMM is building the scaffolding before it raises the flag. It is a more disciplined approach than many Kenyan political launches have managed. The 2027 election remains nine months away, long enough for alliances to form and dissolve several times over. But Friday’s NDC established one thing clearly: the Linda Mwananchi Movement is a serious political project, not a holding vehicle. It has a name designed to resonate with an electorate exhausted by economic hardship, a senator with the platform and temperament to carry that message, and a mandate to build the alliances that presidential contests require. Whether it can translate all of that into votes when it counts is the question Kenya will spend the next nine months answering. For now, Sifuna’s movement has announced itself — loudly, deliberately, and with considerable structural seriousness. The campaign, in every sense that matters, has begun. title: Ruto gathers Nairobi’s broad-based leaders at State House to accelerate housing, roads and markets
description: With polls showing public scepticism about the UDA-ODM alliance and the 2027 election looming, Friday’s State House meeting was as much about political consolidation as it was about development By Janet Mwathi President William Ruto yesterday hosted leaders from Nairobi under the broad-based government arrangement at State House, announcing plans to accelerate affordable housing, modern markets, road development, drainage improvement, and water and sanitation expansion across the capital in what his administration framed as a coordinated push to make Nairobi more liveable and attractive to investors. The meeting brought together leaders from the ruling United Democratic Alliance and the Orange Democratic Movement, whose March 2025 political cooperation agreement formed the foundation of the broad-based arrangement that has defined Kenya’s governing coalition for the past twenty months. That the two parties’ Nairobi delegates were seated together at State House on a Friday afternoon in November 2026 — nine months before the country goes to the polls — was not purely a matter of urban planning. It was a carefully staged demonstration that the alliance holds, at a moment when polling data suggests the public is far from convinced. “We identified priority development programmes, whose implementation we agreed to accelerate, including affordable housing, modern markets and road development to ease traffic congestion,” Ruto said in a statement posted on his X account following the engagement. The priorities align with longstanding concerns among Nairobi’s residents and business community — a city of more than five million people whose infrastructure has struggled to keep pace with its growth, whose roads flood seasonally, and whose informal markets remain among the most congested and poorly serviced on the continent. The ambition is not new. Successive administrations have promised Nairobi transformation, and the gap between announcement and delivery has historically been wide. What distinguishes the current moment is the political urgency that accompanies the promise. The 2027 general election is close enough to feel, and Nairobi — with its dense population, its media scrutiny, and its capacity to shape national political narratives — is a prize that no serious presidential contender can afford to concede. Ruto appears acutely aware of this. The State House meeting follows a pattern of intensified engagement with key constituencies in recent weeks, and the choice to host Nairobi’s broad-based leadership collectively, rather than through separate party channels, reinforces the administration’s message that UDA and ODM are functioning as a unified governing force. Whether that message is reaching voters is a different matter. A Trends and Insights for Africa poll released this month found that 43 per cent of Kenyans oppose the broad-based government arrangement, against 32 per cent who support it. The numbers carry a particular sting in Nyanza, historically ODM’s heartland, where 44 per cent of respondents opposed the arrangement and only 38 per cent backed it. For ODM leader Raila Odinga — currently serving as African Union Commission Chairperson — and for the party’s domestic leadership, those figures represent a genuine electoral liability. The base that has sustained ODM across five election cycles is sending a signal that its patience with the alliance is not unlimited. This is the central tension the broad-based government must navigate between now and August 2027. The arrangement delivered political stability after the turbulence of the 2022 post-election period and gave both parties a platform for governance. But stability secured at the top of the political structure does not automatically translate into popular legitimacy at the grassroots. Voters in Kisumu, Siaya and Homa Bay who backed Odinga repeatedly on promises of opposition and change did not mandate their representatives to govern alongside the man their candidate ran against. The Nairobi development agenda is therefore doing double duty. It is a genuine policy programme — Nairobi’s infrastructure deficit is real, its flooding a recurring public health crisis, its road congestion a daily economic drag — and it is a political instrument designed to demonstrate that the broad-based arrangement delivers tangible results for ordinary people. If the housing units are built, the markets upgraded and the roads dualised before the election, the administration will have a material argument to make. If they remain at the level of announced priorities without implementation timelines or confirmed budgets — and Friday’s statement specified neither — the optics risk reinforcing the scepticism the polls already capture. The broader diplomatic context adds another dimension. On Thursday, Ruto hosted more than forty European Union heads of delegation and ambassadors at State House, in engagements marking fifty years of Kenya-EU diplomatic relations. The discussions covered trade, investment, job creation and market access — a signal that the administration is simultaneously pursuing international economic partnerships while managing domestic political consolidation. The two tracks are not unrelated: visible foreign investment in Nairobi’s infrastructure would strengthen the government’s development narrative considerably. For ODM’s Nairobi leadership, the State House meeting represents a calculated bet — that association with a credible development programme in the capital will outweigh the cost of the alliance’s unpopularity in the party’s traditional strongholds. It is a bet that grows riskier the closer Kenya gets to polling day, and the TIFA numbers suggest the window for it to pay off is narrowing. Ruto, for his part, has governed with enough political dexterity to understand that announcements without delivery are a gift to opponents. The question Friday’s meeting leaves unanswered — and the question Nairobi’s residents will be asking in the months ahead — is not what has been prioritised, but when the first foundation is poured, the first market rebuilt, and the first road widened. In an election year, the gap between a State House communiqué and a construction site is measured not in kilometres but in votes. title: Ruto commits to KSh38.7B Kiambu Road dualling and new Nairobi-Thika Expressway
description: The president’s pledge to Kiambu leaders signals an infrastructure push in the Nairobi Metropolitan Area — but one key project remains mired in feasibility studies By James Mwangi President William Ruto on Friday pledged to prioritise the dualling of Kiambu Road and the construction of a new Nairobi-Thika Expressway, committing his administration to two of the most consequential road infrastructure projects in the Nairobi Metropolitan Area during a meeting with Kiambu County leaders at State House, Nairobi. The announcements carry both developmental and political weight. Kiambu is among the most densely populated counties in Kenya, its road network under daily pressure from commuter traffic, commercial vehicles and an expanding urban population that has long outgrown the infrastructure built to serve it. For residents who spend hours each week on congested routes into Nairobi, the commitments — if delivered on schedule — would represent a tangible improvement in daily life. “We are giving priority to key infrastructure projects in Kiambu County, including the dualling of Kiambu Road and the construction of the Nairobi-Thika Expressway, to ease transport and improve connectivity within the Nairobi Metropolitan,” Ruto said. He framed the investments within his administration’s broader equity agenda, adding: “We are deliberate and intentional in ensuring that every part of Kenya benefits equitably from our transformation agenda. No county, no community and no region will be left behind. Usawa ni Sawa.” The Kiambu Road project is the more advanced of the two. Cabinet approved the KSh38.7B scheme in November 2025, with the Kenya National Highways Authority confirming plans to upgrade the 23.5-kilometre Pangani-Muthaiga-Kiambu-Ndumberi corridor from a two-lane road into a four-lane dual carriageway, flanked by two-lane service roads, pedestrian walkways and six footbridges. New bridges, overpasses and interchanges are planned at key junctions including Kamiti Road, Banana Road and the Northern Bypass, while two bypasses around Kiambu Town will divert through-traffic away from the town centre. The National Land Commission has already published notices for the compulsory acquisition of eleven land parcels in Nairobi and Kiambu counties to facilitate the works. The Nairobi-Thika Expressway presents a more complicated picture. Ruto announced in February 2026 that construction of the approximately 60-kilometre elevated route — running from the Museum Hill Interchange in Nairobi to Thika Town — would begin in September. That timeline has since slipped. Deputy President Kithure Kindiki acknowledged in October 2026 that the project was still undergoing final design and feasibility studies, a disclosure that places a question mark over the administration’s earlier schedule. The expressway is designed to run above the existing Thika Superhighway, offering motorists an additional route without disrupting traffic on the road below — a technically ambitious proposition that may partly explain the delays. Both projects sit within a wider government infrastructure programme targeting connectivity across the Nairobi Metropolitan Area. The administration’s argument — that improved roads unlock economic growth, reduce travel times and attract investment — is well-founded in principle. The test, as with every infrastructure pledge in Kenya’s political history, lies in execution. With the August 2027 general election drawing closer, the pressure to show concrete progress on the ground, rather than announcements at State House, will only intensify. title: Defiant BABU OWINO sets record straight on stepping down for GACHAGUA's DCP candidate in 2027 Nairobi Gubernatorial race.
description: Saturday, November 14, 2026 - Embakasi East MP Babu Owino has ruled out stepping aside for Embakasi North MP James Gakuya in the contest for Nairobi governor in the 2027 General Election. The Mwananchi Party leader maintained that he has no intention of withdrawing from the race to pave the way for another opposition candidate. Speaking about the possibility of backing Gakuya, who is seeking the seat on a Democracy for the Citizens Party (DCP) ticket, Babu dismissed the proposal, describing himself as a front-runner. "How do you step down in a race that you are already winning? “You are already a lion, and these other people are tortoises; they are still crawling. “How would you step down? I don't even want them to step down. “I want to defeat these people because I have hope Nairobians will punish these people once and for all," he said. The outspoken legislator also promised to resign within one year if elected governor but fails to deliver on his campaign pledges. He further vowed to dismantle cartels controlling Nairobi's garbage collection, water supply and roads sectors. His declaration comes amid growing calls for opposition leaders to rally behind a single candidate to avoid splitting their support. Babu's position also puts him on a collision course with Gachagua, who has maintained that DCP will field candidates across Nairobi, with the governor's seat among its key priorities. Meanwhile, Governor Johnson Sakaja has moved from UDA to ODM and intends to seek re-election, while Kasarani MP Ronald Karauri has joined UDA to pursue its gubernatorial ticket. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Mguu Niponye! The moment chaos broke out as President RUTO was attending the Maa Cultural Festival in Narok (VIDEO)
description: Saturday, November 14, 2026 - The annual Maa Cultural Festival was thrown into disarray after supporters allied to Narok Governor Patrick Ole Ntutu and Narok West MP Gabriel Tongoyo clashed at Sekenani Gate in Narok West. The dramatic confrontation reportedly erupted shortly after President William Ruto arrived at the festival, turning what was supposed to be a colourful cultural celebration into scenes of chaos. In a video circulating online, attendees are seen scampering for safety as the rival groups engage in a fierce confrontation, with some individuals hurling chairs at each other. Several chairs were overturned in the ensuing commotion as frightened festival-goers scrambled to get away from the violence. Maa Cultural Festival brings together members of the Maa community to celebrate their shared heritage, traditions and cultural identity. However, the confrontation between the rival political camps threatened to overshadow the cultural event, particularly given the presence of President Ruto. Watch the video. Kenyan DAILY POST.

author: shamlal puri
title: BRITAIN TO HONOUR HEROES OF THE MAKERS OF HISTORY WITH BLUE PLAQUES
description: By SHAMLAL PURI, Senior Editor – UK & Associate Publisher Britain has a unique way of honouring her heroes of yesteryear with blue plaques erected on the walls where they either lived or made history. These blue plaques will better reflect our nation, the British Government said in an announcement. Among the heroes is Kenya’s founding father and first president, Mzee Jomo Kenyatta, who lived in London as a student and during the freedom struggle. Indian freedom fighter and the Father of the Nation, Mahatma Gandhi, also has a plaque in his honour in London. An announcement from the Department for Digital, Culture, Media and Sport and its Secretary, Lisa Nandy, MP, states that the Changes driven by the Culture Secretary will open up the scheme to a wider range of people, places and stories across England. Nominations for a National Blue Plaque are now open on Historic England’s website, and interested people are invited to submit their suggestions. Several diaspora names are included on the current list, which is yet to be finalised. The National and Greater London Blue Plaques schemes are being expanded to celebrate more inspirational people from across Britain, with nominations now open to the public, the Government has announced. New criteria will allow blue plaques to be placed on buildings that have been substantially altered or replaced since a historical person or group was connected to them, including homes, shops, workplaces, community buildings and streets. Previously, the criteria required a person or group to be associated with a building that still existed and had not been altered beyond recognition. However, many brilliant people or groups throughout history have been connected to buildings that have since been redeveloped or demolished, including terraced houses and industrial factories. The changes will remove this barrier, opening the scheme to a wider range of people, places and stories, and helping ensure more of Britain’s diverse history is represented. These include people connected to lost music and performance venues, former residents of demolished homes, and workers and innovators connected to former factories and workshops. To be honoured with a blue plaque, a person or group must have significantly contributed to human welfare or happiness and/or made an exceptional contribution to their field. Sites for a blue plaque must have a strong connection to a historical person who has been dead for at least 20 years, or to a group formed at least 20 years ago that is no longer functioning. This year, £100,000 has been given to Historic England to support the programme and provide grants for community groups and grassroots organisations researching and developing nominations that address historic underrepresentation and improve geographical reach. Current projects include a partnership between charity Creative Lives and local archives across the East of England to uncover and share overlooked stories. Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy said: Throughout our history, it has been ordinary, extraordinary people who have built our country and created lasting change. From millworkers who fought for fair wages, safe working conditions and the rights of women to the Windrush generation who helped shape our NHS, transport, manufacturing industries and more – too often their contributions have been airbrushed from our national story. Until now, it was difficult to commemorate their achievements with a blue plaque. These rules were outdated, unfair, and do not reflect who we are as a nation. That’s why we have changed the rules so that we can properly commemorate the heroes who shaped our communities and changed our country for the better. I hope people across the country will come forward and nominate the people whose contributions are a vital part of our national story, and deserve to be told and remembered. Professor David Olusoga Hon FBA: English history has been shaped by women as well as men, by the poor as well as the wealthy, and by people across England, not just those who lived in London. These welcome changes will liberate Historic England and English Heritage to celebrate the stories of England’s hidden heroes with their beloved blue plaques. Ellie Djerir, Historic England’s Head of Participation Programmes, said: Every community has people whose stories deserve to be remembered, but some of the buildings connected to them no longer stand. By widening the criteria of the National Blue Plaque Scheme, we can now celebrate more of the people who have shaped our history, wherever they lived and worked. With the opening of this year’s nomination window, we’re looking forward to seeing the people that the public put forward for a plaque, and working with community groups across the country to help bring those stories to light. Matt Thompson, English Heritage’s Conservation, Curatorial and Learning Director, said: English Heritage feels this change will offer greater flexibility to recognise a wider range of individuals whose achievements deserve to be celebrated. Our charity has long been committed to addressing the historic under-representation within the scheme, and we have made significant progress. This work will continue, and this change will bring more opportunities to enrich the scheme and the streets of London. Run by Historic England on behalf of DCMS, the National Blue Plaque Scheme builds on the success of the London blue plaque scheme and local schemes across the country. Launched in 2023, the scheme extends across the country, with twelve plaques now placed from Plymouth to Liverpool. The London scheme, run by English Heritage, will also adopt the updated criteria from this round of nominations. Recent people honoured by the National Blue Plaque Scheme include Daphne Steel, the first Black matron in the NHS; George Harrison, the lead guitarist of The Beatles; and Reverend Wilbert Awdry, creator of Thomas the Tank Engine. Applications are now open for both schemes until 13th January 2027. Blue plaques from these nominations will be unveiled in 2027. At the time of writing, the full list of blue plaques erected under the National scheme is: Daphne Steele; first Black matron in the NHS – Ilkley, West Yorkshire The post BRITAIN TO HONOUR HEROES OF THE MAKERS OF HISTORY WITH BLUE PLAQUES appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: shamlal puri
title: World travel and tourism at a crucial turning point:
description: INCREDIBLE! PASSION FOR TRAVEL CONTINUES UNDAUNTED DESPITE GLOBAL POLITICAL UPHEAVALS By SHAMLAL PURI, Senior Editor, UK & Associate Publisher Travel is changing fast. Here’s where the industry turns disruption into opportunity, as scores of countries turned up in full force for this year’s World Travel Market (WTM). WTM in London is the world’s most influential travel and tourism event, where the global travel trade gathers to do business, share insights, and shape the industry’s future. For almost five decades, it has united everyone from government ministers and global CEOs to emerging leaders and the next generation of travel professionals. This is the essential platform where influential voices, high-profile brands, and the industry’s most powerful buyers connect, collaborate, and define what comes next. WTM generates more than £2.8 billion worth of business. More than 55,000 visitors descended on the London ExCeL Centre for the 2026 edition of the World Travel Market (WTM), the spectacular global marketplace for the tourism industry. They proved beyond doubt that even if politics have turned some regions into battlefronts, the tourism industry has not pulled down its shutters. From Abu Dhabi to Zimbabwe, from Algeria to Zambia, they gathered under one roof in central London for their annual jamboree, showcasing their best sights and sounds to tourists from around the world. A total of 3,775 companies from 128 countries exhibited at this spectacular annual fixture. Kenya, Uganda, Tanzania, Ghana, Zimbabwe, and Senegal were among the African countries well represented. The Middle East had a powerful representation too – United Arab Emirates: Dubai, Abu Dhabi, Sharjah, Ras Al Khaimah were out in full force, as were Jordan, Saudi Arabia, Bahrain, among others. From the vibrant cultures of Southeast Asia to the majestic wildlife of Africa and the breathtaking landscapes of Australia, visitors savoured everything from the splendour of blue skies to the beautiful beaches of the world’s islands… in pictures and videos played continuously at the various stands. There were also live displays of dancing and cultural fiestas. The three-day event was delivered with an action-packed programme not only for the travel industry but also for the thousands of visitors who turned up to walk around the ExCeL Centre to see each country displaying its best in sights, sounds and culture. Event Director Chris Carter Chapman was upbeat about this year’s event, describing it as bringing the world of travel together in a year of challenge and uncertainty. He said this year’s WTM “delivers our largest show footprint in our 46-year history”, with the latest addition being the launch of WTM Travel Tech, which he called “our new show-within-a-show.” “Technology is no longer a specialist corner of travel; it is reshaping how our industry operates, and how people book and experience the world.” This year, Travel Tech had its dedicated hall, alongside the Future Stage and Innovation Highway, creating a much bigger platform for AI, data, payments distribution and technologies changing travel, Mr Chapman welcomed the Egyptian Tourist Authority as the 2026 WTM’s premier partner. Egypt has participated in WTM since its maiden event in 1980. Egypt is a popular destination for international tourists. Last year, almost 19 million international visitors travelled to Egypt. In the first eight months of 2026, 12.7 million visited Egypt, and there are indications that by 31st December Egypt would have possibly broken last year’s record, with over 20 million visitors, as many people still have to plan their Christmas holidays. This year’s WTM had more than 200 speakers and over 70 content sessions with expert insights. Excitement filled the air on the first day of the event as singing and dancing filled the air when the doors opened. From the grand opening ceremony with Premier Partner Egypt to the launch of the WTM Global Travel Report and the buzz across WTM Trend Fest, the tone was set for an exciting three days. On the opening day, more than 30,000 people passed through the doors of the ExCeL Centre. The opening day brought many opportunities for the exhibitors, who spared no effort to attract visitors to their stands, offering brochures and bags of goodies. The much-awaited WTM Global Travel Report revealed interesting statistics. Dave Goodger, Managing Director, EMEA Tourism Economics, said, “Travellers are more aware in 2026 than ever before. Leisure travel remains a key priority in consumer budgets, even as travellers adapt how and where they visit in response to ongoing disruption and cost-of-living pressures. The industry is on course for another record year.” A new record was set with 1.57 billion international arrivals, according to the report, despite disruption from conflict and squeezed household budgets. Growth is expected to accelerate into 2027, it notes. Visitors spent a whopping US$7.8 trillion, a 9% increase over 2025, in destination spending, both domestic and international, on 23.9 billion visitor nights. However, the report notes growth in 2026 is more modest, as 3% of travellers avoided long-haul trips mainly due to higher fares and safety concerns. They preferred Europe. An interesting statistic: 37% travelled abroad to relax, compared with 31% in 2025. The report is upbeat and optimistic; long-haul travel is set to rebound in 2027. Visitors are looking for both value and luxury; some 56% said they were interested in both budget and premium travel experiences. In Brazil, for example, the 2027 World Cup holds high hopes. The football tournament will run for a month from 24 June in eight cities, from Fortaleza in the north to Porto Alegre in the south, while showcasing the capital, Brasilia, which is in the centre of the vast country. “Brazil will be in the spotlight,” said Alisson Andrade, International Markets Coordinator at Embratur, Brazil’s national promotional arm. “We understand hosting big events is a turning point.” Potential international visitors will be able to firm up their travel plans from 11 December, when the fixtures are announced and tickets go on sale. title: My culinary arts journey at Kenyatta University: Four years of heat, hustle and growth
description: Esther Wanjiru reflects on four transformative years studying culinary arts at Kenyatta University — the triumphs, the failures and the lessons that forged a professional. By Esther Wanjiru Esther Wanjiru will sit her final examinations in roughly three months, bringing to a close a four-year journey that has been as intense and transformative as the kitchens she has trained in. Pursuing a degree in Culinary Arts at Kenyatta University has not been merely an academic endeavour — it has been a test of endurance, creativity, discipline and self-discovery. This is her story: the hits, the misses and the opportunities that have shaped her into the culinary professional she is becoming. When she first joined the programme, the vision was romantic — beautifully plated dishes, the warm applause of satisfied guests, the glamour so often portrayed in culinary shows. Reality arrived swiftly and without ceremony. The kitchen is not glamorous. It is hot, fast-paced and unforgiving. The opening months came as a genuine shock. Standing for hours on end, handling sharp tools, working under pressure and meeting strict deadlines pushed her far beyond any comfort zone she had previously known. But it was in that discomfort that growth quietly began. Among the biggest hits of the journey has been mastering foundational skills. Knife work, for instance, is not simply about cutting ingredients — it is about precision, safety and efficiency. Learning classical cooking techniques, understanding flavour profiles and appreciating the science behind food fundamentally transformed the way she approaches the craft. There is a particular confidence that comes with knowing not just what to do, but why it works. That shift — from following recipes to genuinely understanding food — stands among her proudest achievements. Exposure has been another significant highlight. Culinary arts extends well beyond the classroom, and through industrial attachments and practical sessions she has worked in real kitchens, engaged with seasoned professionals and experienced the full demands of the hospitality industry at close range. These experiences opened her eyes to the remarkable diversity within the field — hotel kitchens, catering operations, food production facilities and entrepreneurial ventures all revealed themselves as viable and exciting paths. They reinforced a truth that is easy to overlook: culinary arts is not simply about cooking. It is about service, management and innovation in equal measure. The journey has had its misses, too. There were moments of outright failure — dishes that refused to cooperate, assessments that fell short of expectation and days when the pressure felt genuinely overwhelming. One practical examination stands out in memory. Everything that could go wrong did go wrong. Timing collapsed, presentation suffered and she left the kitchen feeling thoroughly defeated. Yet those painful moments became her most instructive teachers. They taught her resilience, humility and the absolute importance of preparation. Failure, it turns out, has a way of building the very qualities that success alone cannot. Financial constraints have also been a persistent reality. Culinary training demands ingredients, equipment and, at times, additional certifications — all of which carry a cost. Balancing academic requirements against financial limitations has never been straightforward. There were moments that demanded creativity not only inside the kitchen but in the management of limited resources. That pressure, difficult as it was, has instilled a resourcefulness she now considers one of her most bankable professional qualities. Time management has emerged as another critical lesson. The programme is demanding, blending theory and practicals in a combination that requires equal and sustained attention. There were days when juggling assignments, kitchen sessions and personal responsibilities felt like trying to manage too many pots on the stove simultaneously. Learning to prioritise, plan methodically and remain disciplined has been essential — not merely for survival but for genuine success. Amidst the challenges, the opportunities have been considerable. Culinary arts rewards passion and creativity in ways that few disciplines can match. She has had the freedom to experiment with different cuisines, fuse unexpected flavours and develop her own distinctive style. The liberty to create — to transform simple, honest ingredients into something meaningful — has been deeply fulfilling. It is in those moments of creation that the original decision to choose this path makes complete and undeniable sense. Networking has been a substantial and sometimes underestimated gain. Engaging with lecturers, professional chefs and fellow students has built connections that reach well beyond the lecture hall or the kitchen. These relationships are not merely social — they are professional networks that will shape the career ahead. Learning from others, exchanging ideas and collaborating under pressure have enriched the experience in ways that no textbook ever could. As the final stretch approaches, the reflection turns not only to what has been learned but to who has been shaped in the process. The discipline is sharper, the resilience is real and the confidence in her abilities has grown steadily. The kitchen has taught patience and meticulous attention to detail. It has demonstrated the value of consistent hard work and the quiet power of showing up, day after day, regardless of how the previous session ended. Looking ahead, the feelings are mixed — genuine excitement tempered by honest anxiety. The transition from student to professional carries its own distinct set of challenges. The industry is competitive and the expectations are high. But the lessons of four years travel with her: the hits that have built confidence, the misses that have strengthened character and the opportunities that have broadened vision. This journey has not been perfect. It has, without question, been worthwhile. Culinary arts has delivered more than a degree — it has given her a sense of purpose and a clearer understanding of who she is. As she prepares to step into the next chapter, she does so with genuine gratitude for the experiences, the lessons and the growth they have produced. The heat of the kitchen has tested her, the hustle has shaped her and the hope keeps her going. This is her story — and it is only just beginning. description: Kenya’s political marketplace is shifting as a more demanding electorate challenges the old brokerage model ahead of the 2027 General Election. By Fredrick Chelimo Kenya is becoming a politically dynamic marketplace, its traditional power brokers declining in influence as a more demanding electorate reshapes the rules of engagement ahead of the 2027 General Election. Beneath the familiar rally circuits, party defections, coalition negotiations and declarations of regional loyalty, something fundamental is changing. The traditional political marketplace — where influential personalities claim the ability to deliver entire communities, constituencies or voting blocs in exchange for financial and political reward — is confronting an electorate that is increasingly difficult to predict. As the old saying goes: a political broker may negotiate access to voters, but only the voter can decide who deserves the mandate. This phenomenon, widely described as political wholesaling, has long occupied a central place in Kenyan electoral politics. Political brokers, community influencers, former elected leaders and self-appointed regional kingpins have presented themselves as custodians of political loyalty. Their proposition is straightforward: provide the resources, recognise our influence, and we shall deliver the votes. The arrangement rests, however, on a questionable assumption — that voters are political commodities whose choices can be negotiated by intermediaries on their behalf. The changing political mood suggests otherwise. Recent opinion surveys examining the popularity, likeability and political standing of prominent Kenyan personalities have unsettled sections of the established political class. Familiar names no longer enjoy automatic public acceptance, while relatively new voices are attracting growing attention. More significantly, economic frustrations — unemployment, taxation, healthcare costs and the rising cost of living — are reshaping how citizens evaluate political leadership. The distinction between popularity and electability has consequently become sharper. A politician may command public recognition, draw large crowds and attract favourable social media attention without necessarily holding the confidence of voters at the ballot box. This is where political wholesalers face their greatest challenge. They may organise meetings, negotiate alliances and assemble impressive delegations, but they cannot guarantee that those attending will vote according to instruction. Attendance is not endorsement. Applause is not commitment. A photograph with a political heavyweight is not an electoral contract. Kenya’s experience mirrors developments in other democracies. In Brazil, social programmes such as Bolsa Família demonstrated how practical poverty-reduction interventions could strengthen political confidence beyond traditional patronage networks. India’s Aam Aadmi Party built substantial support through its emphasis on anti-corruption, education and accessible public services. South Korea’s candlelight demonstrations showed how organised citizens could demand accountability beyond the reach of established political elites. Kenya has its own lessons. The 2022 General Election demonstrated that established alliances and presumed ethnic voting patterns could be disrupted. William Ruto’s victory illustrated the possibilities of building a coalition around economic messaging and perceived political exclusion. Ethnicity, party machinery and patronage remain influential nonetheless. The lesson is not that traditional politics has disappeared, but that its ability to guarantee electoral outcomes is diminishing. Three developments explain this transition. First, the economic experience of ordinary Kenyans has become a political scorecard. A farmer wants affordable agricultural inputs, reliable markets and reasonable returns. A young person wants employment and opportunity rather than endless campaign promises. A parent wants affordable education, while a person with a disability expects accessible healthcare, economic participation and respect for constitutional rights. Political rhetoric becomes irrelevant when it cannot respond to these everyday realities. Second, digital communication has weakened the monopoly previously enjoyed by political intermediaries. Citizens can now interrogate statements, compare promises against performance and challenge political narratives almost immediately. Political communication is no longer controlled exclusively by those who claim to speak for entire communities. Online popularity, however, must not be mistaken for genuine electoral support. Third, voters are growing impatient with political blame games. Politicians blame predecessors; predecessors blame successors; and government officials cite inadequate resources. Yet citizens want straightforward answers: What did you promise? What did you accomplish? Where did you fail, and what will you do differently? This presents a particular challenge to former governors, ministers, legislators and senior public officials seeking another term in office. Experience is an advantage only when accompanied by demonstrable results. Previous positions should invite accountability, not permanent political entitlement. For aspiring politicians, the implications are substantial. The successful campaign of tomorrow must be built around credibility, public engagement and measurable commitments rather than expensive delegations and negotiated voting blocs. Candidates must understand their constituencies before presenting manifestos. They must engage farmers, traders, young people, women, professionals, persons with disabilities and other community groups to identify genuine priorities. Their proposals should be realistic, financially explainable and consistent with the constitutional responsibilities of the offices they seek. Political organisations must equally reconsider the role of grassroots representatives. Community leaders should facilitate dialogue, communicate public concerns and strengthen participation — not claim ownership of people’s votes. A campaign that only reports favourable opinions to its candidate is a political liability. Leaders need honest intelligence, not manufactured enthusiasm. Financial transparency, integrity and continuous public accountability must become central to political organisation. Campaign resources should support legitimate mobilisation, research, voter education and genuine public engagement — not inducements designed to compromise electoral choices. The 2027 General Election will test more than political alliances and financial muscle. It will test whether established leaders can reinvent themselves, whether emerging personalities can translate popularity into credible organisation, and whether political parties can offer practical alternatives to the electorate. Public dissatisfaction with an incumbent does not automatically translate into support for the opposition. Equally, popularity among young people does not guarantee national electoral reach. Successful political leadership requires credibility, competence, organisation, policy clarity and the capacity to unite diverse interests. Kenya is not witnessing the death of political brokers. It is witnessing a possible decline in the political value of those who mistake influence for ownership and mobilisation for authority. The modern voter is not demanding a perfect politician — only an honest, accessible and competent leader who understands that public office is a responsibility, not a commercial investment. title: Water problems in the modern world: a global threat to the future of humanity
description: By: Absamatova Iroda Abstract This article discusses the problem of water scarcity, which is becoming increasingly relevant in the modern world, its causes, and its environmental, economic, and social consequences. The rational use of water resources, pollution of freshwater sources, climate change, population growth, and the impact of human activities on water reserves are analyzed. Attention is also paid to the importance of water-related problems in the Central Asian region, particularly in Uzbekistan, the tragedy of the Aral Sea, and environmental responsibility towards future generations. The article substantiates the necessity of saving water, protecting water resources, and strengthening international cooperation. Keywords: Water scarcity, freshwater, environmental problem, climate change, global warming, water resources, Aral Sea, environmental security, sustainable development, water conservation, Central Asia. Introduction Water is the beginning of life, an invaluable gift of nature, and one of the most important conditions for the existence of humanity. Human life cannot be imagined without water. Every day, we use it for drinking, preparing food, maintaining cleanliness, agriculture, industry, and many other fields. However, unfortunately, humanity does not always appreciate the value of this resource, which is essential for its existence. In today’s era of globalization, the world is facing numerous problems. These include climate change, environmental crises, food security, and the depletion of natural resources. Among these problems, water scarcity occupies a special place. This is because water-related problems directly affect not only nature but also human health, the economy, agriculture, social stability, and the future of countries. According to the United Nations, in 2024, 2.2 billion people worldwide were unable to access safely managed drinking water services. This figure shows that the water problem is not limited to certain regions but is a serious issue facing all humanity. Therefore, talking about water today means not simply discussing a natural resource, but thinking about the future of humanity, the future of our children, and the fate of our planet. Main Body Water Scarcity — A Pressing Problem of the Modern World Although a large part of the Earth’s surface is covered with water, most of it consists of salt water. Freshwater reserves suitable for human consumption and daily needs are quite limited. A large part of the available freshwater is also located in glaciers and underground layers. For this reason, usable water resources are becoming increasingly important in meeting the needs of the world’s population. Several factors contribute to the emergence of water scarcity. Firstly, as the world’s population increases, the demand for drinking water and food products also rises. Secondly, large amounts of water are used in industrial enterprises and agriculture. Thirdly, due to climate change, droughts are intensifying in certain regions, and the amount and seasonal distribution of precipitation are changing. In addition, the pollution of water sources by household waste, industrial wastewater, and chemical substances is further deepening the problem. Most regrettably, in some regions, people are forced to travel long distances to find clean drinking water. Climate Change and Its Impact on Water Resources Today, global climate change is recognized as one of the most important causes of water-related problems. Rising temperatures are leading to the melting of glaciers, increased evaporation, and changes in natural phenomena such as droughts and floods. In particular, glaciers in mountainous regions are the main sources of water for many rivers and streams. The shrinking of glaciers may cause changes in river flows and lead to problems with water supply in the future. Water scarcity is not limited only to a shortage of drinking water. It also leads to a decline in agricultural productivity, an increase in food prices, and a deterioration in living conditions in certain regions. Thus, climate change and water-related problems are processes that are closely interconnected. Water Problems and Human Health Water is vital for the human body. Processes such as metabolism, regulation of body temperature, transportation of nutrients, and elimination of harmful substances take place with the participation of water. The lack of clean drinking water and the use of contaminated water pose serious risks to human health. Under such conditions, the likelihood of the spread of intestinal infections, diarrhoea, dysentery, hepatitis A, and other infectious diseases increases. Children, elderly people, and individuals with weakened immune systems are particularly more vulnerable to water-related diseases. From this point of view, the water problem is not only an environmental issue but also an important medical and social issue. Ensuring that every person has access to safe drinking water is necessary for building a healthy society. Water Problems in Central Asia and Uzbekistan Water scarcity is also one of the pressing issues for Central Asian countries. In our region, agriculture, people’s livelihoods, and economic development largely depend on the waters of major rivers such as the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya. Uzbekistan’s geographical location and climatic conditions make the rational use of water resources particularly important. Population growth, the extensive area of irrigated land, water losses during water use, and climate change may create additional pressure on water supplies in the future. In this regard, the tragedy of the Aral Sea is a particular lesson. During the last century, as a result of the improper and excessive use of water resources, a large part of the Aral Sea gradually dried up. Its consequences had a negative impact not only on nature but also on public health, economic activities, and the social life of the region. The environmental situation that emerged in the Aral Sea region clearly demonstrates what consequences human attitudes towards nature can lead to. This historical experience shows the necessity of taking long-term interests into account when using water. title: PUBG MOBILE teams up with Davido as new Flash version launches globally
description: The gaming giant partners with the Afrobeats superstar to broaden access to its Battle Royale platform across Africa and beyond. By Elizabeth Angira PUBG MOBILE has partnered with global Afrobeats superstar Davido in a collaboration that brings together music, gaming and African youth culture, coinciding with the worldwide launch of PUBG MOBILE FLASH, a lighter version of the platform designed to reach a significantly wider audience of smartphone users across the globe. The partnership carries an unusual dimension: Davido is not simply a celebrity endorser. He is a PUBG MOBILE player himself, with a stated passion for squad tactics and close-range combat gameplay. His involvement, the company says, is rooted in genuine affinity with the game rather than contractual association alone — a distinction the brand has been keen to emphasise as it seeks to build credibility with Africa’s discerning gaming community. The collaboration reflects a broader cultural shift across the continent, where mobile gaming has become a defining feature of youth identity. For a generation that plays, creates and connects primarily on mobile devices, the presence of one of Africa’s biggest music stars on the battlegrounds carries direct resonance with how young Africans engage with digital culture today. Gaming is no longer a pastime on the margins — it is a central thread in the social fabric of African youth life, and PUBG MOBILE is positioning itself firmly within that conversation. PUBG MOBILE has recorded more than one billion downloads worldwide, establishing itself as one of the most recognised names in mobile gaming through its Battle Royale format, which centres on immersive shooting gameplay and competitive multiplayer engagement. PUBG MOBILE FLASH builds on that foundation by reducing the initial download size and optimising performance across a wider range of smartphone specifications. Players who were previously unable to run the full version can now access the core Battle Royale experience without compromise to the essential gameplay that has defined the brand’s global reputation. Jeff Tange, PUBG MOBILE’s Marketing Manager, was clear that PUBG MOBILE FLASH is not a simplified or diminished product. “PUBG MOBILE FLASH is a new way to experience the game,” Tange said, noting that players across both versions can connect and compete with one another, preserving the social dimension that underpins the platform’s enduring appeal. He added that the launch reflects the brand’s commitment to expanding access to premium mobile gaming, particularly across African markets where reaching a broader base of smartphone users represents a meaningful and long-term growth opportunity. Alongside the FLASH launch, the company has introduced the 30BG Card Drop campaign, through which players can complete in-game missions, earn draws and collect exclusive Davido, City and Holiday cards for a chance to win prizes. These include concert tickets to Davido’s Oriade show, an Infinix HOT 70 Pro 5G+ handset and limited-edition 30BG merchandise. Players can also win Davido-themed items by downloading the game and participating in associated in-game activities. For Davido, the partnership connects his music platform with an interactive global gaming community, adding a cultural dimension that extends the collaboration well beyond conventional brand endorsement. His involvement builds a bridge between an international gaming phenomenon and Africa’s vibrant entertainment and youth landscape — one that his fanbase, spread across the continent and the diaspora, inhabits daily. PUBG MOBILE said the Davido partnership and the FLASH launch together form part of a sustained push to deepen its presence in African markets. The company has previously invested in server infrastructure, network optimisation, community operations and creator support programmes on the continent. These include the Next Star influencer initiative and the PDP creator programme, both designed to grow local content creation and encourage player participation in shaping game content from the ground up. From Version 4.5 onwards, PUBG MOBILE said it would intensify localisation efforts in Africa by incorporating local artists, music and cultural references directly into the game. Customised songs, music videos, voice packs, outfits and avatar frames are among the tools the company intends to deploy. The stated ambition is for African players to see their own cultural expression genuinely reflected within the game, rather than simply consuming content produced for markets elsewhere. The move signals a maturing approach to the African market — one that goes beyond surface-level representation and attempts to embed local culture into the product itself. Whether that ambition translates into sustained player growth will depend on execution, but the appetite on the continent is not in question. Africa’s gaming audience is young, connected and growing rapidly, and PUBG MOBILE’s decision to anchor its latest global launch to one of the continent’s most recognisable faces suggests it understands where the opportunity lies. Further details of the music collaboration component of the Davido partnership are expected in a subsequent campaign phase. title: Mahlangu turns 91: A legacy of resilience, art and grace in Mpumalanga
description: The Emthambothini artist who defied doubt to build a celebrated craft and a lasting community legacy marks a remarkable birthday. By Themba Emanuel Mashobane Dr. Esther Mahlangu’s hands once worked in silence, overlooked by the very community she called home. In the quiet corners of her village in Emthambothini, Mpumalanga, while critics were loud and recognition slow, she poured her spirit into her art — and refused to let bitterness take root. She turned 91 yesterday, and the celebration was a testament to what perseverance, grace and an unselfish heart can build over a lifetime. Rather than allowing rejection to harden her, she let it fuel her. Piece by piece, her work began to speak a language the world could not ignore. What started as a solitary passion in a small village grew into a celebrated craft known far beyond South Africa’s borders. She rose above the whispers of those who once dismissed her, proving that true talent cannot remain hidden forever. Yet her greatest masterpiece is not the art itself — it is her grace. Despite her international recognition, she carries no pride and holds no grudges against those who once doubted her. With open hands and a generous heart, she continues to pass her skills to others, ensuring the craft endures for generations to come. The fruits of her perseverance are today undeniable. Even her own family, who watched her long and difficult journey, has embraced the art she fought so hard to protect. What was once a misunderstood dream now sustains a household and feeds a community. She did not simply create art. She built a legacy — and paved a road that others now walk with pride. title: The role of artificial intelligence in the modern world
description: By: Zilola Sayfiddinova Alisher Introduction In the twenty-first century, technological development has become one of the most influential factors shaping human civilization. Among the numerous innovations that have transformed modern society, Artificial Intelligence (AI) occupies a particularly important position. It is rapidly changing the way people live, work, communicate, learn, and interact with the world around them. Artificial Intelligence is no longer a concept associated only with science fiction or advanced scientific laboratories; it has become an essential part of everyday life. Artificial Intelligence can be defined as the ability of computer systems and machines to perform tasks that traditionally require human intelligence. These tasks include learning from experience, analyzing information, recognizing images and speech, understanding languages, solving problems, and making decisions. Through technologies such as machine learning, deep learning, natural language processing, and computer vision, AI systems are becoming increasingly sophisticated and capable of performing complex operations. Today, artificial intelligence is used in various fields, including education, medicine, science, agriculture, industry, transportation, business, and communication. Its rapid development creates new opportunities for economic growth, scientific discoveries, and social progress. At the same time, it raises important questions concerning employment, privacy, security, ethics, and human responsibility. The purpose of this article is to examine the role of artificial intelligence in the modern world, explore its practical applications in different areas of human activity, identify its major advantages and challenges, and discuss its potential influence on the future of society. Main Part Artificial Intelligence in Education Education is one of the fields in which artificial intelligence has created significant opportunities for improvement and innovation. Traditional educational systems are gradually integrating digital technologies to make the learning process more effective, accessible, and student-centered. AI-powered educational platforms can analyze students’ learning progress, identify their strengths and weaknesses, and provide personalized learning materials. This approach allows students to study at their own pace and receive additional support in areas where they experience difficulties. Intelligent tutoring systems, online learning applications, automated assessment tools, and digital assistants are examples of how artificial intelligence is transforming education. Artificial intelligence also provides valuable opportunities for teachers. Educators can use AI tools to prepare lesson plans, develop educational exercises, create presentations, generate assessment questions, and organize interactive learning activities. These technologies help reduce the time spent on routine tasks and allow teachers to focus more on students’ individual needs, creative thinking, and intellectual development. Moreover, AI-based translation and language-learning applications make foreign language education more accessible. Students can practice pronunciation, improve vocabulary, receive grammatical explanations, and communicate with intelligent virtual assistants. Such opportunities are particularly important in an increasingly interconnected world where multilingual communication has become essential. However, artificial intelligence should not replace teachers or reduce the importance of human interaction in education. Teachers play an irreplaceable role in developing students’ moral values, social skills, creativity, independent thinking, and emotional intelligence. Therefore, the most effective educational approach is to combine modern AI technologies with professional teaching methods and human guidance. The Role of Artificial Intelligence in Healthcare Healthcare is another important sector experiencing remarkable changes due to artificial intelligence. Medical professionals and researchers increasingly use AI systems to analyze medical data, identify diseases, improve diagnostic procedures, and support treatment decisions. One of the most valuable applications of AI in medicine is medical image analysis. Intelligent systems can examine X-rays, MRI scans, CT images, and other medical examinations to help specialists identify abnormalities. These technologies can assist in detecting certain diseases at earlier stages, allowing patients to receive timely medical attention. Artificial intelligence also contributes to the development of personalized medicine. By analyzing medical histories, genetic information, and other health-related data, AI systems can help researchers and healthcare professionals understand individual patient needs and explore more suitable treatment approaches. Furthermore, AI technologies are being used in pharmaceutical research, where they can help scientists analyze chemical compounds, identify potential drug candidates, and accelerate certain stages of medicine development. In hospitals, intelligent systems can support patient management, appointment scheduling, and the organization of medical information. Despite these advantages, AI cannot independently replace the professional knowledge, experience, and ethical responsibility of doctors. Medical decisions require careful human evaluation, especially when patients’ lives and well-being are involved. Therefore, artificial intelligence should function as a supportive instrument that improves healthcare services under appropriate professional supervision. Artificial Intelligence in Business and the Economy The influence of artificial intelligence on business and economic development is becoming increasingly significant. Modern companies use AI technologies to improve productivity, reduce operational costs, analyze market trends, and provide better customer services. One of the major advantages of AI in business is its ability to process enormous amounts of information within a short period. Companies can use these analytical capabilities to understand consumer behavior, predict market demands, identify business opportunities, and make more informed decisions. In the banking sector, artificial intelligence helps identify unusual financial transactions, detect potential fraud, and improve customer support services. Chatbots and virtual assistants can answer frequently asked questions and provide information to customers at any time of the day. Manufacturing industries also benefit from AI-powered automation. Intelligent machines and robots can perform repetitive tasks with high precision, monitor production processes, and identify technical problems. This improves efficiency, reduces certain human errors, and contributes to the development of modern industrial systems. However, the expansion of automation also creates challenges for the labor market. Some traditional occupations may change or become less common as machines take over routine tasks. Consequently, employees need to develop new professional skills, improve their digital literacy, and adapt to changing economic conditions. In this context, lifelong learning and professional development are becoming increasingly important.
