title: Israel’s post-election crisis: Netanyahu and Eisenkot clash over national unity government as nuclear threat looms
description: Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot trade public accusations over coalition negotiations, exposing deep divisions in Israeli politics ahead of a critical government formation deadline. By David Kimani Benjamin Netanyahu and Gadi Eisenkot, two of Israel’s most prominent political figures, are engaged in a sharp and increasingly public dispute over the formation of a national unity government, with both men accusing the other of bad faith as the country enters one of its most consequential political periods since the last general election. The confrontation, playing out on social media and in the Knesset, cuts to the heart of Israel’s post-election reckoning — a nation navigating fractured politics, an existential security threat from Iran and a population exhausted by division. The stakes could scarcely be higher. Israel heads into the critical government formation period with no settled coalition, a contested Knesset speakership and a former prime minister who, by Eisenkot’s account, lost the election but refuses to accept its full political consequences. For observers of Israeli politics, the standoff is both familiar and newly dangerous — familiar because Netanyahu has survived every previous political crisis through tactical manoeuvre, dangerous because the geopolitical context in which this one unfolds is unprecedented in its severity. Eisenkot, a former Chief of Staff of the Israel Defence Forces and now leading the charge to form an alternative government, did not mince his words. He dismissed Netanyahu’s public call for immediate coalition negotiations as a calculated distraction. “Netanyahu calls for negotiations after they have already been scheduled,” Eisenkot said in a statement posted to his official social media account. “He claims he wants unity, but disgraces a state ceremony in the Knesset and divides and incites as if there were no tomorrow.” Eisenkot was explicit about his conditions for any power-sharing arrangement under his leadership: acceptance of his stated principles and a complete break with what he described as extremist political partners. Netanyahu, for his part, framed the conversation in dramatically different terms. In his own public statement, he described a recent meeting with Eisenkot in warmer language, invoking years of professional acquaintance stretching back to Eisenkot’s tenure as IDF Chief of Staff. “This meeting only strengthened my understanding of how essential it is to establish a national unity government,” Netanyahu said, arguing that only a broad coalition encompassing all parties committed to Israel as a Jewish state would be capable of confronting the security challenges ahead. He made no reference to preconditions. The centrepiece of Netanyahu’s public argument was Iran. He warned with striking directness that the Iranian regime, which he characterised as one that “did not hesitate to murder many thousands of its own people,” was once again seeking to advance its nuclear programme. “It will use nuclear weapons against us the moment it manages to resume uranium enrichment and the accelerated development of nuclear weapons,” he said, invoking the codenames “Am Kelavi” — meaning Brave People — and “Shaagat Ha’ari” — meaning Lion’s Roar — as examples of past operations that had, in his account, averted immediate threats. A narrow government, or one dependent on parties he characterised as supporters of terrorism, would, he argued, be incapable of meeting that threat. The language of existential danger has long been part of Netanyahu’s political vocabulary, but analysts who follow Israeli politics closely note that the current moment is not merely rhetorical. Iran’s nuclear ambitions remain a live and unresolved threat. Israeli military and intelligence services have repeatedly identified uranium enrichment acceleration as a red line. Whether or not one accepts Netanyahu’s framing of the coalition arithmetic, the underlying security concern he raises is widely shared across the Israeli political spectrum, including by Eisenkot himself. What divides the two men is not the diagnosis but the prescription. Eisenkot contends that a unity government built around Netanyahu and his current allies — particularly those from the Religious Zionism bloc — would not be a government of genuine national reconciliation but rather a continuation of the same political configuration under a different name. His conditions, he has made clear, are not negotiating positions but prerequisites. The Tuesday Knesset vote to appoint Matan Kahana — a former lieutenant colonel, squadron commander and Sayeret Matkal commando — as Knesset speaker represented, in Eisenkot’s framing, an immediate and concrete test of Likud and Religious Zionism’s stated commitment to democratic cooperation. “If they are indeed committed to genuine political partnership, as they claim, they must allow a proper democratic process to take place on schedule,” he said. The Knesset speakership is not a ceremonial matter. Control of the speaker’s chair shapes legislative agendas, determines which motions reach the floor and, in a parliament as finely balanced as Israel’s, can materially affect a government’s ability to function. The contest over that position is therefore not a sideshow — it is a direct proxy battle for the larger coalition struggle being waged in public statements and behind closed doors simultaneously. Netanyahu’s appeal to unity carried an emotional register as well as a strategic one. He invoked the image of ordinary Israelis — naming individual citizens, Elisha Midan alongside Elisaf Peretz, Talik Gvili alongside Shira Shapira — joining forces across their differences in service of a shared national future. It was language designed to reach beyond the political class, to appeal directly to a public that, by most polling measures, is deeply fatigued by years of electoral instability and political polarisation. Israel has held multiple elections in recent years without producing durable governing majorities. The country’s proportional representation system, combined with an increasingly fragmented party landscape, has made coalition-building a prolonged and painful exercise in which ideological distance between potential partners is frequently enormous. The current impasse fits that pattern — but the external environment gives it an urgency that previous formations did not carry to the same degree. What comes next will be determined not by the volume of public statements but by whether the gap between Eisenkot’s conditions and Netanyahu’s position can be bridged in negotiations. title: IsiDonodono wins double awards in a landmark week for isiNdebele literature
description: Themba Emanuel Mashobane’s celebrated poetry collection claimed two prestigious honours in a single day, cementing its place as a trailblazer for South Africa’s marginalised languages. By Themba Emanuel Mashobane IsiDonodono, the award-winning isiNdebele poetry collection by Themba Emanuel Mashobane, claimed two prestigious literary awards on the same day last Friday, 7 November, in what has become a remarkable run of recognition for a book that has now won three awards and received seven nominations since its publication. The first award came at The Book Behind The Awards (TBBA) ceremony held in Howick, KwaZulu-Natal, under the Umngeni Municipality, where IsiDonodono won in the category of Best isiNdebele Book. The second followed the same evening at The Castle of Good Hope in Cape Town, in a ceremony hosted by SHOFAR Books. That two major awards fell on the same date underscored the growing national profile of a collection that began as a manuscript entry and has since travelled the length of the country. The book, which contains 67 poems written in isiNdebele, was previously a winning manuscript at both the ANFASA and DSAC awards in 2025 before being published by ePublishing and Digital Displays. It is structured in the form of a textbook, with Mashobane providing literary analysis and explanatory notes alongside the poems — an approach that makes it both a creative work and a scholarly resource for readers and students of the language. For Mashobane, the awards carry a purpose that extends beyond personal achievement. “I use these awards to promote isiNdebele, which is one of the most disadvantaged languages in South Africa when compared with other indigenous languages,” he said. “Award nominations pave the way for me to promote my book, my genre and to network with writers from different regions and various languages.” His broader concern is access. Mashobane noted that self-published authors are frequently sidelined from both national awards and opportunities enjoyed by those backed by traditional publishing houses. Private awards that partner with established brands, he argued, provide an important platform for independent voices to showcase their work and reach new audiences. He urged emerging writers to pursue such opportunities actively, treating local awards not as validation alone but as a practical tool for market visibility and professional connection. IsiDonodono continues to demonstrate that a language once considered peripheral can, in the right hands, produce work of national distinction. TBBA 2026 WINNER’S . title: Detectives raid a guest house and arrest a fake KDF recruiter who fleeced jobseekers Ksh 1.1 million - Was conducting fake medical tests (PHOTOs)
description: Sunday, November 15, 2026 - Detectives have arrested a man accused of masquerading as a Kenya Defence Forces (KDF) officer and fleecing unsuspecting jobseekers of KSh1.1 million in fake recruitment fees. The suspect, identified as Brian Shem Maboni Achieng, was arrested at Cereda Guesthouse in Shibale Trading Centre, Nambale, Busia County, following credible intelligence received by detectives. According to DCI, officers raided the guesthouse and found the suspect holed up in a room with a 22-year-old woman who had been brought there by her mother in the hope of securing a KDF recruitment slot. Another young woman had similarly been brought to the premises by a parent, with both families hoping to secure their daughters' enlistment into the military. Preliminary investigations indicate that the suspect had been posing as a KDF officer with the purported ability to secure recruitment slots, collecting KSh1.1 million in cash from the victims' parents on different dates between September and November 2026. But what detectives discovered inside the room was even more disturbing. suspect had allegedly drawn blood and urine samples from one of the women under the guise of conducting a KDF medical examination. Among the items recovered were two syringes, one containing a blood sample and another containing clear fluid, a black dual-head stethoscope, an Omron blood pressure machine, surgical spirit and cotton wool. Detectives also seized a laptop, computer mouse and other electronic accessories, as well as white T-shirts bearing the inscriptions CODE 87243 and CODE 624513. Further recoveries included Kenyan and Ugandan national identity cards, a Ugandan driving permit and a VISA card, all bearing the suspect's photograph, alongside two mobile phones. suspect is currently in custody undergoing processing ahead of arraignment, while the recovered items have been detained as exhibits to support ongoing investigations. DCI has cautioned members of the public against falling prey to individuals masquerading as recruitment agents for the disciplined services and demanding money in exchange for enlistment. agency reiterated that KDF recruitment is conducted through officially announced and transparent procedures, not backdoor deals or cash inducements. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Kalenjin man arrested in connection with the murder of a senior police officer after being on the run for nearly 3 years - DCI reveals how detectives finally tracked him down
description: Sunday, November 15, 2026 - Detectives have arrested a murder suspect who had been on the run for nearly two years and nine months following the brutal killing of a senior police officer in Laikipia County. The suspect, identified as Onesmas Kipkoech Tiony, is accused of murdering Inspector Prosper Ojiambo Wandera, who was then the Deputy Officer Commanding Rumuruti Police Station. According to the DCI, the chilling incident happened on February 16, 2024, when Inspector Wandera was found lying in a pool of blood in the Maundu Meri area of Rumuruti Town. senior officer had sustained a deep stab wound on the left side of his chest, pointing to a violent end. suspect reportedly fled the scene and went into hiding, but detectives never abandoned the search for him. Through painstaking investigations, forensic analysis and follow-up on leads, Homicide detectives eventually narrowed down the search and launched a manhunt that culminated in his arrest. On Saturday, November 14, 2026, a coordinated operation involving Homicide detectives, DCI Laikipia West and officers from Rumuruti Police Station led to the raid of the suspect’s hideout and his eventual arrest. During the operation, detectives also recovered a motorcycle believed to have been used by the suspect to flee the scene after the murder. motorcycle has since been secured as an exhibit. suspect is currently in police custody, undergoing processing ahead of his arraignment in court. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Portugal honour Cristiano Ronaldo with special number 7 shirt redesign
description: The Portuguese Football Federation has permanently altered the design of its iconic number 7 shirt in an emotional tribute to one of football’s greatest ever players. By Pascal Okoth Portugal have introduced a special redesign of their iconic number 7 shirt as a permanent tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo, celebrating the extraordinary legacy of a man who transcended football and became the defining symbol of Portuguese sporting greatness across more than two decades of international service. The Portuguese Football Federation (FPF) announced the gesture yesterday, describing it as an effort to immortalise the significance of a number that has become utterly inseparable from Ronaldo’s name, his achievements and his immeasurable contribution to the game in Portugal and beyond. It is a rare honour — the kind reserved not merely for great players, but for those who reshape what a nation believes is possible on a football pitch. Ronaldo’s relationship with the number 7 shirt stretches back to his earliest days representing Portugal, a bond that deepened with every goal, every tournament and every record broken along the way. He retired as Portugal’s all-time leading scorer and the most capped player in the history of the national team, having appeared at multiple World Cups and European Championships and lifted the UEFA European Championship trophy in 2016 — Portugal’s first major international title — in what many consider the crowning achievement of his international career. The number 7 itself carries a mythical weight in football. From the great wingers of the British game to the continental maestros who wore it with flair and purpose, the shirt number has long been associated with brilliance, speed and the capacity to change a match in a moment. For Portugal, however, it means something specific and deeply personal. It means Ronaldo — the boy from Madeira who left home as a teenager, conquered club football at the highest level with Manchester United, Real Madrid and Juventus, and never stopped returning to pull on the red and green of his country with everything he had. The FPF’s decision to alter the shirt’s design rather than simply retire the number reflects a thoughtful distinction. Retiring a number takes it off the pitch entirely; this tribute keeps the 7 alive in Portuguese football while marking it permanently with the weight of what Ronaldo achieved in wearing it. Future players who pull on that shirt will carry with them a visible reminder of the standard set by the man who wore it before them — a responsibility and an inspiration in equal measure. The tribute has been warmly received across the football world, with supporters, former teammates and football administrators praising the federation for the sensitivity and creativity of the gesture. For Portuguese fans who watched Ronaldo grow from a gifted but raw teenager into the most prolific scorer in the history of international football, the redesign carries genuine emotional resonance. It is not simply a commercial or ceremonial act — it is an acknowledgement that some legacies are too large to be left only to memory and statistics. Ronaldo himself has spoken often about what representing Portugal means to him, describing the national team as a source of immense pride that no club achievement could replicate. That attachment, sustained over a career of extraordinary length and consistency, is precisely what makes the FPF’s tribute feel earned rather than sentimental. The number 7 shirt will continue to be worn by Portugal players in the matches ahead. But it will now carry a design that tells anyone who sees it exactly what that number has meant — not just in the record books, but in the hearts of a nation that watched one of their own become, by any measure, the most remarkable footballer their country has ever produced. For Portugal, the number 7 no longer belongs only to football. It belongs to Cristiano Ronaldo. title: ODM tops KSh 2.26B political parties fund as UDA and Jubilee trail behind
description: The Orange Democratic Movement has received the single largest share of Kenya’s political parties funding, edging out the ruling UDA in the latest allocation covering 47 parties. By Yvonne Wambui The Orange Democratic Movement (ODM) has emerged as the biggest beneficiary of Kenya’s KSh 2.26 billion Political Parties Fund, receiving KSh 801.85 million — the largest single allocation among 47 political parties that participated in the 2022 General Election, according to a report by the Registrar of Political Parties tabled before Parliament yesterday. The figure positions ODM, now led by Oburu Odinga following the death of his younger brother, the late Raila Odinga, ahead of President William Ruto’s ruling United Democratic Alliance (UDA) and the Jubilee Party in what is one of the most consequential annual distributions of public money to Kenya’s political landscape. The fund exists to support parties in running their operations, maintaining structures and promoting democratic participation — and the scale of the allocations this cycle underscores just how unevenly that support is distributed across the political spectrum. ODM’s total allocation comprises a primary disbursement of KSh 421.22 million, a supplementary allocation of KSh 380 million and a carried-forward balance of KSh 634,896 from the previous financial period. The combination of a primary grant and a supplementary top-up pushed ODM’s total marginally above UDA’s, a gap that is likely to sharpen debate about how the formula rewards electoral performance and parliamentary representation. UDA, which controls the presidency and commands a significant parliamentary bloc, received KSh 788.74 million — placing it second, albeit by a relatively narrow margin. Jubilee Party, now associated with former Interior Cabinet Secretary Fred Matiang’i following its dramatic political realignment in recent years, secured KSh 184.89 million, making it the third-largest recipient. Together, the three parties absorbed approximately 79 per cent of the total funds distributed, leaving the remaining 44 parties to share the balance — a concentration of resources that critics argue entrenches the dominance of established political outfits at the expense of newer and smaller formations. Among the mid-tier beneficiaries, Wiper Democratic Movement-Kenya, led by former Vice-President Kalonzo Musyoka, received KSh 98.81 million, reflecting its sustained organisational base in lower Eastern Kenya. The Democratic Action Party-Kenya (DAP-K), associated with Eugene Wamalwa, was allocated KSh 43.20 million. The United Democratic Movement received KSh 36.83 million, Ford-Kenya was allocated KSh 35.33 million, and the Kenya African National Union (KANU) — once the country’s sole legal party and now a shadow of its former self — received KSh 32.89 million. The allocations are determined under the Political Parties Act using a formula that weighs the number of votes a party obtained at the previous general election alongside the number of elected representatives it fields across all levels of government. That formula inherently favours parties with broad national reach and strong parliamentary representation, which explains why ODM and UDA dominate the distribution despite their very different positions — one in government, one navigating a post-Raila future with considerable uncertainty about its long-term political direction. What makes this cycle’s figures particularly noteworthy is the context in which they land. Political parties across the country are actively preparing for future electoral contests, and financial resources at this stage carry outsized strategic importance. Access to party funding determines whether grassroots structures can be maintained, whether local offices remain operational and whether parties can sustain the kind of continuous engagement with voters that translates into electoral strength. For smaller parties scraping by on allocations in the tens of millions, the gap between their resources and those of the top three is not merely financial — it shapes their entire capacity to compete. ODM’s position at the top of the table is also significant given the party’s current moment. The death of Raila Odinga — the towering figure who built ODM into a national force over two decades — has left the party at a crossroads. Oburu Odinga inherits both the leadership and the challenge of holding together a coalition that was, in many respects, built on his brother’s singular political personality. The KSh 801.85 million allocation provides a substantial financial platform from which to attempt that consolidation, but money alone will not resolve the deeper questions of identity and direction that now confront the party. For UDA, the second-place finish in funding despite holding the presidency and a parliamentary majority reflects the technicality of how the formula operates — ODM’s stronger performance in the 2022 vote in certain categories, combined with the supplementary disbursement, nudged it ahead. It is a distinction the ruling party’s strategists will note, though UDA’s proximity to state resources through its position in government gives it advantages that do not appear in the Registrar’s report. The tabling of this report before Parliament also reopens broader questions about accountability. Kenya’s Political Parties Act requires that parties submit audited accounts detailing how public funds are spent, but enforcement of that requirement has historically been inconsistent. With KSh 2.26 billion of taxpayer money now distributed, the scrutiny on how each party accounts for its allocation will inevitably intensify — as it should. Kenyans have a right to know whether these funds are strengthening genuine democratic structures or simply sustaining party bureaucracies with little accountability to ordinary members and voters. The report now sits before Parliament, and the conversation it triggers about equitable distribution, formula reform and financial accountability is one that Kenya’s political class can no longer afford to have only on paper. title: The poll shock, opposition realignment and the gathering storm ahead of 2027
description: A statistical tie between Ruto and Sifuna, a fractured opposition seeking unity and mounting institutional questions are reshaping Kenya’s electoral landscape with 2027 drawing steadily closer. By Fredrick Chelimo “The political fortunes of a nation are rarely determined by the loudest voices in its political arena, but by the silent conversations taking place in the homes, workplaces and communities of ordinary citizens. When those conversations begin to change, even the most established political arrangements must reconsider their foundations.” Kenya’s political landscape is displaying unmistakable signs of a competitive and complicated electoral season as the country moves through the week of November 16–22, 2026. The latest presidential opinion poll, renewed debate over opposition unity, emerging political movements, regional rivalries and growing scrutiny of public institutions have combined to create an atmosphere in which almost every political engagement carries an electoral undertone. The events of the past week are significant precisely because they reveal a shifting relationship between political leadership, public perception and the traditional methods through which electoral support has been built and negotiated. The most consequential development is the TIFA Research survey released on November 12, which placed President William Ruto and Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna at 31 per cent each in preferred presidential choice for 2027. Kalonzo Musyoka registered nine per cent, Fred Matiang’i five per cent and Rigathi Gachagua four per cent, while 15 per cent of respondents remained undecided. Conducted between October 26 and November 5 among 2,036 adults across all 47 counties, the survey has generated considerable political debate. These figures measure stated preference at the time of interviews — they are neither an election result nor a definitive prediction of voting behaviour, and they should be read as such. The reaction from Kenya Kwanza leaders has itself been revealing. Senate Majority Leader Aaron Cheruiyot and other government-aligned politicians have challenged the suggestion that Ruto and Sifuna are operating at comparable levels of public support. Yet opinion polling should not be treated as a political endorsement, nor dismissed simply because its findings are inconvenient. Its real value lies in identifying changing public attitudes, stimulating debate and encouraging political institutions to examine honestly the reasons behind those shifts. Equally, the opposition should resist the temptation to interpret a statistical tie as an electoral victory. The 15 per cent undecided electorate, the constitutional presidential threshold and the practical challenges of coalition-building remain critical variables. What makes the findings particularly interesting is Sifuna’s emergence as a national political personality beyond his traditional parliamentary and ODM constituency. His Linda Mwananchi platform appears to be attracting citizens seeking a different kind of political conversation — one centred on accountability, economic opportunity and generational renewal. However, translating personal popularity into a sustainable political organisation requires considerably more than public enthusiasm. The November 13 delegates’ conference, which proceeded after the Political Parties Disputes Tribunal declined to stop it, focused on organisational restructuring, nomination rules and coalition negotiations. Crucially, delegates deferred key leadership appointments, leaving Sifuna’s formal elevation unresolved. The distinction between a popular political personality and an established political institution will define the movement’s next phase. Opposition unity has simultaneously gained renewed momentum following former President Uhuru Kenyatta’s appeal to opposition principals to subordinate individual ambitions to a common political purpose. Kalonzo Musyoka’s November 14 declaration that he is prepared to sacrifice his presidential ambition in support of a single opposition candidate is a significant development. His insistence that he will remain in the opposition regardless of the outcome of negotiations provides a clearer indication of his publicly stated position — though the gap between public declarations and durable political agreements remains wide and historically familiar in Kenyan politics. The intervention of Opiyo Wandayi, who urged Kenyatta to step back from active political engagement, has introduced another dimension to the debate, raising an important constitutional and democratic question about the continuing role of retired presidents in national political discourse. Retirement from public office does not extinguish citizenship or the freedom to express political opinions, and that distinction matters. At the regional level, the confrontation during the Maa Cultural and Tourism Festival at Sekenani in Narok on November 14 deserves serious reflection. The clash involving rival supporters associated with Governor Patrick Ntutu and Nairobi West MP Gabriel Tongoyo briefly disrupted an occasion intended to celebrate cultural heritage and promote tourism. President Ruto’s presence did not prevent the confrontation, and security officers were forced to intervene. The incident illustrates the growing difficulty of separating cultural institutions from competitive electoral politics — a difficulty that will only intensify as 2027 approaches. The controversy surrounding the Kenya Pipeline Company share transaction adds another layer of institutional concern. Ndindi Nyoro’s questions about the transaction and Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi’s defence of the sale of a 25 per cent stake to private investors have opened a wider debate about public asset management, transparency and national economic interests. The government maintains the transaction was commercial and above board, but the public deserves access to relevant valuation, ownership and governance arrangements. Trust in public institutions is built through transparency, not assertion. The distribution of KSh 2.26 billion in political party funding offers yet another perspective on the changing environment. ODM received approximately KSh 801.85 million, UDA KSh 788.74 million and Jubilee KSh 184.89 million — the three parties together accounting for approximately 79 per cent of total disbursements. Audit concerns about inadequate records and party offices that existed only on paper raise legitimate questions about whether public resources are genuinely strengthening democratic participation or merely sustaining political bureaucracies. Looking ahead, the IEBC’s announcement on November 11 that 105 fully registered political parties had submitted certified nomination rules for the 2027 General Election marks a significant institutional step, shifting attention towards the integrity of party primaries, candidate selection and compliance with electoral law. The quality of these internal processes will carry considerable implications for the credibility of the eventual national contest. Ultimately, Kenya’s political weather must be assessed not merely through rallies, declarations and shifting alliances, but through the substance The post The poll shock, opposition realignment and the gathering storm ahead of 2027 appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: No Ronaldo, no party: Denmark deliver 4–1 reality check to Portugal
description: A night planned as a celebration of Cristiano Ronaldo’s legacy turned into a sobering lesson as Denmark dismantled Portugal 4–1 in the UEFA Nations League at Braga. By Andalo Christine Ingutia Portugal’s carefully choreographed tribute to Cristiano Ronaldo was yesterday gate-crashed by a ruthless Denmark side who showed no interest in sentiment, handing the hosts a stunning 4–1 defeat in the UEFA Nations League at the Estádio Municipal de Braga — their heaviest home loss in the competition’s history. The evening had been designed as an emotional farewell to Ronaldo’s international legacy, with Portugal’s players and their mascots taking to the pitch in shirts bearing his iconic number 7, while supporters unveiled a breathtaking stadium display honouring the forward’s extraordinary contribution to Portuguese football. It was a night built for warmth and celebration. Denmark, however, had not read the script. Pierre-Emile Højbjerg broke the deadlock in the 43rd minute, stepping up to convert from the penalty spot after VAR confirmed a handball by Portugal defender Rúben Dias. It was a clinical, composed finish that set the tone for everything that followed — and Portugal never truly recovered. Denmark returned from the break with greater intent and sharper teeth. Rasmus Højlund, one of Europe’s most dangerous young strikers, took centre stage with a devastating seven-minute double that effectively killed the contest. He first volleyed home Mikkel Damsgaard’s cross in the 50th minute, all timing and technique, before firing a low, precise effort past Diogo Costa in the 57th minute to put the visitors firmly in control. The Braga crowd, so electric before kick-off, had fallen into a stunned silence. The evening’s misery was completed in the 75th minute when Joachim Andersen rose highest from a corner to power a header into the net, making it four and emphatically ending any Portuguese hope of a comeback. Bernardo Silva provided a late consolation in the 94th minute, but it was exactly that — a consolation, with no bearing on a result that told an uncomfortable story about where this Portugal side currently stands without the man they had spent the evening honouring. Portugal head coach Jorge Jesus was characteristically blunt when asked whether Ronaldo’s absence had contributed to the defeat. “Missing what? He’s no longer on the national team, so what’s missing? The only thing missing is his presence here to keep me company,” Jesus said. It was a deflection dressed as a quip, but it also contained a pointed challenge to his players — that the Ronaldo era is over and the responsibility of carrying Portugal forward rests entirely with those now in the squad. There is an irony in all of this that is hard to ignore. The night was meant to draw a line under the Ronaldo chapter with grace and gratitude, to send him off with the full-throated affection of a nation he served for more than two decades. Instead, it exposed with unusual clarity the size of the vacuum his retirement has left — not because Portugal lack quality, but because replacing a player of Ronaldo’s psychological force and goalscoring certainty is not something that happens in one match, or one season, or perhaps even one generation. The result, painful as it is, does not alter Portugal’s standing in Group A4. They remain top with 12 points and have already secured their place in the quarter-finals. Denmark move to nine points, keeping alive their own qualification hopes heading into the final round of group fixtures. Portugal travel to Cardiff to face Wales on Tuesday, while Denmark host Norway in Copenhagen. For Denmark, it was a statement — a victory on Portuguese soil that announced their own ambitions loudly and without apology. For Portugal, it was a reality check delivered on the worst possible night. The tributes to Ronaldo were genuine and deserved. But football, as it always does, moved on before the applause had even faded. The post No Ronaldo, no party: Denmark deliver 4–1 reality check to Portugal appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Modern Uzbekistan, timeless traditions: Preserving national identity in a changing world
description: As Uzbekistan embraces modernisation and global connectivity, one university’s weekly tradition asks a quietly profound question — what does development cost if it erases the culture it was meant to serve? By Odilov Muhammadamin Uzbekistan is developing at a pace and confidence that would have been difficult to imagine a generation ago — new infrastructure, deepening diplomatic ties, expanding international partnerships and a younger generation with opportunities their parents never had. Yet alongside these achievements, a question that refuses to be drowned out by the noise of progress keeps surfacing: how does a nation modernise without losing the very thing that makes it distinctly itself? It is not a uniquely Uzbek dilemma. Every society navigating rapid change faces some version of it. But in Uzbekistan, where culture is not an abstract idea but something woven, literally, into daily life, the stakes feel particularly vivid. Traditional Uzbek clothing represents one of the most immediate and beautiful expressions of that heritage. The richly coloured Atlas and Adras fabrics, the carefully embroidered do’ppi — the traditional skullcap — the elegant chopon robe and the many other elements of national dress have been passed down through generations not as museum pieces, but as living markers of identity, craftsmanship and cultural pride. These garments carry within their patterns and textures a record of who Uzbeks are and where they come from. They are not merely decorative. They are a language. That language has been heard well beyond Central Asia. The late Oscar de la Renta, one of the most celebrated fashion designers of the twentieth century, drew inspiration from Central Asian ikat patterns, incorporating their geometric complexity and colour richness into his international collections. It was a reminder that what is rooted in tradition need not be parochial — that the specific can speak to the universal. In 2017, UNESCO formally recognised the Margilan Crafts Development Centre’s work in safeguarding the traditional production of Atlas and Adras fabrics, lending international weight to what Uzbek artisans have known for centuries. None of this means that global fashion trends are unwelcome. Among young Uzbeks, international styles are popular and their enthusiasm for them is entirely natural. Cultures have always exchanged ideas about how people dress, and that exchange is part of what keeps traditions alive rather than frozen. The question is not whether to engage with the modern world, but how to do so without allowing the pressures of globalisation to quietly hollow out what is most distinctly one’s own. This is precisely the philosophy at the heart of Alfraganus University’s guiding motto: “Zamonaviy ta’lim va sharqona tarbiya uyg’unligi” — the harmony of modern education and Eastern values. The phrase is not merely a slogan. It reflects a genuine institutional commitment to producing graduates who are professionally equipped for a competitive world while remaining grounded in the cultural and moral traditions that give that professional life its meaning. Real education, the university argues, is not limited to academic achievement. It also shapes the kind of person a student becomes — someone who carries their heritage forward with understanding and pride, not embarrassment. That commitment finds a practical and joyful expression every Friday, when Alfraganus University observes Milliy kun — National Dress Day. For more than a year, students have been encouraged to wear elements of Uzbek national clothing to university: an Atlas or Adras outfit, an embroidered do’ppi, garments featuring traditional ornaments. The tradition has become more than a dress code. It is a weekly act of cultural affirmation, a reminder that heritage does not belong only in ceremonial contexts or behind exhibition glass. It can walk into a lecture hall, sit at a desk and open a textbook. Preserving traditional clothing does not demand that every Uzbek wear national dress daily or turn their back on contemporary fashion. It asks something more sustainable and more meaningful — that people understand the significance of what they have inherited, support the artisans who keep those skills alive and ensure that future generations receive that inheritance with its value intact. A nation that moves confidently into the future while remaining anchored in its past is not caught between two worlds. It has found the harder and more rewarding thing: a way to be both. Uzbekistan’s future is modern. Its roots are timeless. The two are not in conflict — not if the choice is made, every Friday and beyond, to carry both forward together. author: the mt kenya times
title: Press freedom in Kenya: Free on paper, difficult in practice
description: Kenya’s Constitution promises world-class press protections — the streets tell a different story. By Mathew Kipkemboi Kenya’s 2010 Constitution is, on paper, a journalist’s charter. Article 33 protects expression. Article 34 guarantees media independence. Article 35 grants access to information. Few countries write these protections more boldly into law. Yet Reporters Without Borders ranked Kenya 117th for press freedom in 2025, recovering only modestly to 106th in 2026, with conditions rated “difficult.” The gap between constitutional promise and lived reality is wide. The evidence is not abstract. During the 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests, journalists were tear-gassed, injured and had equipment destroyed. In June 2025, the Communication Authority ordered broadcasters to pull live protest coverage off-air until courts intervened. On October 20 this year, a Royal Media Services investigative journalist was arrested while reporting on fuel price protests. Each incident is not merely an attack on a reporter — it is a direct violation of the Constitution those same officials swore to uphold. This is not a new fight. Since Gutenberg’s press around 1440, the powerful have sought to control what the public knows. Today the tools are surveillance, internet shutdowns and cybercrime laws — but the impulse is identical. The encouraging signs exist. Courts suspended the broadcast shutdown. Criminal defamation was struck down. The system still has teeth. But a press free in law yet battered in practice is not truly free. A public that cannot see clearly cannot govern itself. Kenya wrote that principle beautifully into its Constitution. The task now is making practice match the promise. author: the mt kenya times
title: How Bahati fooled Kenya: The million-shilling ‘wedding’ that was really a campaign launch
description: A gospel star, a fake wedding and KSh 10 million — Bahati’s Mathare 2027 debut raises a question that will follow him to the ballot. By Justus Sware Kenyans waited weeks for Bahati and Diana Marua’s white wedding. Hand-delivered invitations, a black-tie dress code, cameras banned, admission pegged at KSh 1 million per guest. On November 6 at the Argyle Grand Hotel in Nairobi, guests arrived expecting vows. They got a podium reading “MP Mathare 2027.” The wedding was never a wedding. It was a campaign launch in a bridal veil. The stunt worked because of its precision. Viral videos of celebrity invitations, deliberate media restrictions and a month-long buildup kept the true nature of the event carefully hidden. On NTV’s Fixing the Nation, Bahati was unapologetic. “I did not say what was to happen,” he said. “They guessed this is a wedding. I used Bahati’s Big Day artistically to get the attention of the nation.” On the money, Bahati claimed total collections reached approximately KSh 10 million — far below the KSh 100 million rumoured — with proceeds directed to his Bahati Cares initiative. Critics were unconvinced. The million-shilling figure was actively promoted, not imagined. Nairobi official Geoffrey Mosiria announced his own free-entry wedding, challenging Bahati to refund the money to Mathare residents. Bahati contested Mathare in 2022 and lost. His 2027 bid leans on a compelling origin story — orphan, gospel star, devoted husband. But he took public affection for that story and monetised it as a political prop. Technically, he never lied. But if he misled the nation about a wedding to win attention, Mathare voters will ask: what else would he do to win a seat? title: Maa festival chaos exposes the fault lines tearing Narok apart ahead of 2027
description: Violence at a cultural celebration attended by President Ruto has laid bare the bitter rivalries and political tensions fracturing the Maasai heartland with elections less than a year away. By David Kimani The Maa Cultural and Tourism Festival in Narok County descended into violence on Saturday when clashes between rival political factions erupted at Sekenani Gate, injuring at least ten people, scattering chairs across the dais and forcing security forces to form a protective cordon around President William Ruto as chaos swept through what was meant to be a celebration of Maasai heritage and cultural pride. The incident lasted only minutes before order was restored, but its significance will outlast the broken chairs and scattered tents by a considerable margin. What unfolded at Sekenani was not a random eruption of crowd disorder. It was a glimpse into the state of Narok County’s politics — fractured, increasingly personal and dangerously volatile — at a moment when Kenya’s broader electoral competition is beginning to reach its most combustible temperature ahead of the August 2027 General Election. The immediate trigger was a confrontation between supporters allied to Narok West MP Gabriel Tongoyo and those of Governor Patrick Ole Ntutu, two figures whose rivalry has been building for months and whose competing ambitions for dominance in one of Kenya’s most politically and economically significant counties have created precisely the kind of pressure that explodes in crowded public spaces. Videos reviewed by The Mt Kenya Times showed groups of people running through the venue, chairs hurled near the main dais, tents damaged and journalists scrambling to protect their equipment as light showers swept across the vast Mara landscape and the atmosphere shifted from celebration to confrontation in a matter of moments. The Presidential Escort Unit and General Service Unit responded swiftly, forming an all-round cordon around Ruto with officers fixing their gaze on the crowd, hands on rifles, expressions locked in professional seriousness. It was a scene that would have been difficult to imagine at a cultural festival a decade ago — and one that recalled an uncomfortably similar moment in May 2026, when a man breached the President’s security during a public address in Ganze, Kilifi County, reaching the presidential dais before officers intervened. That incident prompted an immediate restructuring of the Presidential Escort Unit: commandant Noah Kirwa Maiyo was transferred and replaced by William Sawe from the Recce Sub-Unit, with further changes made to the unit’s deputy commandant and officers serving in specialised formations. The National Police Service had not issued a statement on the Sekenani incident by the time of publishing. Governor Ole Ntutu and Narok Senator Ledama Ole Kina appealed for calm from the podium, persuading the rival groups to return to their seats and allowing the festival to resume. But the resumption of a cultural programme cannot paper over what the violence revealed about the depth of Narok’s political tensions or the degree to which electoral ambition has begun to corrode institutions and occasions that once stood apart from partisan rivalry. Inside the venue, a separate confrontation had already ignited before the chairs began flying. Nominated Senator Hezena Lemaletian had spoken about divisions within the Orange Democratic Movement, prompting Ole Kina to challenge her aggressively from the floor — an exchange that set portions of the crowd chanting “Wantam,” a pointed expression of discontent directed at the Ruto administration. The chant, which has become something of a shorthand for anti-government sentiment in parts of the country, landing at a cultural festival attended by the President himself, carried an unmistakable political charge. Ole Kina later placed blame for the broader tensions on former Cabinet Secretary Joseph Ole Lenku, adding a further layer of complexity to a feud that is as much about personal history and accumulated grievance as it is about ideological difference or electoral strategy. Ruto condemned the violence the following day at a church service, calling on communities to embrace issue-based politics and move away from personal rivalries that, in his words, served neither the people nor the county’s development. It was the correct message to deliver, and the setting — a Sunday church service, the morning after the chaos — gave it a degree of moral weight. Whether it lands with any durability in Narok’s political environment is a genuinely open question. The deeper story here is about what Narok represents in the architecture of Kenyan electoral politics as the country moves towards its next defining democratic moment. The county sits at the intersection of Maasai cultural identity, significant tourism revenue from the Maasai Mara — one of Africa’s most visited wildlife destinations — land politics of extraordinary complexity and a 2027 electoral contest that is shaping up to be fiercely fought at every level, from the governor’s seat to Parliament to the presidential race itself. When a cultural festival becomes a battleground, it is a signal that the boundary between community life and electoral competition has effectively collapsed — and that the consequences of that collapse are being felt not by politicians, who leave in motorcades, but by ordinary Kenyans who came to celebrate their heritage and found themselves running from thrown chairs. This pattern is not unique to Narok. Across Kenya, the political class is already operating in full campaign mode with elections less than a year away, using every available platform — church services, funerals, harambees, cultural gatherings — as proxies for electoral positioning and mobilisation. The result is an accelerating colonisation of community life by political rivalry, in which the occasions that once provided neutral ground for people to come together are increasingly weaponised. The burden of that dynamic falls on communities, not on the politicians whose ambitions drive it. For the Maasai community specifically, the Maa Cultural and Tourism Festival carries a significance that extends well beyond any electoral cycle. title: Omari demands KSh 30M and public apology from former MP over alleged defamatory video
description: City lawyer Danstan Omari has given Vincent Kemosi Mogaka 48 hours to retract statements he says falsely portrayed him as incompetent, dishonest and professionally worthless. By Elizabeth Angira Danstan Omari, a prominent city lawyer and managing partner of Danstan Omari & Associates Advocates, has issued a demand letter to former MP Vincent Kemosi Mogaka seeking KSh 30 million in compensation, a full public apology and the immediate deletion of a video he says contained malicious and defamatory statements about his character and professional career. The letter, dated November 13 and signed by Advocate Martina Swiga, centres on a public address delivered by Mogaka in Ekegusii and later posted on his Facebook page, “Hon. Kemosi Mogaka,” on September 15. According to the letter, Mogaka urged the public not to listen to Omari, alleged he had engaged in deceitful conduct in 1993, claimed he was dismissed from employment and ridiculed him for pursuing legal education at an advanced age. Mogaka also allegedly claimed Omari had never won a single case in court. Omari’s firm has rejected every allegation as false, malicious and reckless. The letter sets out his professional record in unambiguous terms: a Bachelor of Laws degree from the University of Nairobi in 2008, admission to the Kenya School of Law in 2009 and admission to the Roll of Advocates on November 4, 2011. He subsequently obtained a Master of Laws degree and between 2012 and 2022 served as a law lecturer at the Catholic University of Eastern Africa. He has practised at the Bar for more than 15 years, representing individuals, corporations, constitutional offices, public institutions and religious organisations in courts and tribunals across the country. The letter argues that the seriousness of Mogaka’s statements is compounded by the public platform on which they were made — reaching not only people who know Omari personally, but his existing clients and prospective ones. The firm maintains that while Mogaka is entitled to hold political opinions and support any leader he chooses, that right stops well short of making false allegations of professional failure and personal dishonesty. “Political differences cannot justify defamatory attacks upon another person’s character and professional standing,” the letter states. Within the 48-hour window, Omari demands that the offending video and Facebook post — along with any other versions circulated — be permanently deleted. He also requires a full, unequivocal and unreserved public apology and retraction, published in both Ekegusii and English, withdrawing each of the specific allegations made. The apology must appear on the same platforms used to disseminate the original statements, with comparable prominence and visibility. A written undertaking that Mogaka will not repeat or circulate further defamatory statements is also required. The KSh 30 million demand is framed as compensation for what Omari describes as grave injury to his personal reputation, professional integrity, dignity, goodwill and legal practice — harm he says was inflicted publicly and without justification. The letter closes with a clear warning: failure to comply within the stipulated period will result in legal proceedings being filed without further notice. By the time of publishing, Mogaka had not publicly responded to the demands. title: University funding in Kenya: A system finally being rebuilt from the ground up
description: From a broken 80% promise to a bold 100% loan model, Kenya’s university funding overhaul is the most consequential education reform in a generation. By Comfort Meredith Kenya’s university funding system has long been built on a promise the government never kept. Under the old Differentiated Unit Cost model, the state pledged to cover 80 per cent of tuition costs. In practice, disbursements fell to between 37 and 40 per cent, forcing students to shoulder 60 per cent — and pushing public universities into cumulative debt of nearly KSh 67B by 2022. The Student-Centred Model introduced in 2023 attempted a fix by sorting students into five income bands, with government covering between 30 and 95 per cent depending on household need. The concept was sounder than its execution — thousands were placed in the wrong bands, compounding the injustice. Education Cabinet Secretary Julius Ogamba has declared both models failures. His proposed Tertiary Education Placement and Funding Bill 2026 merges HELB, the Universities Fund Board and the TVET Funding Board into a single authority. Under the new model, government will cover 100 per cent of tuition for all KUCCPS-placed students — including those at KMTC’s 71-plus campuses. The full amount is a loan, repayable once graduates enter employment, with minimum monthly repayments of KSh 5,000 for formal employees and KSh 1,500 for low-income earners. For 2026/2027, KSh 22.12B has been disbursed. Semester fees now range from KSh 5,814 to KSh 75,000. The bill is expected before Parliament by December 2026. Kenya has rebuilt this system twice and failed both times. The third attempt must deliver. title: Perfectionism can become an expensive form of procrastination
description: The pursuit of perfect preparation often costs more than the mistakes it was meant to prevent. By Margaret Nekesa There is a difference between preparing carefully and preparing endlessly without ever acting. Research, planning and practice serve a purpose — but they become counterproductive the moment they permanently replace the action they were meant to support. Consider two people starting an online business. The first spends months comparing platforms, studying branding and researching successful entrepreneurs. The second picks a simple product, builds a basic version and puts it in front of real customers. The second person makes mistakes, faces criticism and discovers the original idea needs rethinking. But they also begin learning what actually matters — customer behaviour, pricing, the unglamorous mechanics of running something real. The first person accumulates theory. The second accumulates experience. This is not an argument against planning. Decisions involving significant financial, legal or personal risk genuinely require preparation, professional guidance and clear thinking. The point is that preparation must have a destination. It should lead somewhere, not circle endlessly back to itself. Small beginnings reduce the pressure to produce something extraordinary immediately. Starting with what is available, then improving through real feedback, is a more honest education than any amount of advance research. Perfection, when used as a standard that must be met before anything begins, quietly becomes an excuse — a respectable-sounding reason to avoid the discomfort of actually starting. Progress rarely comes from getting everything right the first time. More often, it comes from having the courage to begin before you feel ready, learning what only experience can teach and improving as you go. title: Political commentator Nuru Okanga hospitalised after roadside attack by unknown assailants
description: Okanga shared photographs of his injuries on Sunday, vowing his spirit remained unbroken and that he would not be silenced. By John Kamau Political commentator Nuru Okanga was yesterday attacked by unknown assailants on his way home and hospitalised with visible facial injuries, sharing photographs of his condition on Facebook and vowing that those behind the assault would not succeed in silencing him. Okanga disclosed the attack in a Sunday post accompanied by photographs showing him bleeding, with a large bandage covering one side of his face near the eye and significant swelling across his features. He did not disclose the location of the attack, the number of assailants involved or what may have prompted it, and it was not immediately clear whether he had reported the matter to police. “I have been attacked by unknown people on my way home. I am currently in hospital,” he wrote. He suggested the assault was intended to silence him, but said his resolve remained firm. “They may have wanted to silence me, but God is my protector. I thank Him for the gift of life. My faith remains unshaken, my spirit is strong, and my journey continues,” he added, invoking Isaiah 54:17 — “No weapon formed against me shall prosper.” He closed his post with a declaration that carried clear political undertones. “We shall not be intimidated, we shall not surrender. God is not finished with me yet! ALUTA CONTINUA! WANTAM!” The attack on a prominent political voice, with no suspects identified and no police statement issued, raises urgent questions that cannot go unanswered. title: Trump, Putin and Xi to hold historic nuclear talks at China summit
description: The leaders of the world’s three biggest nuclear powers will meet in Shenzhen next week in a trilateral encounter that could reshape the global arms control landscape for a generation. By James Mwangi United States President Donald Trump, Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping will hold a historic trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in Shenzhen, China, this week, the White House confirmed yesterday — the first time the leaders of the world’s three largest nuclear powers have met simultaneously since the Cold War redrew the boundaries of global politics. White House spokeswoman Olivia Wales announced the meeting to reporters, framing it as a centrepiece of Trump’s broader Indo-Pacific tour. “The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous,” Wales said. The language was careful and the ambitions deliberately measured — a senior American official, speaking anonymously to news agencies AP and Reuters, confirmed that no formal agreement was expected to emerge from the talks. But in diplomacy, the significance of a meeting is not always measured by what is signed at its conclusion. Sometimes it is measured simply by the fact that it happens at all. Trump arrives in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day Apec summit, which brings together the 21 member economies of the Asia-Pacific grouping. On Thursday, he will hold bilateral talks with Xi — their fourth meeting since Trump returned to the White House in January 2025 — before the three-way encounter that Wales described with unusual formality: “President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People’s Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation.” The phrasing, with its deliberate use of full titles, signalled that Washington intends this moment to carry symbolic weight even if its immediate practical outcomes remain limited. The backdrop against which the three men will sit down together is one of the most precarious in the history of nuclear diplomacy. The last major arms control treaty between the United States and Russia — the New START agreement — expired in February, leaving the world’s two largest nuclear arsenals without the verification mechanisms, inspection protocols and mutual guardrails that have underpinned strategic stability for decades. The collapse of that framework did not happen overnight. It was the culmination of years of deteriorating relations, suspended inspections during the Ukraine conflict and a broader unravelling of the arms control architecture that was painstakingly constructed to manage the existential risks of the Cold War. The United Nations has repeatedly urged Washington and Moscow to negotiate a successor agreement without delay, warning that the absence of a framework creates dangerous ambiguity about intentions and capabilities on both sides. Trump has indicated he is open to a new deal — but only on his own terms, and crucially, only if it includes China. Beijing has traditionally resisted being drawn into bilateral US-Russia arms control discussions, arguing that its arsenal is too small to warrant inclusion in frameworks designed for the two superpowers. That position has become harder to sustain as China’s military modernisation programme has accelerated, with the Pentagon estimating that Beijing’s nuclear stockpile has grown significantly in recent years and is projected to continue expanding. Whether the Shenzhen meeting will produce any movement on that fundamental disagreement remains to be seen. Iran is understood to be on the agenda — a point of genuine convergence of concern for all three leaders, albeit from very different directions — while Ukraine is notably absent from the confirmed discussion topics, a conspicuous omission that reflects the continuing sensitivity of the conflict and the difficulty of finding common ground between Washington and Moscow on a war that has defined European security for three years. What is already clear is that the meeting itself represents a significant diplomatic achievement for Trump, who has staked much of his foreign policy identity on his claimed ability to deal directly and personally with authoritarian leaders whom his predecessors struggled to engage. His relationship with Putin has been a source of persistent controversy at home and deep unease among America’s European allies, who have watched with anxiety as the administration has at times appeared to prioritise rapport with Moscow over solidarity with Kyiv. His engagement with Xi has been more transactional — defined largely by the trade war that dominated his first term and has continued to shape the economic relationship between the two superpowers in his second. The Shenzhen summit is also the latest in a sequence of events that illustrate the degree to which the geopolitical centre of gravity has shifted eastward. That the most consequential diplomatic encounter of the current moment is taking place in southern China, on Xi’s home territory, is itself a statement about the changed architecture of global power. A generation ago, a meeting of this significance would almost certainly have taken place in a European capital or on neutral ground chosen to reflect a rough parity of influence. Today, Shenzhen — a city that barely existed forty years ago and now stands as one of the world’s great technology and financial hubs — provides the stage. Trump’s tour will begin with an Association of Southeast Asian Nations summit in the Philippines on Tuesday before he travels to China, giving Washington an opportunity to reinforce relationships across a region where American influence has faced sustained challenge from Beijing’s expanding economic and military footprint. Wales described the trip as one that would “secure historic wins for the American people and advance America’s interests in the Indo-Pacific” — language that reflects both the ambition of the administration’s aims and the domestic political imperative of framing any engagement with rivals as a victory. title: Waiguru leads Kindiki in running mate poll as Ruto’s 2027 ticket takes shape
description: A Swiss Poll International survey has placed Kirinyaga Governor Anne Waiguru ahead of Deputy President Kithure Kindiki as the preferred running mate for President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election, in findings that are already reshaping the conversation about Kenya’s next electoral contest. By Daniel Karanja Kirinyaga Governor Anne Waiguru has emerged as the leading preferred running mate for President William Ruto in the 2027 General Election, commanding 42 per cent support in a Swiss Poll International survey that places her ahead of Deputy President Kithure Kindiki at 31 per cent and Homa Bay Governor Gladys Wanga at 13 per cent — findings that land at a moment when Kenya’s pre-election political calculations are intensifying by the week. The poll, conducted nationally, offers the clearest public snapshot yet of how Kenyans are thinking about the question of who should stand beside Ruto on the 2027 ticket — and its results carry implications that extend well beyond a simple popularity ranking. They touch on regional arithmetic, gender politics, the future of the Deputy President’s position, and the broader strategic question of what kind of coalition Ruto needs to build if he is to retain the presidency in what is shaping up to be the most competitive Kenyan election in a generation. Waiguru’s 42 per cent showing is striking for several reasons. She is a two-term governor of Kirinyaga County, a former Cabinet Secretary for Devolution and Planning under President Uhuru Kenyatta, and one of the most recognisable political figures in the Mount Kenya region — a vote-rich bloc whose support will be fiercely contested in 2027. Her profile combines executive experience at both national and county level with a political resilience that has seen her survive an impeachment attempt, a series of legal battles and the shifting loyalties of a region whose political direction has rarely been more uncertain. For Ruto, whose relationship with the Mount Kenya establishment has been complicated by the fallout with Kenyatta and the subsequent realignment of figures such as former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, the idea of a running mate who can anchor the region carries obvious strategic appeal. Kindiki, at 31 per cent, occupies a fundamentally different position in this calculation. As the sitting Deputy President, he is not merely a potential running mate — he is already on the ticket, elevated to the position following Gachagua’s controversial impeachment in late 2024. His poll numbers reflect a figure who has had relatively little time to establish an independent public profile in the role, having spent much of his tenure navigating the institutional aftermath of his predecessor’s removal while managing a demanding security portfolio. His academic background — he is a distinguished constitutional law scholar and former Vice-Chancellor of the University of Nairobi — commands respect, but respect and electoral warmth are different currencies, and the poll suggests Waiguru currently holds more of the latter. Wanga’s 13 per cent is the most politically nuanced figure in the survey. As governor of Homa Bay County, she represents a constituency that sits at the heart of ODM’s traditional support base in Luo Nyanza. Her appearance in a poll about Ruto’s preferred running mate reflects two possibilities that are not mutually exclusive: genuine cross-community admiration for her governance record, and the complex negotiations between Kenya Kwanza and ODM that have characterised the broad-based government arrangement. Whether Wanga’s figure represents a serious political pathway or simply a measure of her personal popularity is a question the coming months will begin to answer. The deeper significance of this poll lies in what it reveals about the structural pressures bearing down on Ruto’s 2027 campaign. The President faces a fundamentally different electoral environment from the one he navigated in 2022. Then, he ran as an insurgent — the hustler candidate challenging the establishment, drawing energy from economic frustration and a generational desire for change. That narrative delivered him the presidency by a margin that was ultimately confirmed by the Supreme Court after a legal challenge. In 2027, he runs as an incumbent with a record to defend, in an economy that has tested ordinary Kenyans severely through the cost-of-living pressures that dominated the 2024 protest movement, and against an opposition that is — however imperfectly — moving towards the kind of unity that eluded it last time. In that context, the choice of running mate is not a ceremonial decision. It is a strategic one that will signal to specific communities, regions and demographic groups whether Ruto’s coalition is broadening or contracting. Waiguru’s strength in the poll suggests that a significant portion of Kenyans see value in a ticket that doubles down on Mount Kenya representation — a reading that prioritises consolidating a base over reaching for new constituencies. Kindiki’s position, by contrast, represents continuity and institutional stability, virtues that carry weight in uncertain times but that may not generate the electoral excitement a competitive race demands. What the poll cannot capture is the internal negotiation that will ultimately determine the ticket. Kenyan running mate selections are rarely decided by public preference surveys alone. They are the product of backroom conversations between regional barons, party structures, financial interests and the kind of political debts that accumulate over years of alliance-building. Waiguru’s public numbers are strong, but public numbers and private commitments are different things. What is clear is that the 2027 ticket question is now firmly open and firmly contested. Gachagua’s departure from the Deputy President’s office removed what many assumed was a settled arrangement and introduced a fluidity into Ruto’s re-election planning that his campaign strategists will be working hard to manage. Every poll that places Waiguru ahead of Kindiki adds pressure to that management exercise and raises questions — however premature — about whether the sitting Deputy President’s position on the ticket is as secure as the institution of his office might suggest. Kenya’s election season has, in effect, already begun. title: Gachagua warns Ruto to respect Kenyatta: ‘In nine months you will also be a former president’
description: The former Deputy President has issued his sharpest personal warning yet to Ruto, framing the treatment of Kenyatta as a measure of the man — and a preview of his own fate. By David Kimani Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua has warned President William Ruto to treat retired President Uhuru Kenyatta with respect, telling him directly that in nine months he too will be a former president and that the courtesy he withholds today will be the courtesy he cannot claim tomorrow. Gachagua made the remarks in a video circulated widely on social media, delivering what has become his most pointed personal challenge to Ruto since his impeachment from the deputy presidency. “Respect the former president,” he said. “In nine months’ time you will also be a former. Respect is mutual.” The statement was brief, deliberate and calculated — the kind of message designed not merely to be heard but to land. The warning comes at a moment of intensifying pre-election tension, with opposition leaders coalescing around the shared position that Ruto’s administration has treated Kenyatta with a contempt unbefitting of a former Head of State. Gachagua, who now positions himself as a central figure in the emerging opposition architecture, has repeatedly invoked Kenyatta’s treatment as evidence of the administration’s character. The subtext of his message is as important as the words themselves. With August 2027 drawing closer, Gachagua is telling Ruto — and telling Kenya — that power is temporary, accountability is not, and that the clock is already running. title: Gachagua breaks silence on Ruto’s attacks: ‘I was mourning — now I have buried my sister’
description: The DCP leader has warned President Ruto that his period of restraint is over, challenging Kenya’s Catholic bishops to confront the President directly over language he says is beneath the dignity of the office. By Grace Wanja Democracy for the Citizens Party leader Rigathi Gachagua yesterday broke his silence over President William Ruto’s recent personal attacks, revealing that he had held back only because he was mourning the death of his sister — and warning that now she has been buried, any further insults from the President will be met with an immediate and full response. Gachagua made the remarks during a church service on Sunday, one day after burying his sister, in what turned out to be one of his most carefully framed public addresses since his impeachment from the Deputy Presidency. The timing and setting were deliberate. By speaking from a church, fresh from grief, he positioned himself not as a combative politician spoiling for a fight but as a man who had shown restraint under provocation and was now simply and reasonably serving notice that the restraint had run its course. His target was specific. Ruto had used a tour of Kisii County to describe Gachagua as a “master of hate,” a “hate man from Texas,” a “chronic liar,” a “conman” and a “fraud” — a sequence of personal attacks delivered from public platforms during official county engagements that drew criticism from several quarters, including the Catholic Church. Gachagua’s response on Sunday was measured in tone but unambiguous in substance. “This week you have been in Kisii, insulting Rigathi Gachagua and Uhuru Kenyatta. You were lucky I was mourning and did not get an opportunity to respond to you,” he said. “But now that I have buried my sister, if you insult us this week, we will respond.” The statement carried a weight that went beyond political point-scoring. Gachagua was making two arguments simultaneously — one personal, one institutional. The personal argument was that he had shown the kind of human dignity in a moment of family grief that he believes his former principal has failed to demonstrate in public office. The institutional argument was more pointed: that the President of Kenya has a responsibility to protect the dignity of the office he holds, not merely for his own sake but for the sake of everyone who aspires to hold it in the future. “He is undermining the dignity and the respect of the institution of the presidency,” Gachagua said. “We want to become presidents of Kenya, and we do not want the respect of the office of the President to go down.” It was a line that served double duty — a criticism of Ruto’s conduct and a quiet declaration of his own ambitions, framed as concern for the institution rather than personal grievance. The Catholic Church had entered the fray days earlier. The Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops, led by chairman Archbishop Maurice Muhatia, issued a statement on Thursday calling on presidential aspirants to avoid tribal, hateful and demeaning language as political exchanges intensified ahead of August 2027. The bishops’ appeal was directed broadly, but its timing — following Ruto’s Kisii remarks — left little doubt about the context in which it was issued. Gachagua welcomed the intervention but redirected it with considerable precision. “I have seen Catholic bishops saying leaders should not use abusive language against each other. And that is right. But let me help them a little. It is not the other leaders who are using abusive language. The person using insults everywhere is the President of the Republic of Kenya,” he said. He then went further, issuing a direct challenge to the bishops to request a formal meeting with Ruto and address his conduct face to face. “We want to tell our Catholic fathers that they are right, but they should get an appointment with William Ruto, with our church leaders, go and sit him down and tell him what he is doing is not presidential,” he stated. He extended the appeal beyond the Catholic Church, calling on bishops of the African Inland Church, the Anglican Church of Kenya and the Presbyterian Church of East Africa to intervene. His appeal to the AIC was particularly pointed, given that Ruto is a worshipping member of that church. “First, AIC, you are the bishops who should go and sit down with him. Tell him that he has embarrassed the church because of the insults coming from his mouth while he is the President of the Republic of Kenya,” Gachagua said. The broader political context in which these exchanges are taking place matters enormously. Kenya is now less than a year from a General Election that is shaping up to be fiercely contested across every level of government. The opposition, however imperfectly, is consolidating — with Gachagua, Kalonzo Musyoka, Martha Karua, Ndindi Nyoro and others moving, however gradually, towards a common platform. Ruto, as the incumbent, faces the challenge of defending a record on the economy and governance that has drawn sustained criticism, while simultaneously managing the internal dynamics of a ruling coalition that has itself been tested by the Gachagua impeachment and its aftermath. In that environment, the register of political speech matters. When a sitting president calls a former deputy president a conman and a fraud from public platforms in a county that he is visiting on what are ostensibly official duties, it sets a tone for political discourse that filters down through every level of public life. When that former deputy president responds from a church, a day after burying his sister, by challenging religious leaders to hold the President to account, the exchange has moved well beyond a personal quarrel. Gachagua left one door open. “If he stops, we will return to policies,” he said. “If he gets into insults, we will meet him there. He is the one to set the agenda because he is the President.” The agenda, for now, appears firmly set. The post Gachagua breaks silence on Ruto’s attacks: ‘I was mourning — now I have buried my sister’ appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.
