title: Ruto demands global finance reform as Africa’s $100B food import bill lays bare a continent’s missed potential
description: to convert their continent’s extraordinary agricultural resources into food security, regional prosperity and freedom from dependency. By Grace Nduta President William Ruto yesterday called for sweeping reforms to the international financial architecture, arguing that Africa’s annual food import bill of more than $100 billion represented not an inevitability but a failure of investment, political will and access to affordable capital that the continent’s legislators had both the power and the obligation to reverse. Speaking at the opening of the Third Global Parliamentary Summit Against Hunger and Malnutrition at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi, Ruto delivered a pointed challenge to delegates from across the continent: a land mass with the soil, the sun, the water and the people to feed the world should not be writing cheques to import the food it is capable of producing. The argument Ruto made was not new in its broad contours — African leaders have spoken of the continent’s agricultural potential for decades — but the specificity and urgency with which he pressed it yesterday suggested a president determined to move the conversation from aspiration to accountability. Africa, he said, did not merely have an agricultural opportunity. It had an agricultural obligation, and the gap between that obligation and current reality was a measure of collective failure. “Our continent spends more than $100 billion annually importing food, loses a substantial share of its harvest after production and directs only a small fraction of commercial lending to agriculture,” Ruto told delegates. “We cannot continue to import what we have the capacity to produce, export raw agricultural commodities while importing processed products, or leave our young people without opportunity in a continent endowed with such extraordinary productive capacity.” The diagnosis he offered was precise. Africa’s agricultural potential, he said, was being strangled by inadequate irrigation, limited access to affordable credit, poor storage facilities, low processing capacity and fragmented markets that prevent farmers from accessing buyers at scale. These are structural failures, not natural ones — and structural failures, he argued, yield to structural solutions, beginning in the legislative chambers where the delegates before him held power. At the centre of his prescription was the African Continental Free Trade Area, which Ruto described as the most consequential institutional opportunity the continent currently possesses for transforming its agricultural economy. The AfCFTA, he said, offered a framework for building an integrated agricultural market of genuine scale — one in which the logic of raw commodity export is replaced by a logic of continental value addition. “Through the African Continental Free Trade Area, we have an opportunity to build an integrated agricultural market in which African farmers feed African consumers, African enterprises process African produce, and African trade creates African prosperity,” he said. He urged parliamentarians to use their legislative authority to dismantle unnecessary trade barriers, harmonise regulatory frameworks, facilitate cross-border investment and build the infrastructure that connects smallholder farmers to regional markets. Ruto also invoked the Kampala Declaration, the continental agri-food framework that entered into force in January this year, which sets targets of increasing agricultural output by 45 per cent by 2035, reducing post-harvest losses by half, tripling intra-African agri-food trade and mobilising $100B in investment. The ambition of those targets, he acknowledged, was not in question. What was in question was whether parliamentarians would translate them into budgets, laws and accountability mechanisms that made them real. His challenge to delegates was unambiguous. “Declarations do not appropriate money. Parliaments do. The Kampala Declaration will succeed or fail not only in summit halls, but in the laws you enact, the budgets you approve and the accountability you demand long after these meetings have ended.” The domestic agricultural argument was accompanied by a broader critique of the international financial system that Ruto has made a recurring theme of his presidency. Africa’s ability to invest in agriculture, infrastructure and climate resilience, he argued, was being directly constrained by the high cost of borrowing, unfair assessments of sovereign risk and growing debt-servicing obligations that crowded out productive expenditure. As evidence of the structural imbalance he described, he cited the fact that despite the continent’s significant renewable energy potential, Africa attracted less than three per cent of global energy investment — a figure that, in his framing, illustrated not Africa’s unattractiveness as a destination for capital but the persistent distortions of a financial architecture designed by and for wealthier nations. “This is why reform of the international financial architecture is essential to the fight against hunger and climate change,” he said. “We need multilateral development banks that lend more and lend longer, fairer assessments of sovereign risk, affordable development and climate finance, and instruments that mobilise private investment at scale.” The demand is one that Kenya has pressed in various international forums, from the Summit for a New Global Financing Pact in Paris to the United Nations General Assembly, and Ruto deployed it here with the authority of a leader who has made it a signature diplomatic cause. Yet he was equally insistent that external reform alone was insufficient. Africa, he said, could not credibly demand fairer access to international capital while failing to mobilise its own. He called on governments to strengthen domestic development finance institutions, channel domestic savings towards productive sectors and build the internal investment capacity that would reduce structural dependence on external financing. “Africa seeks not charity, but fair access to capital and the opportunity to turn its vast resources into shared prosperity,” he said. The closing note he struck was one of conditional optimism, grounded not in what Africa had been given but in what it had chosen to do or not do with what it already possessed. “Africa has the resources. Africa has the people. Africa has the potential. What we must now demonstrate is the political will to turn that potential into production, production into prosperity, and prosperity into freedom from hunger.” The continent has heard that call before. title: Sifuna wins court battle as High Court clears Linda Mwananchi Movement rebrand
description: A bid to block the implementation of the Nairobi Senator’s National Delegates Conference resolutions has collapsed, freeing the path for The Equitable Party’s transformation into the Linda Mwananchi Movement. By James Mwangi Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna yesterday secured a significant legal victory when the High Court declined to block the implementation of resolutions passed at his party’s National Delegates Conference last Friday, clearing the way for The Equitable Party to be formally rebranded as the Linda Mwananchi Movement ahead of the 2027 General Election. The ruling removes what had been an immediate legal obstacle to one of the more visible political repositioning exercises currently under way in Kenya’s rapidly shifting pre-election landscape. Sifuna announced the outcome on his official X account, characterising the case as politically motivated. “The case by Ruto’s minions seeking to block the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties from implementing decisions of the Friday NDC has collapsed,” he wrote. The Senator did not name the petitioners directly in his post but described them as individuals aligned with President William Ruto — an allegation that the government has not publicly addressed. The dispute centred on resolutions adopted at the party’s National Delegates Conference held on 13 November 2026, through which delegates approved the transition from The Equitable Party to the Linda Mwananchi Movement. The rebrand is not merely cosmetic. The Linda Mwananchi Movement has been positioned by Sifuna as the institutional vehicle for his presidential ambitions in 2027, and the name itself — which translates broadly as “the movement of ordinary citizens” — carries a deliberate populist message aimed at urban and working-class voters, particularly in Nairobi where Sifuna holds his Senate seat and commands a significant political following. Following the court’s refusal to grant the blocking order, Sifuna moved quickly to signal that the rebrand would proceed without delay. “It’s full steam ahead for now. We know Kasongo will not give up, but every hurdle he puts in our way, we shall surmount,” he said, in a reference that indicated the legal contest may not be entirely concluded. The name Kasongo, cited by Sifuna in his post, appears to be associated with the party challenging the NDC resolutions, though the precise identity and standing of the petitioners in the case were not set out in detail in Sifuna’s public statement. He also took a moment to acknowledge the lawyers who had represented the party’s interests. “Salute to our overworked legal team. Msichoke, tutapumzika State House” — a Swahili phrase meaning, in substance: do not tire, we will rest at State House — a line that doubles as both gratitude and a declaration of presidential intent. The legal skirmish, though resolved in Sifuna’s favour for now, illustrates the increasingly combative environment in which Kenya’s opposition parties are operating as the August 2027 election approaches. Legal challenges to party resolutions, NDC processes and registration decisions have become a recurring feature of the political calendar, with rival factions and, in some cases, actors alleged to have government connections, using the courts and the Office of the Registrar of Political Parties as terrain for pre-election warfare. The pattern reflects a broader reality: that in Kenya’s current political moment, the battle for 2027 is being fought not only at rallies and in coalition negotiations, but in courtrooms and before regulatory bodies. For Sifuna, the successful defence of his NDC resolutions matters for reasons that go beyond the immediate rebrand. The Linda Mwananchi Movement needs to demonstrate organisational credibility — a functioning party structure, a verifiable membership base and a clear programmatic identity — if it is to compete seriously in a presidential field that is becoming more crowded by the month. The IEBC’s published electoral timelines place party primary nominations between 17 March and 10 April 2027, with presidential candidate registration opening on 29 May. That calendar leaves limited room for protracted legal distractions. Sifuna has built a national profile that extends well beyond his Nairobi base, with networks across both Luo Nyanza and Western Kenya giving him reach into regions that will be fiercely contested. His pitch — grounded in economic populism, anti-establishment rhetoric and the politics of ordinary Kenyan livelihoods — is calibrated for a moment when the cost of living remains the dominant concern of voters across the country. Whether the Linda Mwananchi Movement can translate that pitch, and Sifuna’s considerable personal political capital, into a credible presidential campaign will depend in large part on the organisational work of the coming months. Yesterday’s court outcome removes one obstacle. Many more lie ahead. The road to State House, as Sifuna himself might say, has never been without its hurdles. title: Trouble for former KTN host REGINA RE’s daughter as DPP approves murder charges against her - She is suspected of stabbing her grandmother over 20 times
description: Tuesday, November 17, 2026 - Former television actress and KTN host Regina Wambui Gitao, popularly known as Regina Re, is facing fresh trouble after the Director of Public Prosecutions (DPP) approved murder charges against her daughter over the killing of her 86-year-old grandmother. The DPP has approved murder charges against Thandie Malaika Wanjiku Gitao, who is accused of killing her grandmother, Dorita Lasinder Macharia. Thandie will be charged with murder contrary to Section 203 as read with Section 204 of the Penal Code. Her mother, Regina Re, and brother, Alton Jimmy Macharia, will also face charges of being accessories after the fact to murder. They are accused of interfering with the crime scene to conceal evidence and cover up Thandie's involvement in the killing. A post-mortem examination conducted on November 3, 2026, established that Dorita died from severe blood loss following multiple sharp-force injuries, including cuts to the face and neck, stab wounds and injuries that severed the external jugular veins. The cause of death was recorded as excessive blood loss resulting from a stab wound to the neck that caused vascular injury. Investigators also recovered clothing belonging to Thandie and the deceased, bloodstained towels and carpet samples, which were submitted to the Government Chemist for forensic analysis. The three appeared before Magistrate Beryl Akinyi, where they sought release to attend Dorita's burial scheduled for Wednesday, November 18. However, the prosecution opposed their release, citing the risk of them absconding court proceedings given the gravity of the offences. The court declined to release them and ordered that they remain in custody at Gigiri Police Station pending plea-taking. Meanwhile, Immanuel Munyeki, who had also been held in connection with the murder investigations, was released on November 12 after the prosecution informed the court that investigators had found no evidence linking him to the killing. The three are expected to appear before the Kibera Chief Magistrate's Court on Wednesday, November 18, 2026, for plea taking. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: “The Old Witch is Dead. We Can Now Have Money”- Details emerge on how former KTN host REGINA RE celebrated after her daughter brutally murdered her mother
description: Wednesday, November 18, 2026 - Chilling details have emerged surrounding the murder of 86-year-old Dorita Lasinder Macharia, whose granddaughter, Thandie Malaika Wanjiku Gitao, is accused of killing her. According to reports, Thandie's mother, Regina Re, was over the moon following the cold-blooded murder. The prosecution reportedly heard that Regina celebrated after her mother died, allegedly saying, "The old witch is dead. We can now have money." Further reports indicate that Regina had separated from her husband and pursued life as an independent woman while building her career in the entertainment and media industry. However, her television fame eventually faded, and claims have emerged that she was struggling financially and living in a bedsitter along Thika Road. Meanwhile, Thandie reportedly lived with her grandmother in a rented two-bedroom apartment, while her brother occupied a separate servant's quarter (SQ) next to the apartment. The brother has also been mentioned in the investigations, with allegations that he was found cleaning blood from the scene after receiving instructions from Regina. It is also alleged that Regina frequently fought with her elderly mother whenever she visited. As previously reported, a post-mortem examination established that the 86-year-old died from severe blood loss following multiple sharp-force injuries, including stab wounds to the neck. Thandie is facing murder charges, while Regina and her son, Alton Jimmy Macharia, are accused of being accessories after the fact to murder over alleged attempts to interfere with the crime scene. The three have denied the charges, and the case is expected to proceed in court. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Xi says China-Vietnam top-level exchanges inject positive energy into regional peace, development
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia SHENZHEN, (Xinhua) — General Secretary of the Communist Party of China Central Committee and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Tuesday met with General Secretary of the Communist Party of Vietnam Central Committee and Vietnamese President To Lam in Shenzhen. In recent years, the top leaders of the two parties and the two countries have maintained close exchanges and reached important consensus on building a higher-level China-Vietnam community with a shared future that carries strategic significance, Xi said. This has helped advance bilateral relations and injected positive energy into regional peace and development, Xi added. The Vietnamese leader is in Shenzhen to attend the 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders’ Meeting, scheduled for Nov. 18-19. During the meeting, Xi expressed willingness to deepen experience sharing with Vietnam, firmly support each other, and strengthen exchanges on self-supervision and self-governance of the parties, so as to ensure continuous progress in both countries’ socialist causes and national development. “As comrades and brothers, China and Vietnam must stand together and weather the storms,” Xi said. Xi also underscored the importance of enhancing mutual trust and solidarity, deepening all-round cooperation, jointly safeguarding peace and stability, and advancing shared development and prosperity. The two sides should properly manage maritime differences and steadily advance maritime cooperation, Xi said. Xi called on China and Vietnam to strengthen coordination within frameworks such as the United Nations, China-ASEAN cooperation and Lancang-Mekong cooperation, and to fulfill their duties as successive hosts of APEC in 2026 and 2027, respectively. Noting that the Vietnamese side views China as its most important strategic support, Lam said that, amid the current complex international situation, his country stands ready to strengthen solidarity and cooperation with China to support the development of both countries. Lam also pledged to work with China to safeguard maritime stability. As the next APEC host, Vietnam will build on the outcomes of APEC “China Year” and continue efforts to advance Asia-Pacific cooperation, the Vietnamese leader added. ■ The post Xi says China-Vietnam top-level exchanges inject positive energy into regional peace, development appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: APEC CEO Summit 2026 kicks off in Shenzhen with focus on regional cooperation, future prosperity
description: Source: Xinhua, Editor: huaxia SHENZHEN, Nov. (Xinhua) — The Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) CEO Summit 2026 opened Tuesday in Shenzhen, south China’s Guangdong Province, bringing together business and political leaders from across the Asia-Pacific and beyond to discuss regional economic cooperation and future development. Under the theme “To Prosper and Win the Future Together,” the two-day event has attracted more than 2,000 representatives from 21 APEC economies and 13 non-APEC economies, including Britain, France, Germany and Switzerland. Participants include representatives from 115 Fortune Global 500 companies, as well as heads of several international organizations and representatives of business associations from Russia, the United States and other economies. U.S. companies make up the largest group among participating companies from economies other than China, accounting for nearly 20 percent of the total. As an important part of the 2026 APEC Economic Leaders’ Week, the summit is expected to launch a Shenzhen initiative this year, marking the first time in the summit’s 30-year history that an outcome document will be issued in the form of an initiative. In his welcome address, Ren Hongbin, chairman of the China Council for the Promotion of International Trade and chair of the APEC CEO Summit 2026, expressed the hope that the dialogue will spark new ideas and forge broad consensus, injecting fresh momentum into the Asia-Pacific community and global growth. Attendees at the summit are discussing the new landscape of the Asia-Pacific economy and opportunities for cooperation. Key topics include crafting a new blueprint for connectivity, building an open and inclusive AI innovation ecosystem, and setting a new paradigm for sustainable development in the Asia-Pacific. Other sessions will focus on advancing the Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific, exploring new paths for digital economy cooperation, the Guangdong-Hong Kong-Macao Greater Bay Area and Asia-Pacific development opportunities, and promoting synergized digital and green transformation. An important event in the APEC calendar, the APEC CEO Summit has been held annually since 1996, serving as the highest-level platform for APEC economy leaders and business representatives to discuss open cooperation and advance regional economic development. As the host of APEC in 2026, China will hold the 33rd APEC Economic Leaders’ Meeting in Shenzhen from Nov. 18 to 19. This year’s gathering, under the theme “Building an Asia-Pacific Community to Prosper Together,” will focus on three priority areas identified by China — openness, innovation, and cooperation. These priorities are “particularly relevant today,” according to Antonio Basilio, director of the secretariat of the APEC Business Advisory Council, a mechanism that allows the regional business community to participate in APEC cooperation and submit policy recommendations to APEC economy leaders. Basilio expects all sides to hold constructive dialogues during the APEC meeting, and enable businesses to conduct trade and investment activities under more coherent, transparent and predictable rules. Working together with other APEC member economies, China has hosted more than 300 APEC meetings and events this year, drawing a cumulative attendance of over 10,000 participants. In the economic and trade field, China and other APEC economies have reached nearly 50 practical outcomes. ■ The post APEC CEO Summit 2026 kicks off in Shenzhen with focus on regional cooperation, future prosperity appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Uzbekistan youth and reproductive health: What a new study reveals
description: A survey of 65 students in Termez exposes critical gaps in gynecological awareness and the urgent need for structured preventive education By Mahmudova E’zoza Abstract Reproductive health constitutes an essential component of individual physical, mental and social well-being. This study aims to provide an initial assessment of respondents’ self-reported awareness of reproductive health issues and to establish the vital role of preventive education, based on a survey administered via Telegram channels. A total of 65 respondents participated. Their demographic profile, regional distribution and educational status were systematically recorded. Approximately 65 per cent of participants considered themselves knowledgeable regarding the survey topics, while the remainder indicated either basic familiarity or an insufficient grasp of the subject. Because findings rely on self-evaluation and a non-probabilistic convenience sample recruited through a digital messaging platform, they cannot be generalised to reflect the objective knowledge level of the broader population. Nonetheless, this research highlights a clear need for systematically structured preventive health education and validated information interventions going forward. Keywords: reproductive health, health literacy, preventive education, survey, awareness, university students, healthy lifestyle. Introduction Reproductive health extends well beyond the mere absence of disease or infirmity within the reproductive system. It encompasses a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being in all matters relating to the reproductive system, its functions and the life processes connected to it. The World Health Organisation identifies reproductive health as a critical pillar of overall human development, placing particular emphasis on equitable access to professional healthcare services and scientifically sound medical information. Awareness in reproductive and gynaecological health involves a working understanding of menstrual cycle physiology, the distinction between normal and pathological reproductive signs, the clinical symptoms of anaemia, the prevention of sexually transmitted infections, cervical cancer screening and prophylaxis, and the importance of timely clinical consultation. Such educational guidance must be delivered in a framework that is age-appropriate, evidence-based and genuinely accessible to the people it is meant to serve. Health literacy, however, is not simply a matter of having heard or read about a medical topic. Functional health literacy requires that individuals understand clinical information, assess its scientific credibility and translate it into sound, informed personal health decisions. A person’s subjective sense of being well-informed does not automatically equate to objective medical competence or practical disease-prevention behaviour — a distinction this study keeps firmly in view. In contemporary public health research, digital platforms — specifically Telegram messaging channels — offer efficient tools for collecting exploratory data across diverse age groups and regions. The voluntary nature of participation, educational background and prior exposure to medical disciplines, however, introduce methodological considerations that require careful acknowledgement. Study aim The primary objective of this investigation is to provide a preliminary descriptive assessment of respondents’ self-perceived awareness of reproductive and gynaecological health, based on a cross-sectional survey administered via Telegram channels, and to establish both the theoretical and practical case for targeted preventive health education. Materials and methods A total of 65 participants were recruited through educational and community Telegram channels. The dataset was analysed according to demographic age categories, geographic origin, educational status and subjective self-ratings of knowledge across core reproductive health domains. The study was designed as a preliminary descriptive survey, with relative percentage distributions calculated against the total sample size of 65. Approximately 65 per cent of participants reported sufficient awareness of the topics presented, while the remainder reported either superficial familiarity or an outright deficit in reliable information. Because convenience sampling via a digital messaging platform was used, the findings cannot be extrapolated to represent the objective knowledge levels of the entire population of Surkhandarya Region or Uzbekistan as a whole. Domain-specific competencies were not evaluated through standardised clinical testing; the data reflect participants’ subjective self-assessments only. Results Age distribution The predominant age bracket was 18 to 21 years, accounting for 47 respondents, or 72.3 per cent of the total. Respondents under 18 years and those aged 40 to 50 each represented 6.2 per cent (four respondents apiece), while the 25 to 39 age group accounted for 15.4 per cent, or ten respondents. The findings therefore largely reflect the perspectives and academic environments of young people and university students. Geographic distribution The majority of participants were based in Termez City, accounting for 58.5 per cent of respondents (38 individuals). Other districts across Surkhandarya Region contributed 27.7 per cent (18 respondents), Tashkent City 12.3 per cent (eight respondents) and Navoiy Region 1.5 per cent (one respondent). While this demonstrates a reasonable geographical spread, non-random sampling prevents regional comparisons or generalised epidemiological extrapolations. Educational profile Approximately 59 participants — representing 90.8 per cent of the cohort — were active university students, with around 50 of those enrolled in medical academic disciplines. This concentration of medical students is a significant factor in interpreting the findings. Individuals undergoing medical training naturally carry higher baseline exposure to biological and anatomical concepts than non-medical or non-student populations, which bears directly on how the awareness figures should be read. Self-assessed reproductive health awareness Approximately 65 per cent of respondents identified themselves as knowledgeable about the reproductive health topics covered in the survey. The remaining proportion acknowledged having only rudimentary familiarity or a meaningful shortage of reliable information. Critically, this 65 per cent figure represents subjective self-perception rather than objectively verified clinical accuracy or demonstrated readiness to manage reproductive health challenges in real-world situations. Discussion The findings reveal that even within a cohort composed predominantly of university students — many of them from medical faculties — a notable proportion continue to experience informational gaps or rely on only basic insights. This underlines the need for systematic, validated and accessible reproductive health education delivered well beyond the walls of medical schools. The World Health Organisation defines health literacy as the composite cognitive and social skills that determine an individual’s motivation and ability to access, understand, evaluate and apply health information. Binary self-reports of being either “knowledgeable” or “not knowledgeable” are therefore insufficient to capture true behavioural readiness. author: the mt kenya times
title: Entertainment’s grip on Kenya’s youth
description: Digital platforms are reshaping how young Kenyans consume content — with consequences that cut both ways By Caren Nekesa Entertainment in Kenya is no longer a pastime. For a generation raised on smartphones and streaming, it is the air they breathe. With young people constituting over 75 per cent of Kenya’s population, they are the country’s dominant consumers of entertainment content. Digital platforms have fundamentally transformed how that content is accessed, shared and internalised — faster, cheaper and in greater volume than any previous generation experienced. The benefits are real. Entertainment provides stress relief and emotional regulation at a time when young Kenyans face mounting academic and economic pressure. It builds social bonds, fosters cultural identity and, increasingly, generates livelihoods. The creative economy — music, comedy, film, digital content creation — is producing genuine employment opportunities for young people locked out of formal job markets. But the risks are equally real and deserve honest scrutiny. Excessive screen time eats into academic performance and personal development. Relentless exposure to idealised lifestyles on social media feeds anxiety, depression and corrosive self-doubt. Some content actively promotes drug abuse and normalises violence, reaching young audiences with little filtering or critical media education to push back against it. The challenge for Kenya’s youth is not to retreat from entertainment but to engage with it deliberately. Balance is not a vague aspiration — it is a discipline, and one that schools, families and content creators all share responsibility for building. Entertainment can empower a generation. Unchecked, it can quietly diminish one. The post Entertainment’s grip on Kenya’s youth appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Let students write: The case for authentic authorship in school drama
description: Kenya’s school drama festival must put learners back in the creative driving seat By Ashford Kimani The requirement that all competitive drama and film entries in Kenya’s school festivals be authored by students is not only timely — it is necessary. It is a call to restore the soul of a platform originally conceived as an educational space for nurturing creativity, originality and authentic student voice. Without this shift, the festival risks becoming an arena where adult brilliance is paraded through borrowed youthful voices, defeating its very purpose. At its core, drama and film in schools are not merely about performance. They are about process — the intellectual and emotional journey of a learner who must conceptualise ideas, structure narratives, experiment with language and ultimately present a piece that reflects their own understanding of the world. When students are sidelined in authorship, that process is disrupted. What remains is performance without ownership, expression without authenticity. Across many stages today, the imprint of adult authorship is difficult to ignore. Themes are often too layered, language too refined and ideological positions too sophisticated to genuinely belong to the learners performing them. Such pieces may win awards, but they raise a fundamental question: whose voice are we actually celebrating? When a student delivers lines crafted by an adult, they are not expressing their own reality — they are echoing borrowed thoughts. That reduces the learner to a vessel rather than a creator. The consequences reach further than the stage. Creativity cannot be taught through substitution. Writing skills cannot be developed through imitation alone. When teachers or external scriptwriters take over the authorship process, learners are denied the opportunity to struggle, to draft, to fail and to improve — the very experiences that build intellectual resilience and artistic confidence. First, the development of critical competencies is undermined. Then comes a subtler but equally damaging effect: an uneven playing field. Schools with access to highly skilled adult writers produce more polished pieces, overshadowing institutions that attempt to remain faithful to student authorship. The competition shifts from a test of student creativity to a contest of adult expertise, demoralising genuine student effort and entrenching a culture of dependency. Perhaps most critically, the practice distorts the purpose of education itself. Education is not about perfection; it is about growth. A flawed but authentic student-written script carries far more educational value than a technically immaculate piece authored by an adult. The former reflects learning in progress. The latter reflects learning outsourced. Advocating for student authorship does not mean excluding teachers from the process. On the contrary, it demands more of them, not less — but in a different capacity. Teachers must transition from scriptwriters to facilitators of creativity. Their role becomes guiding learners through idea generation, helping structure narratives, refining language and providing constructive feedback. That is the essence of effective pedagogy: supporting without overshadowing, guiding without dictating. This conviction is personal as well as professional. While in Form Two, Ashford Kimani authored a Kiswahili shairi. It was not perfect, but it was his own. It reflected his thoughts, his linguistic ability and his interpretation of the themes he had engaged with. With teacher guidance, he refined it and performed it with confidence. The experience was transformative — not simply because of the poem itself, but because it taught him that his voice mattered. That is precisely the kind of empowerment the festival should seek to cultivate in every learner who walks onto a competitive stage. For the student-authorship policy to succeed, it must be backed by practical enforcement. Declaring that items should be student-authored is not sufficient on its own. Schools could be required to submit drafts showing the evolution of a script from initial concept to final product. Learners could be asked to defend their work before adjudicators, explaining their creative choices and thematic intentions. Such measures would not only verify authenticity but also deepen the learning experience considerably. Teacher training workshops should be prioritised alongside enforcement. Many educators default to writing scripts themselves not out of any intent to circumvent policy, but because they lack practical strategies for facilitating student writing at a competitive level. Equipping teachers with mentorship skills would bridge that gap and bring practice into genuine alignment with policy intent. Ultimately, the debate is not about denying students access to quality work. It is about redefining what quality means within an educational context. True quality, in this setting, lies not in linguistic perfection or dramatic complexity but in authenticity, originality and learner growth. A student-written piece may lack the polish of an adult-authored script, but it carries something far more valuable: the imprint of a young mind in the process of becoming. If Kenya’s school drama and film festival is to remain committed to its educational mandate, it must be bold enough to prioritise authenticity over spectacle. It must create an environment where learners are not just performers but creators — where their voices are not borrowed but owned. Let students write. Let them stumble through drafts, wrestle with ideas and discover the power of their own expression. In doing so, the festival will not only preserve its integrity but fulfil the deeper purpose it was always meant to serve: nurturing thinkers, creators and confident individuals ready to engage with the world in their own voice. author: the mt kenya times
title: Are Kenya’s university graduates ready for the job market?
description: Degrees are multiplying but employability is not keeping pace — and the gap is widening. By Charles Wafula Kenya produces thousands of university graduates every year. Too many of them leave campus underprepared for what awaits them. The disconnect between classroom learning and workplace expectations is well documented and stubbornly persistent. Employers consistently flag deficits in communication, teamwork, problem-solving and digital literacy among fresh graduates — skills that academic syllabuses still treat as secondary to theoretical knowledge. The result is a generation credentialled on paper but underpowered in practice. The labour market compounds the problem. Employment opportunities have not grown at anything close to the rate of graduate output, forcing many young professionals into roles unrelated to their fields of study or into prolonged unemployment. Internship experience, which most employers now treat as a baseline requirement, remains inaccessible or poorly structured for a significant proportion of students. The solutions are not complicated. Universities must embed practical, industry-linked training into curricula rather than offering it as an afterthought. Employers should invest in structured graduate programmes rather than demanding experience that the system does not provide. Government must create conditions — through policy, incentives and direct support — that make youth employment a business priority, not a corporate social responsibility gesture. Students, too, carry responsibility. Waiting for institutions to act is a luxury that Kenya’s job market does not allow. Skills development, entrepreneurial thinking and practical exposure must begin long before graduation day. A degree should be a launchpad, not a waiting room. Kenya cannot afford to keep producing graduates the economy is not equipped to absorb. The post Are Kenya’s university graduates ready for the job market? appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Mofokeng double sinks Harambee Stars as Bafana Bafana win in Nairobi
description: Relebohile Mofokeng scored twice in the second half to hand South Africa a 2-1 victory over Kenya at Nyayo National Stadium. By Andalo Christine Ingutia Harambee Stars suffered a 2-1 defeat to South Africa in their 2027 Africa Cup of Nations Group D qualifier at Nyayo National Stadium in Nairobi on Tuesday, with Orlando Pirates forward Relebohile Mofokeng stealing the show with a second-half brace that proved the difference between two evenly matched sides. Playing in front of a passionate home crowd, Kenya started with purpose and defensive discipline, pressing forward in the opening exchanges and looking determined to register their first win of the qualifying campaign. South Africa, however, were organised and patient at the back, absorbing the early pressure and gradually imposing themselves on the contest. The first half was tight and physical. Kenyan defender Rooney Onyango picked up a yellow card in the 27th minute as the tempo rose, but neither side could find a breakthrough before the break. Both goalkeepers were largely untroubled, and the match headed into the interval goalless. Bafana Bafana returned from the dressing room with sharper attacking intent, and their greater urgency in the second half began to tell. The breakthrough came in the 68th minute when Mofokeng punished a defensive error inside Kenya’s penalty area to put the visitors ahead. It was a moment of clinical opportunism from the 20-year-old, and it changed the shape of the contest entirely. Kenya responded by pushing men forward in search of an equaliser, opening up space that South Africa were only too willing to exploit on the counter. Harambee Stars created chances but struggled to test the visitors’ goalkeeper with any real conviction, and the longer the game went on, the more vulnerable they looked at the back. The tie appeared settled in the 86th minute when Mofokeng struck again, completing his brace and extending Bafana Bafana’s lead to 2-0. It was a composed, well-taken finish that underlined why the youngster is regarded as one of the most exciting attackers on the continent. Kenya, to their credit, refused to capitulate. Two minutes later, substitute Ryan Ogam pulled one back after a sharp assist from Adam Wilson, sending a ripple of renewed energy through the stands and setting up a tense final few minutes. The home faithful roared their side forward, but South Africa held firm to secure all three points. The 2-1 result gives Bafana Bafana a 4-3 aggregate advantage across the two November fixtures, following the sides’ 2-2 draw in Johannesburg on Friday, 13 November. More significantly, the victory lifts South Africa to the top of Group D with 10 points from four matches, moving one point clear of second-placed Guinea. Kenya remain third in the group with just two points and are still searching for a first qualifying win. However, the result carries limited consequence for Harambee Stars in terms of tournament participation — Kenya have already secured automatic qualification for the 2027 AFCON finals as co-hosts alongside Uganda and Tanzania. For coach Benni McCarthy, though, the performance will be a source of frustration. Conceding twice from individual errors and failing to convert home advantage into points are habits that will need correcting before the continental tournament begins. With the final qualifying fixtures scheduled for March 2027, Kenya have time to sharpen their game — but McCarthy will know that the standard required at AFCON will be considerably higher than what was on display yesterday. South Africa, by contrast, travel home with momentum, a place at the top of their group and confirmation that Mofokeng, in the right conditions, is capable of deciding matches on his own. author: the mt kenya times
title: Blow to Ruto as three Mt Kenya MPs abandon UDA for Gachagua’s DCP
description: Three sitting MPs cross to the former deputy president’s party, deepening the battle for Mt Kenya ahead of 2027. By Yvonne Wambui President William Ruto suffered a significant political setback in the Mt Kenya region yesterday after three Members of Parliament abandoned his United Democratic Alliance and joined former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s Democracy for the Citizens Party, sharpening what is fast becoming one of Kenya’s most consequential political rivalries ahead of the 2027 General Election. The three legislators who announced their departure from UDA are Gabriel Kagombe, MP for Gatundu South, Wachira Karani, MP for Laikipia West, and Rahab Mukami, the Nyeri Woman Representative. Their decision to cross to Gachagua’s DCP signals growing fractures within the ruling party’s Mt Kenya base — a region that was central to Ruto’s victory in the 2022 General Election and remains critical to his re-election prospects. The timing is pointed. With under a year to polling day, political leaders across the country are making calculated decisions about where to place their allegiances, and Mt Kenya is shaping up as the most closely watched battleground. For Ruto, the defections raise uncomfortable questions about his grip on a bloc that delivered for him four years ago. For Gachagua, the gains could not have come at a better moment. The former deputy president, who was removed from office following a parliamentary impeachment in 2024, has been methodically constructing his political base through DCP. Attracting three sitting MPs — each with an established constituency — provides the party with credibility, visibility and momentum it has been working to build. Kagombe’s Gatundu South constituency carries particular symbolic weight, sitting at the heart of the late President Jomo Kenyatta’s political legacy and deep within Mt Kenya’s political core. Karani’s Laikipia West and Mukami’s Nyeri county seat add geographic spread to the DCP’s expanding footprint, strengthening the party’s claim to represent a cross-section of the region rather than a narrow faction. The defections are also a reflection of a broader pattern emerging in Kenyan politics. As 2027 approaches, elected leaders are increasingly willing to reconsider party affiliations when the political calculus shifts. Loyalty, in this environment, is transactional — and the three MPs’ move suggests that for some in Mt Kenya, the calculation has already changed. UDA still controls a significant number of elected representatives in the region, and the ruling party retains the considerable advantages of incumbency — state resources, patronage networks and the institutional weight of government. However, losing sitting MPs publicly, in a region of this strategic importance, is not easily dismissed as routine political noise. The more pressing question for the ruling party is whether these three departures are an isolated event or the visible tip of a wider discontent. Within UDA’s Mt Kenya caucus, there will be MPs watching the reaction closely, weighing their own futures and calculating their options. If the party does not move quickly to stabilise its position in the region, further movement cannot be ruled out. Gachagua, for his part, has shown he understands the importance of momentum. Each high-profile addition to DCP changes the conversation — transforming the party in public perception from a vehicle of personal grievance into a credible political force capable of winning seats, attracting talent and presenting a genuine electoral challenge. Yesterday’s announcement was a carefully staged demonstration of exactly that. The contest unfolding in Mt Kenya is about more than two political heavyweights settling a personal score. It is about the future shape of Kenyan politics — about whether the dominant coalition that brought Ruto to power in 2022 holds together or fractures under the pressure of competing ambitions and unmet expectations. Mt Kenya’s voters have shown in previous election cycles that they are neither passive nor monolithic. They respond to leadership, to perceived benefit and to the confidence that their region will have genuine influence in government. If Gachagua succeeds in persuading enough of them that DCP offers a more credible path to that influence, the electoral arithmetic for 2027 could shift in ways that matter. Whether yesterday’s defections mark the beginning of a sustained political migration or represent the outer limit of DCP’s current appeal in the region remains an open question. What is no longer in question is the seriousness of the challenge Gachagua is mounting — and the pressure that challenge is placing on a president who cannot afford to take his home region for granted. The battle for Mt Kenya has begun in earnest. The next twelve months will determine who wins it. title: Nairobi senator Edwin Sifuna met Canada’s top diplomat in Kenya
description: A closed-door meeting at the Canadian High Commission signals growing foreign interest in Kenya’s political trajectory ahead of 2027. By Anne Njeri Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna, leader of the Linda Mwananichi Movement, met Canadian High Commissioner Joshua Tabah, Deputy High Commissioner Julanar Green, and First Secretary for Political Affairs Siobhan Kerr at the Canadian High Commission in Nairobi yesterday, in a closed-door engagement that underlines the deepening diplomatic interest in Kenya’s rapidly evolving political landscape ahead of the August 2027 general election. The meeting comes at a charged moment. With political realignments accelerating, coalition negotiations intensifying and the electoral commission under scrutiny over technology procurement, Western missions in Nairobi are paying close attention to how Kenya’s democratic institutions hold up under pressure. Sifuna, one of the opposition’s most prominent voices in the Senate, is well placed to offer foreign diplomats an unfiltered reading of the political temperature. Canada, which has consistently supported democratic governance and electoral integrity across East Africa, has a direct interest in ensuring Kenya’s 2027 transition is credible and peaceful. No statement was issued following the meeting. The post Nairobi senator Edwin Sifuna met Canada’s top diplomat in Kenya appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Gachagua brands Ruto’s ‘Usawa ni Sawa’ a cover for ethnic appointments
description: The DCP leader’s latest broadside over senior public service jobs cuts to the heart of one of the most combustible issues heading into the 2027 election. By David Kimani Democracy for the Citizens Party leader Rigathi Gachagua yesterday attacked President William Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa” campaign, accusing the government of using an equality slogan to mask a pattern of ethnically skewed appointments at the highest levels of Kenya’s public service. Gachagua’s remarks came shortly after the Teachers Service Commission named Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer. In a sarcastic post on X, the former Deputy President linked Ayabei’s appointment to other recent selections — Ronoh Kibet as KenGen Managing Director and Chief Executive Officer, and Lydia Sitienei Chelagat’s nomination as Data Commissioner, which is awaiting parliamentary approval. All three appointees are from the Kalenjin community. “To start with, Ruto cannot tell anybody about Usawa. He’s a con. He’s deceptive,” Gachagua said. The remarks were pointed in their target. “Usawa ni Sawa, Mbele Pamoja” — equality is fair, forward together — is Ruto’s rebranded campaign message for 2027, a deliberate pivot from the bottom-up “hustler nation” rhetoric that carried him to State House in 2022. For Gachagua, the slogan is not a governing philosophy. It is a political instrument designed, in his telling, to neutralise Mt Kenya’s legitimate grievances while systematically concentrating economic and institutional power elsewhere. The allegation is not new, but its persistence gives it weight. Gachagua, who was impeached in October 2024 after facing charges that included accusations of promoting ethnic divisions, has repeatedly accused his former boss of favouring members of his community in public appointments. Government allies have defended the selections, maintaining that the individuals were picked on merit through competitive recruitment processes. That defence is the standard response — and it is the response that Gachagua is methodically working to undermine. His strategy is accumulation. Each appointment, taken in isolation, can be explained away. Assembled into a pattern and placed before a Mt Kenya electorate already primed to see economic grievance in institutional decisions, they become a political narrative with real electoral traction. Mt Kenya delivered approximately 2.9 million votes for Ruto in 2022 — roughly 41 per cent of his national tally of 7.1 million. The region has long been Kenya’s most influential political kingmaker, having produced three presidents. Ruto cannot afford to lose it, and Gachagua knows it. The “41 vs 1” charge — the accusation that Ruto is reviving the politics of isolating one community against the rest of the country — is the most incendiary weapon in Gachagua’s arsenal. It resurrects the darkest chapter of Kenya’s pre-2007 political rhetoric, and its deployment ahead of 2027 is a calculated escalation. Whether it reflects genuine grievance, political strategy or both, it will resonate in every household, church and market in central Kenya. Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa” message was designed precisely to defuse this kind of attack — to reframe his presidency as one of national inclusion rather than ethnic patronage. Yesterday’s exchange suggests that reframing has not taken hold where it matters most. The battle for Mt Kenya’s 7.4 million voters has entered its most dangerous phase. title: Why Ruto’s State of the Nation address today carries more weight than any before it
description: With the 2027 election closing in and Kenyans demanding answers on the cost of living, President Ruto faces Parliament today in the most politically charged address of his first term. By David Kimani President William Ruto will today deliver his State of the Nation Address to a joint sitting of the National Assembly and Senate at Parliament Buildings in Nairobi, in what is shaping up to be the most consequential speech of his presidency — one that will be heard not only as a constitutional obligation but as the opening salvo of a re-election campaign that has already begun in everything but name. Parliament confirmed the address in a formal notice issued yesterday, 17 November 2026, citing the constitutional requirement under Article 132 of the Constitution of Kenya, which obliges the president to address a special sitting of Parliament once every year. The provision requires Ruto to report on measures taken and progress achieved in realising the national values and principles of governance enshrined under Article 10, as well as to submit reports on Kenya’s progress in meeting its international obligations. Speaker of the National Assembly Moses Wetang’ula also highlighted Article 247, which separately requires the president to provide Parliament with an annual report on the state of national security — making today’s address a dual-purpose constitutional exercise with both domestic and strategic dimensions. On paper, it is routine. In practice, nothing about today’s address is routine. Kenya is nine months from a general election. The political temperature is rising by the week. Coalitions are forming and fracturing simultaneously. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua, impeached and ousted barely a year ago, is building a rival political base in the Mt Kenya region with a speed that has unsettled the ruling Kenya Kwanza administration. The opposition, fragmented but vocal, is sharpening its critique of the government’s economic record. And ordinary Kenyans — the ones who voted in August 2022 with specific, urgent expectations — are waiting to hear whether this administration has delivered on the promises that brought it to power. That is the real audience for today’s address. Not the lawmakers seated in the chamber. Not the diplomats in the gallery. Not the political commentators parsing every sentence for tactical meaning. The real audience is the Kenyan voter who is paying more for unga, struggling to find work for their children and wondering whether the bottom-up economic model — the centrepiece of Ruto’s 2022 campaign — was a governing philosophy or a campaign slogan. Ruto is expected to address the cost of living, employment, economic growth, healthcare reforms, education, agriculture and infrastructure development. These are not abstract policy categories. They are the daily lived realities of millions of Kenyans, and the gap between what was promised and what has been delivered will be measured not in percentage points or GDP figures but in the price of cooking oil, the availability of fertiliser and the accessibility of affordable credit for small traders and farmers. The Kenya Kwanza administration came to power on an explicitly pro-poor, pro-hustler platform. Its economic transformation agenda was built around expanding opportunities for those at the bottom of the economic pyramid — the mama mboga, the boda boda operator, the small-scale farmer, the informal trader. Three years into the administration, the question being asked in markets, churches and barber shops across the country is a simple one: has the hustler nation actually improved the lives of hustlers? The honest answer is mixed, and Ruto will need to navigate that complexity carefully today. There have been genuine achievements. Infrastructure investment has continued at scale, with significant road projects, the expansion of affordable housing and progress on universal health coverage. The government’s agricultural interventions — subsidised fertiliser, improved seed programmes and expanded irrigation — have produced measurable results in certain counties. Digital financial services and government-to-person payment systems have improved the efficiency of some social transfers. But the challenges have been equally real and, in many cases, more visible than the achievements. The cost of living has remained stubbornly high. Youth unemployment persists at levels that represent both an economic crisis and a political risk. The tax burden introduced through successive finance bills — including the controversial 2023 Finance Act, elements of which were struck down by the courts following deadly protests — left a residue of public anger that has not fully dissipated. The government’s relationship with young Kenyans, in particular, was tested severely in mid-2024 and has required sustained effort to repair. It is against this backdrop that today’s address takes on its full political weight. Ruto is not merely reporting to Parliament. He is making an argument to the electorate — constructing a narrative of progress, resilience and forward momentum that he will carry into the 2027 campaign. The challenge is that the narrative must be credible. In an era of social media scrutiny, real-time fact-checking and an energised civil society, a presidential address that glosses over failure or overstates achievement will be dismantled within hours of delivery. The security dimension of today’s address adds another layer of complexity. Under Article 247, Ruto is required to report on the state of national security — a provision that will draw attention to the security situation in several parts of the country, including the ongoing challenges in parts of the Rift Valley and the broader question of how the government is addressing the conditions that generate insecurity in the first place. Security, in Kenya’s political context, is never a purely technical matter. It is deeply intertwined with land, ethnicity, resource allocation and the perception of whether the state is equally present and equally protective across all communities. Parliament will subsequently have the opportunity to debate the address and assess the government’s progress. That debate, in the current political climate, will be lively. title: Nairobi’s KSh86.9B debt crisis: How stalled projects and unpaid bills are strangling county suppliers
description: Parliament is now proposing a national government bailout as Nairobi’s mounting obligations threaten to choke businesses and derail devolution’s economic promise. By Grace Wanja Nairobi County accounts for more than half of Kenya’s KSh172.5B in county pending bills, with KSh86.9B owed to suppliers and 57 stalled projects making it the worst performer among all 47 counties, according to a new Parliamentary Budget Office report. The figures, covering the period to June 2026, lay bare the scale of a fiscal crisis that has been building quietly beneath the surface of devolution for years — one that is now threatening to undermine business confidence, destabilise suppliers and contractors, and raise serious questions about financial governance at the county level as Kenya heads into a general election in which devolution’s record will be a central point of contest. Of the KSh172.5B total stock of pending bills held across all counties, KSh71.7B had remained unpaid for more than three years as of June 2026. That figure alone — obligations outstanding for over three years — speaks to a structural problem that goes beyond cashflow difficulties or delayed disbursements from the national government. It points to a pattern of spending commitments that counties have been unable or unwilling to honour, with suppliers and contractors bearing the cost. Nairobi’s position within that picture is in a category of its own. The county owes KSh49.1B of the total pending bills stock — more than half of the national county figure — with nearly a third of that accumulated in the 2025/26 financial year alone, amounting to KSh46.7B. A further KSh30.6B is aged between one and two years, and KSh22.9B between three and four years. The layering of these figures tells a story not of a single crisis but of accumulated defaults across successive financial years, each one compounding the last. The human dimension of these numbers is easily lost in the aggregation. Behind every unpaid bill is a business — a construction firm, a medical supplier, a road contractor, a cleaning company — that delivered a service or completed a project on the expectation of payment. Many of these are small and medium enterprises for which delayed government payments do not merely affect profitability; they threaten survival. Staff go unpaid. Bank loans fall into default. Supply chains freeze. The Parliamentary Budget Office is explicit on this point, noting that Nairobi’s level of pending bills creates a significant risk for businesses and economic activity in the county and beyond. The proposed remedy is as notable as the diagnosis. Parliament is suggesting the introduction of a matching financing arrangement between the national government and Nairobi County — either a one-for-two model, in which the national government contributes one shilling for every two settled by the county, or a one-for-one arrangement under which the national government matches every shilling the county pays. Under the more generous version, the national government would effectively absorb half of Nairobi’s outstanding obligations. The Budget Office argues that clearing the bills by 2030 would improve liquidity for suppliers and strengthen business confidence across the broader Nairobi economy. The proposal is pragmatic but politically loaded. It amounts to an acknowledgement that Nairobi County, the seat of Kenya’s capital and economic engine, cannot clear its own debts without central government intervention. That is a significant admission, and one that will not be lost on the county’s political leadership as the 2027 election approaches. County governance — and the question of whether devolution has delivered value for money — is increasingly a live electoral issue, and Nairobi’s pending bills crisis hands critics a substantial line of attack. The stalled projects data sharpens the concern further. Nairobi leads all counties with 57 incomplete projects, followed by Kakamega at 26, Baringo at 23, Machakos at 22 and Kilifi at 10. The Parliamentary Budget Office is insisting that viable stalled projects be completed before new ones are initiated — a recommendation grounded in straightforward economic logic. A project that is 70 per cent complete generates no economic return until it is finished. Beginning a new project while the existing one sits idle doubles the waste and compounds the inefficiency. What the report ultimately captures is a governance gap that devolution, now in its second decade, has not closed. The constitutional promise of county governments was accountability, proximity and responsiveness. Pending bills that sit unpaid for three years and construction sites that lie dormant for want of political will represent a failure of all three. With the 2027 election nine months away, every county governor will face voters who can point to a half-built hospital, an unpaid contractor or a development promise that never materialised. In Nairobi, there are 57 of them. That is not a statistic. It is a ballot paper. title: Oburu meets Ruto at State House as ODM sets its price for 2027 support
description: With Raila gone and elections nine months away, ODM is negotiating hard — and its message to UDA is blunt: nothing is for free. By James Mwangi Orange Democratic Movement leader Oburu Oginga held talks with President William Ruto at State House in Nairobi yesterday, as the two parties moved to consolidate their working relationship ahead of the August 2027 general election — with ODM making clear it expects a formal power-sharing agreement in return for its support. The meeting comes at a delicate moment for ODM. The party is navigating a politically sensitive transition following the death of its longtime leader Raila Odinga in October 2025, with Oburu — Raila’s elder brother — now steering its negotiations with the ruling United Democratic Alliance. The broad-based arrangement between the two parties was initiated in March 2025, when Ruto and Raila signed a ten-point cooperation framework covering governance, national unity, devolution, anti-corruption efforts and the rule of law. With Raila gone, the question of whether that framework survives — and on what terms — is one of the defining political questions of the pre-election period. Senior ODM officials were unambiguous on Tuesday about where the party stands. National Chairperson Gladys Wanga, Deputy Party Leader Simba Arati and Director of Elections Junet Mohamed said any arrangement with UDA must be anchored in a formal agreement, not goodwill. The party had already prepared its conditions, they said, and would negotiate from a position of political strength. Junet was the most direct. “ODM is not an NGO. It is a political party that has been formed to capture and exercise political power. That is why the party leader has said, what do we want? Power,” he declared. He acknowledged that Ruto had delivered development projects in ODM strongholds but was explicit that projects alone would not satisfy the party’s ambitions. “We will form the government together with UDA and we will negotiate with UDA. Nothing is for free. Our support for UDA must count for something and we must share power,” he said. Junet drew a sharp boundary around ODM’s traditional strongholds, identifying Nyanza, Western, Nairobi, North Eastern and the Coast as areas where the party would tolerate no interference from coalition partners. “We will defend those strongholds to death. And we will not spare anybody who comes to interfere with the strongholds of ODM,” he warned — a signal directed as much at smaller parties within the broad-based arrangement as at any external challenger. His framing of ODM’s position in government was equally pointed. “We are in a broad-based government by right, we are not vagrants. We did not go for a walk. We went to form a government with UDA,” he said, firmly rejecting any suggestion that the party’s presence at the table was a concession rather than a negotiated entitlement. The stakes of these negotiations are substantial. ODM controls significant voting blocs in regions that Kenya Kwanza did not carry convincingly in 2022. Nyanza in particular delivered heavily against Ruto in the last election. If ODM delivers those votes to the incumbent in 2027 — and delivers them actively rather than passively — the electoral arithmetic shifts meaningfully in Ruto’s favour in what is already shaping up as a fiercely competitive race. The complication for Ruto is that ODM’s demands are structural rather than transactional. The party is not asking for a single ministerial appointment or a targeted development fund. It is asking for a defined seat at the governing table — shared authority, clear roles and a political roadmap that commits UDA to genuine partnership. Whether UDA is prepared to offer terms on that scale, without compromising its own internal coalition dynamics, is the central question the two parties must resolve before the campaign season begins in earnest. There are pressures on both sides. Within ODM, divisions over the party’s political direction since Raila’s death have not fully settled. The leadership is pushing for a structured pre-election agreement, but not every faction is convinced that alignment with Ruto represents the right path. Managing that internal debate while simultaneously negotiating with UDA requires considerable political skill. For Ruto, the calculation is different but no less demanding. Absorbing ODM’s support without alienating existing Kenya Kwanza partners — many of whom regard ODM’s strongholds as territory to be contested, not conceded — is a balancing act that leaves little room for error. On 13 November, Ruto hosted leaders from both parties at State House, where they agreed to strengthen their structures and coordinate their political machinery, particularly in Nairobi. Yesterday’s meeting with Oburu continued that conversation at the highest level. But ODM’s public statements on Tuesday made plain that the talking phase has a deadline. Kenya’s 2027 election will not be won in August. It is being won or lost in rooms like these. title: Ruto hosts Western Kenya leaders at State House ahead of regional development tour
description: The president’s pre-visit briefing signals that Western Kenya is firmly on the 2027 electoral map — and the government wants its development record heard. By Jane Njeri President William Ruto met government officials, governors and Members of Parliament from Western Kenya at State House in Nairobi yesterday, ahead of a development tour of the region scheduled for later this week. The meeting covered progress in agriculture, infrastructure and industrial investment across Busia, Kakamega, Vihiga and Bungoma counties. Ruto pointed to reforms in the sugar sector as a tangible marker of delivery, saying revived public factories had improved both farmer incomes and worker pay. “Farmers are producing more and earning more while workers are paid every month,” he said. The government also highlighted ongoing investment in roads, affordable housing, healthcare, industrial parks and an economic processing zone — a package framed as evidence of transformation rather than promise. The visit comes as Western Kenya assumes growing significance in Kenya’s pre-election calculations. With ODM negotiating its terms for supporting Ruto’s re-election bid and opposition formations actively courting the region’s vote, the president’s tour carries clear political weight alongside its development optics. Delivery, not dialogue, will determine which argument lands. title: Maraga and Karua back single opposition candidate as 2027 race sharpens
description: Senior opposition figures insist unity is achievable — but cracks are already visible over who should carry the ticket. By Grace Wanja Former Chief Justice David Maraga and People’s Liberation Party leader Martha Karua yesterday declared their commitment to fielding a single presidential candidate against President William Ruto in the 2027 general election, while their host Caleb Amisi openly backed Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna for the opposition ticket — exposing the fault lines the two leaders were trying to paper over. Speaking at a gathering hosted by People’s Renaissance Movement leader Amisi in Kitale, Trans Nzoia County, Maraga and Karua sought to reassure supporters that the opposition would settle its differences and present a united front ahead of the August 2027 polls. Both leaders accused the Kenya Kwanza administration of presiding over declining governance standards and deepening corruption, framing the election as a battle between an exhausted public and an administration they argue has failed to deliver. “Kenyans are tired, and if we want to remove Kasongo we must field one candidate — we will not fight each other, we must agree so the work gets done,” Karua said, using the opposition’s coded reference for Ruto. Her message was clear: personal ambition must yield to collective purpose, or the opposition risks handing Ruto a second term by default. Maraga was equally direct about what is at stake. “Next year’s vote is between the people and Kasongo. Do not worry — we will agree,” he said, before delivering a stark warning about the consequences of another five years under the current administration. “If Kasongo comes back there will be no Kenya, no country. Kenya will end as a country. I will finish corruption so we can have medicine in our hospitals,” he declared — a remark that blended genuine alarm about governance with an unmistakable personal pitch. Karua, who has built her political identity around anti-corruption advocacy, did not shy from staking her own claim even as she preached consensus. “Kenya is in this mess because of corruption. The person to clean it up is not someone else — it is Mama Martha Karua,” she said, leaving little ambiguity about her own presidential ambitions. That both she and Maraga called for unity while simultaneously positioning themselves as the natural flagbearer captures the central paradox of opposition politics in Kenya at this moment: everyone agrees a single candidate is necessary, but agreement on who that candidate should be remains elusive. The unity message was further complicated by Amisi himself. The People’s Renaissance Movement leader broke ranks with the evening’s dominant theme, openly endorsing Linda Mwananchi Movement leader Edwin Sifuna for the presidential ticket. “We want Edwin Sifuna to be given the ticket — and we as PM must also be at that decision-making table, or we will break the table,” Amisi warned, signalling that smaller parties within the opposition coalition intend to be active participants in the selection process, not passive bystanders. His remarks illustrated the structural challenge facing the opposition as it heads into the most consequential phase of its pre-election planning. The coalition is not short of presidential material — it is short of a mechanism for choosing between it. Without a credible, agreed process for settling on a flagbearer, the calls for unity risk remaining precisely that: calls, rather than commitments. Ruto, watching from State House, will have noted the evening’s contradictions with interest. Nine months from polling day, the opposition’s arithmetic remains dangerously unsettled.
