title: TSC stands firm on Ayabei appointment as Gachagua’s tribalism claims are rejected
description: The commission says 27 years of institutional experience made Cheptumo Ayabei the best candidate — but the row has exposed the raw nerves of Kenya’s pre-election politics. By Jane Njeri The Teachers Service Commission yesterday rejected former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s allegations that the appointment of Cheptumo Ayabei as its new Secretary and Chief Executive Officer was driven by ethnic considerations, defending the selection as the outcome of a transparent, competitive and legally compliant recruitment process. TSC Chairman Dr Jamleck Muturi John confirmed in a statement dated 17 November 2026 that Ayabei emerged as the best candidate among five shortlisted applicants interviewed on 16 November 2026, following a recruitment exercise that attracted 124 applicants. The commission published the names of all applicants and shortlisted candidates in newspapers and on its official website, Muturi said, in line with its commitment to transparency and accountability. “We are mandated to recruit the CEO of TSC. We follow procedures. On July 1, 2025, the seat fell vacant. We commenced the process in May 2025 and advertised the position on social media, newspapers and our website,” Muturi explained. He added that the process was briefly interrupted by a court-issued restraining order, before resuming on 28 September 2026 following a judicial instruction to proceed. Five candidates were shortlisted from over 140 applicants, with interviews conducted on 16 November 2026. “Cheptumo was the best and was appointed CEO. He had a sterling career at TSC, where he joined as a finance officer before rising to Director of Finance and Accounts,” the commission stated. Ayabei brings more than 27 years of experience at TSC, having joined the institution in 1999. He is also notable as the first person with a disability to head the commission, and hails from Baringo County. Gachagua’s response was swift and scathing. The DCP leader claimed on social media that “TSC gave the job to a number-four candidate who scored less than 70 per cent,” framing the appointment as the latest evidence of what he describes as a systematic pattern of ethnic favouritism under President William Ruto’s administration. He linked Ayabei’s appointment to two other recent selections — Ronoh Kibet as KenGen Managing Director and Lydia Sitienei Chelagat’s nomination as Data Commissioner — all involving individuals from the Kalenjin community, arguing that the cumulative picture undermines Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa” equality campaign. Opposition figures and members of the public questioned whether Ayabei was the most deserving candidate and alleged possible political influence by President Ruto — claims the TSC has rejected as unfounded. The commission did not directly address Gachagua’s specific claim about scores, but maintained that its interview and selection process followed established legal and procedural requirements under the Constitution and the Teachers Service Commission Act, 2012. The row is about more than a single appointment. It is the latest episode in a deepening political contest over the distribution of public service positions ahead of the August 2027 general election — a contest in which every senior appointment is being read through an ethnic and political lens by an electorate primed to scrutinise the composition of the state. Ruto’s “Usawa ni Sawa, Mbele Pamoja” — equality is fair, forward together — is the president’s rebranded campaign message for 2027, a deliberate pivot from the bottom-up “hustler nation” narrative of 2022. Gachagua has accused Ruto of using the slogan to deflect criticism over uneven development and alleged disparities in public appointments, saying bluntly: “To start with, Ruto cannot tell anybody about Usawa. He’s a con. He’s deceptive.” The TSC, for its part, is an institution that manages the employment, compensation and discipline of Kenya’s more than 350,000 public school teachers — arguably the largest single professional workforce in the country. Its CEO wields significant institutional influence. That the appointment has become a flashpoint in the ethnic arithmetic of pre-election politics says as much about the temperature of Kenya’s current political environment as it does about the specific merits of the recruitment process. In a pointed response on social media, presidential digital advisor Dennis Itumbi framed the appointment as proof that Ruto is “practically implementing Usawa ni Sawa,” citing Ayabei’s selection as evidence of merit-based recruitment across communities. That the government felt compelled to respond through its own digital machinery underscores how politically loaded the moment has become. Ayabei himself has been largely silent publicly. His record speaks through the institution — he first applied for the TSC CEO position in 2015, was shortlisted among four candidates and lost to Nancy Macharia. He did not give up, and a decade later, the job is his. Whether that story of persistence and institutional loyalty is enough to settle the political noise is another matter entirely. In Kenya’s current climate, no appointment arrives without a political price tag attached. title: Economics: The key to a better future
description: By: Shonazarov Shohjaxon Economics plays a significant role in our daily lives and the development of every country. It is the study of how individuals, businesses, and governments use limited resources to meet people’s needs and wants. Economics is not only about money; it is also about improving living standards and creating opportunities for future generations. One of the main goals of economic development is to improve people’s quality of life. When a country’s economy grows, businesses expand, new jobs are created, and people’s incomes increase. For example, when governments invest in education, healthcare, technology, and infrastructure, society becomes more developed and productive. Another important factor is international trade. Countries exchange goods and services to develop their economies and build strong relationships. This allows businesses to reach new markets, attract foreign investment, and create more employment opportunities. Moreover, modern technology helps companies produce products more efficiently and reduce production costs. However, economic growth also brings certain challenges. Inflation, unemployment, poverty, and income inequality are serious problems that many countries face today. Governments must develop effective economic policies to control inflation, support small businesses, and provide equal opportunities for citizens. A balanced economy should create wealth while ensuring that its benefits reach different groups of society. In addition, sustainable economic development is becoming increasingly important. Countries should use natural resources responsibly, protect the environment, and invest in renewable energy. Economic progress should not destroy the environment for future generations. In conclusion, economics is the foundation of a strong and successful society. A healthy economy creates opportunities, reduces poverty, and improves people’s lives. True economic success is not measured only by money, but also by people’s happiness, well-being, and quality of life. title: Rodri delivers brutal Champions League reality check: ‘Our chances of winning are zero’
description: Manchester City midfielder Rodri warns Barcelona they are nowhere near UEFA Champions League contenders and must raise their level significantly before dreaming of European glory By Pascal Okoth Rodri has delivered a strikingly candid assessment of Barcelona’s chances of winning the UEFA Champions League, insisting the club’s current level falls well short of what is required to be considered genuine contenders for European football’s most coveted prize. The Spain international made no attempt to soften his words. “Our chances of winning the Champions League are zero,” he said, in comments that have since reverberated across European football. It was a remarkable statement — not because it came from an opponent, but because it reflected the kind of honest self-appraisal that is rarely heard from within a dressing room carrying the weight of expectation that surrounds Barcelona. Rodri’s assessment cuts to the heart of a tension that has followed the Catalan club throughout the season. Despite the considerable excitement around their performances in certain matches, he believes there remains a significant gap between where Barcelona are and where they need to be when the Champions League enters its most demanding phase. “We need to raise our level and maintain it over time, so that by March and April, we have real chances of competing for titles,” he said. “And then we’ll have to raise it even further if we want to win everything.” Those months — March and April — are where Champions League campaigns are truly decided. The knockout rounds separate the genuinely elite from the merely talented, demanding consistency, tactical discipline, mental strength and the ability to perform under sustained pressure. Rodri’s point is clear: promising performances in November count for little if they cannot be replicated when the stakes are highest. He also challenged the very idea of discussing favourites before trophies have actually been delivered. “There’s no point talking about whether we’re favourites or not,” he said. “For me, until we win those titles, especially the Champions League, we cannot consider ourselves favourites.” It is a position grounded in results rather than reputation — and one that implicitly acknowledges the distance between Barcelona’s historical standing and their current European reality. That reality is worth examining. Barcelona last lifted the Champions League trophy in 2015, when they defeated Juventus 3–1 in the final in Berlin under Luis Enrique. In the eleven years since, their European campaigns have been defined more by painful eliminations than deep runs. The 4–0 collapse against Paris Saint-Germain in 2017, the astonishing 4–0 reverse at Liverpool in 2019 and a bruising 8–2 defeat to Bayern Munich in 2020 all left lasting marks on the club’s continental reputation. More recent campaigns have brought improvement in patches, but not the sustained excellence that Champions League success demands. Rodri’s comments, then, are not merely a talking point — they are a diagnosis. Barcelona, he suggests, must address their defensive vulnerabilities, sharpen their decision-making in key moments and develop the collective resilience that separates clubs who dream of winning the Champions League from those who actually do. There is no shortage of quality within the squad. Players of genuine international calibre populate the roster, and the club’s financial recovery has allowed significant investment in recent years. But individual talent and institutional prestige, as Rodri rightly notes, do not automatically translate into European success. The Champions League is littered with examples of star-laden squads that fell short when it mattered most. What Barcelona require, in his view, is a sustained elevation of their collective standards — not a single impressive performance or a run of three or four victories, but a consistent, identifiable level of output maintained across months of competition. For the club’s supporters, Rodri’s words will sting. Barcelona’s fans have waited more than a decade to see their team reclaim European football’s ultimate prize, and patience has worn thin through years of near-misses and embarrassments. But there is also something refreshing in the candour. It strips away the noise of expectation and forces an honest conversation about where this squad genuinely stands. The coming months will provide the clearest answer yet. Barcelona’s performance between now and the end of the season will determine whether Rodri’s assessment proves prophetic — or whether the club finds the consistency and character to prove him wrong. For now, his message is unambiguous: reputation is not enough. The Champions League must be earned. title: Sex before marriage: Have we abandoned our values in the name of modernity?
description: A generation navigating sexual freedom without moral anchors risks confusing liberation with the quiet erosion of values that once held communities together By Jackline Kathure There was a time when sex was sacred, intimacy belonged to marriage, and abstinence was respected rather than ridiculed. That time feels distant now — and the distance deserves honest examination. Traditional African societies understood sex as carrying cultural, moral and social weight beyond physical pleasure. Marriage provided its proper foundation. Discipline and responsibility were public expectations, not private eccentricities. That framework had real failures — forced marriages, silenced abuse, gender inequality — but its emphasis on commitment and boundaries served a purpose worth remembering. Today’s reality looks markedly different. Universities are grappling with rising rates of unintended pregnancies, sexually transmitted infections and the emotional wreckage of relationships built on pressure rather than affection. Reproductive health services are increasingly visible across student neighbourhoods — necessary, but symptomatic of deeper questions going unasked about prevention, education and personal responsibility. Most troubling is the creeping belief that sex is compulsory proof of love. Some young people face partners who present physical intimacy as the ultimate test of commitment. But genuine love accommodates boundaries, patience and personal conviction. If someone makes sex a condition for staying, the real question is whether they value you — or simply what they can take from you. Abstinence, meanwhile, is increasingly mocked. That is not progress — it is simply pressure wearing a modern mask. This conversation must never become a vehicle for shaming those who have made different choices. Dignity belongs to everyone. Freedom without responsibility is not liberation. It is a different kind of trap. title: Kenya warns against using children to solicit donations in online fundraisers
description: The State Department for Children Services cautions organisations and individuals that exposing minors in digital fundraising campaigns risks exploitation, abuse and irreversible harm to their dignity By Yvonne Wambui Kenya’s State Department for Children Services has issued a stern warning to organisations and individuals against using children’s photographs, videos and personal stories to solicit donations through online fundraising campaigns, citing serious concerns over the protection of children’s rights, privacy and dignity. The warning comes as social media platforms become an increasingly popular vehicle for raising money on behalf of vulnerable children and families facing financial hardship. Many Kenyans have turned to online fundraising to seek assistance with medical bills, school fees, food and other basic needs — a trend that, while driven by genuine goodwill, has raised uncomfortable questions about how children are being portrayed in the process. The department cautioned that exposing minors to public scrutiny in the name of financial assistance could leave them vulnerable to exploitation, abuse and other forms of harm. The Principal Secretary for Children Services urged organisations, well-wishers and individuals to find responsible ways of supporting children in need without placing their private lives on public display. At the centre of the concern are fundraising campaigns that rely on emotionally charged photographs, videos and personal accounts of children’s suffering to attract sympathy and encourage public contributions. Though such campaigns may succeed in raising significant funds, the exposure carries consequences that can outlast the financial benefit. Images and personal details shared online do not simply disappear once a fundraising target has been met — they can remain accessible indefinitely, beyond the control of the families or organisations that originally posted them. Children are particularly vulnerable in this regard. They may not fully appreciate the long-term implications of having their photographs and personal struggles circulated on social media, nor are they in a position to give meaningful, informed consent to such exposure. The department stressed that children should not be treated as instruments for attracting public sympathy or generating financial contributions. Their welfare, safety and best interests must remain the overriding priority in every charitable activity. The warning also reflects the broader challenge of protecting children’s rights in a digital environment where information travels instantly and widely. Once a photograph or personal detail is uploaded, controlling its distribution becomes virtually impossible, increasing the risk of misuse by those with harmful intentions. Charitable organisations have been called upon to adopt ethical fundraising practices that safeguard the identities and personal information of minors. The department encouraged organisations to explore alternative approaches to communicating the needs of vulnerable children — approaches that convey urgency and generate support without unnecessarily exposing private lives to public consumption. The issue equally raises important questions about the responsibilities of parents, guardians and institutions when sharing children’s information online. Good intentions, the government maintains, do not justify practices that compromise children’s fundamental rights. The desire to secure financial assistance, however sincere, cannot override a child’s right to dignity and protection. Online fundraising has undeniably become a lifeline for many struggling Kenyan families, particularly those confronting costly medical treatments or urgent school-related needs. The government does not dispute its value. What it insists upon is that such assistance be delivered in a manner consistent with the rights and dignity of the children it is intended to help. As digital fundraising continues to grow in popularity across Kenya, the message from government is unequivocal: supporting vulnerable children and protecting them are not competing obligations — they are one and the same. title: Kenyans still pay the same for diesel even as global prices fall 6.1%
description: Kenya’s diesel import costs rose 6.7% in October despite a drop in world prices, with KCh 4.6B in government support preventing a pump-price increase — but analysts warn the relief may be temporary By Grace Wanja Kenya’s diesel pump price has held steady despite a 6.1% fall in global oil prices, with the government deploying KSh 4.6 billion from the Petroleum Development Levy Fund to absorb a sharp rise in the country’s actual import costs — a measure that has spared motorists and commuters an immediate price shock but raised serious questions about how long the cushion can hold. Analysis by EBC Financial Group reveals the apparent contradiction sitting at the heart of Kenya’s fuel pricing: while the world price of diesel fell in October, the landed cost — what Kenya actually paid to bring diesel into the country — rose 6.7%, climbing from USD 1,065.38 to USD 1,137.09 per cubic metre. The gap between global market movements and what Kenyan consumers eventually pay at the pump is not accidental. It is the product of cargo timing, shipping costs, insurance charges and the averaging methodology used by the Energy and Petroleum Regulatory Authority, which bases its pump-price calculations on cargoes unloaded at Mombasa port up to the ninth of each month. Diesel bought weeks earlier at higher prices therefore continues to shape what consumers pay long after international markets have moved on. David Precious, Senior Market Analyst at EBC Financial Group, explained the disconnect plainly. “A fall in the world price does not mean Kenya’s diesel costs fall at the same time,” he said. “Kenya pays for the diesel that actually arrives, and that diesel was bought earlier. Cargo timing, shipping and insurance can all widen the gap between the world price and what Kenya pays.” The exchange rate contributed little to the October increase. The Kenyan shilling depreciated by just 0.2% against the dollar during the period, moving from KSh 129.91 to KSh 130.17, ruling out currency movement as a meaningful factor in the rising import bill. The global supply picture adds further complexity. The International Energy Agency reported on 13 November that overall oil supply is recovering and expected to exceed demand in the fourth quarter. Diesel, however, occupies a different position within that market. European diesel prices fell 11% from their early-October peak but remain 77% above pre-war levels, and the IEA has indicated that diesel could remain in short supply into 2027. A broad recovery in crude oil production does not automatically translate into cheaper refined diesel for importing nations such as Kenya. To prevent the rising import cost from reaching drivers and passengers, EPRA kept the maximum pump price unchanged at KSh 227.76 per litre in Nairobi until 14 December, drawing on the Petroleum Development Levy Fund to cover a potential increase of KSh 10.54 per litre. The fund, built from a levy of approximately KSh 5.40 on every litre of petrol and diesel sold, collects around KSh 2.4 billion monthly. This month’s deployment of KSh 4.6 billion — nearly double the fund’s regular monthly intake — signals the scale of intervention required to hold the line. Treasury Cabinet Secretary John Mbadi had indicated in early November that the fund was withheld in October in anticipation of rising European energy demand as the continent entered winter. Its deployment this month has provided immediate relief, but the arithmetic of that decision carries its own risks. A fund collecting KSh 2.4 billion a month cannot sustain KSh 4.6 billion monthly disbursements indefinitely without additional support or a reduction in import costs. A second layer of relief comes through tax policy. The Tax Laws Amendment Act 2026, signed into law on 16 October, maintains value added tax on fuel at 8% rather than the standard 16%, for a 90-day period from 14 October, with the possibility of a further 90-day extension. The Central Bank of Kenya acknowledged at its October meeting that these combined interventions were easing inflationary pressure across the economy. That pressure remains significant. Annual inflation rose to 7.3% in October from 6.8% in September, sitting just below the CBK’s upper threshold of 7.5%. Over the past year, diesel prices have risen 32.5%, transport costs 17.1% and food prices 10.2% — a chain of increases that has already reshaped household budgets across the country. In May, a single EPRA review pushed diesel up KSh 46.29 per litre to KSh 242.92 in Nairobi, prompting matatu owners to announce a 50% fare increase that illustrated precisely how rapidly fuel costs ripple outward into the daily lives of ordinary Kenyans. The timing of the next decisions makes December a particularly consequential month. The CBK’s Monetary Policy Committee meets on 9 December, five days before EPRA’s current pricing period expires and a new import cost assessment takes effect. The CBK will therefore set its interest rate position without knowing whether the diesel import costs driving inflationary pressure are easing or continuing to climb. Precious offered a measured but pointed warning. “Holding the pump price steady has a cost of its own: KSh 4.6 billion this month, against the roughly KSh 2.4 billion a month that the fund is reported to collect,” he said. “If support at this scale continues, the fund may need topping up. And if import costs stay high while support is reduced, the pump price may rise in one larger step instead of gradually.” For Kenyans, the relief at the pump is real but conditional. Diesel moves the lorries carrying food to market and the matatus carrying workers to their jobs. Keeping its price stable matters enormously. What matters equally is whether the government can sustain that stability — or whether December’s review will deliver in a single announcement the increase that October and November managed to avoid. title: Greenland Girls School shows Kenya how to rescue young mothers from the education crisis
description: One school’s decision to combine childcare with classroom learning offers a transformative model for how Kenya can turn its teenage pregnancy crisis into an opportunity for intergenerational change By Ashford Kimani Greenland Girls School tells a story that is equal parts inspiring and unsettling — inspiring because it proves what becomes possible when an education system chooses compassion over exclusion, and unsettling because it lays bare how many young girls are still falling through the cracks of a system that, in theory, exists to protect them. Teenage pregnancy remains one of the most persistent disruptors of girls’ education in Kenya. Thousands of girls are pushed out of school every year — not always because policy demands it, but because society quietly enforces it. Shame, stigma, poverty and the absence of support converge to make returning to school feel impossible. The result is a silent crisis: young mothers whose academic journeys end abruptly and whose futures are permanently altered before they have had a fair chance to begin. What makes Greenland remarkable is its refusal to accept that outcome as inevitable. The school reimagines education in a way that acknowledges reality rather than denying it. By allowing young mothers to continue learning while providing childcare within the school environment, it removes the single greatest barrier to re-entry: who looks after the child while the mother is in class. That question, so simple to articulate and so devastating when left unanswered, has ended the educational dreams of countless girls across Kenya. This is not merely an administrative adjustment — it is a philosophical shift. Conventional schooling models are rigid by design, expecting learners to conform to pre-existing structures regardless of their circumstances. Greenland inverts that logic entirely. It reshapes the structure to fit the learner, and in doing so, restores dignity to girls who have too long been defined by misfortune rather than potential. The impact extends well beyond the individual. When a teenage mother is given a genuine second chance at education, she regains agency over her own life. She becomes economically empowered. She alters the trajectory of her child’s future. Education, in this context, is not merely personal advancement — it is intergenerational intervention, breaking cycles that would otherwise repeat themselves across decades. Yet the existence of such a school also raises uncomfortable questions. Why should this model be the exception rather than the rule? Kenya already has a re-entry policy allowing girls to return to school after giving birth. On paper, the policy is progressive. In practice, it is inconsistently implemented and routinely undermined by entrenched cultural attitudes that no policy document has yet managed to shift. Many schools remain ill-equipped or simply unwilling to accommodate teenage mothers. There are no childcare facilities, no counselling systems and often no institutional willingness to try. Even where doors are technically open, the environment can be quietly hostile. A young mother may face ridicule from peers, judgement from teachers and sustained pressure from her community to abandon her education altogether. Technically re-enrolled but practically unsupported, she is set up to fail a second time. This is where the deeper lesson of Greenland lies. Creating a safe space matters, but it is not sufficient on its own. What these learners need is an enabling ecosystem — academic instruction alongside psychosocial support, mentorship and practical life skills. They need an environment that consistently communicates a message too rarely delivered: motherhood does not cancel potential. For educators and school leaders, this presents both a challenge and an opportunity. The challenge is an honest reckoning with institutional bias. It is easy to invoke discipline and moral standards; it is considerably harder to practise restorative education. The opportunity, however, is genuinely transformative. Schools that adopt more inclusive approaches do not lower their standards — they expand their definition of who deserves the chance to meet them. Discipline should never be confused with exclusion. The purpose of education is not to filter out those who stumble but to guide them back onto the path. Teenage mothers are not disruptions to the system. They are evidence that the system must evolve. The broader societal dimension cannot be ignored either. Preventing teenage pregnancy must remain a priority, requiring comprehensive sexuality education, meaningful community engagement and stronger protection against gender-based violence. Prevention and support, however, must advance together. Focusing on one while neglecting the other produces an incomplete and ultimately inadequate response. The Greenland model offers a clear way forward. It demonstrates that with intentional design, genuine empathy and institutional commitment, a point of crisis can become a point of recovery. It challenges policymakers to move beyond declarations and invest in the structures that make re-entry not merely permissible but genuinely feasible. The true measure of an education system is not how well it serves the privileged. It is how effectively it rescues the vulnerable. Greenland Girls School has chosen, quietly and deliberately, to be measured by that standard. title: Alcoholism among Kenyan youths: A growing social and public health crisis
description: With over a million young Kenyans trapped in alcohol dependency, the country faces a generational emergency that unemployment, illicit brews and silence are quietly making worse By Charles Waruingi Over one million Kenyans aged 18 to 35 are struggling with alcoholism, with Central and Western regions bearing the heaviest burden. The scale of the crisis demands more than concern — it demands action. Unemployment is the most powerful accelerant. Young people who cannot find work despite completing their education face prolonged frustration and idleness. Alcohol becomes an escape. Cheap illicit brews — particularly chang’aa — deepen the trap. Unregulated, often laced with toxic substances and priced within reach of the poorest, these drinks are destroying lives in low-income communities across the country. Peer pressure and popular culture have normalised what should alarm us. Music, celebrity culture and social media increasingly portray excessive drinking as glamorous. For impressionable young people already searching for belonging, the message lands hard. Untreated mental health struggles complete the cycle. Depression, anxiety and trauma push young people toward alcohol as self-medication. But alcohol does not heal — it compounds. Dependency deepens. The original wound remains. The consequences reach far beyond individual drinkers. Families fracture. Children are neglected. Productivity collapses. Contaminated brews cause blindness, organ failure and death. Road accidents and violence claim lives that could have been saved. Reversing this requires three urgent responses: strict enforcement against illegal brewing and irresponsible alcohol advertising; accessible, affordable rehabilitation and mental health services in every county; and meaningful youth employment through vocational training, entrepreneurship and internship programmes. Kenya cannot afford to lose this generation to a preventable crisis. The bottle should never be the only door left open. title: Martha Karua backs book exposing Kenya’s constitutional gap as 2027 elections loom
description: Senior politician Martha Karua endorses Marilyn Muthoni Kamuru’s new book “Unconstitutional,” reigniting debate over Kenya’s unmet constitutional promises ahead of a defining election year By James Mwangi Martha Karua attended the launch of Marilyn Muthoni Kamuru’s new book, Unconstitutional, on Tuesday, lending her political weight to a publication that challenges Kenya’s failure to fully implement its 2010 Constitution. Karua, one of Kenya’s most prominent voices on constitutional governance and the rule of law, described the launch as an important moment for national reflection. “We gave ourselves a progressive Constitution in 2010, yet so many of its promises remain works in progress,” she said. “From accountability and access to justice to the two-thirds gender principle, there is still a considerable gap between what we agreed as a country and what we actually practise.” The timing is charged. With Kenya’s August 2027 General Election drawing nearer, questions about constitutional fidelity, institutional accountability and gender representation are moving from academic debate into live political contest. The two-thirds gender rule — never implemented despite a 2010 constitutional deadline — remains one of the most visible symbols of that gap between promise and practice. Kamuru’s book arrives as opposition formations sharpen their governance critiques and voters begin measuring incumbents against constitutional benchmarks. “Well done, Marilyn, for keeping these important conversations alive,” Karua added. Some conversations refuse to wait. The post Martha Karua backs book exposing Kenya’s constitutional gap as 2027 elections loom appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Sifuna’s sisters rally at LMHQ as Linda Mwananchi Movement builds its 2027 momentum
description: A family show of solidarity at movement headquarters signals the personal bonds driving Kenya’s most watched emerging political force ahead of next year’s elections By James Mwangi Edwin Sifuna’s sisters visited the Linda Mwananchi Movement headquarters yesterday, in a show of personal solidarity that the Nairobi Senator said he would never take for granted. Sifuna acknowledged the visit publicly, expressing heartfelt gratitude to his sisters for their commitment to the movement he leads. “I see your efforts, deeply appreciate your commitment and will never take your love and support for granted,” he said. The visit, modest in form but pointed in timing, comes as the Linda Mwananchi Movement accelerates its national expansion ahead of Kenya’s August 2027 General Election. With county offices being established across all 47 counties, a diaspora tour underway in the United States and high-profile political figures joining its ranks, the movement is methodically converting grassroots energy into organised political infrastructure. Family solidarity has long carried symbolic weight in Kenyan politics, where personal networks and community trust frequently determine electoral outcomes. Sifuna’s public acknowledgement of his sisters’ support reflects a deliberate effort to humanise a movement that has otherwise trained its messaging on constitutional accountability, democratic governance and youth empowerment. As Kenya’s political temperature rises ahead of 2027, even the smallest gestures are being read for meaning. author: the mt kenya times
title: Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement expands its influence
description: With county offices, diaspora outreach and high-profile recruits, Nairobi Senator Edwin Sifuna is building a national political machine with 2027 firmly in its sights By Job Mwavuwa Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement is rapidly positioning itself as a serious political force, intensifying grassroots mobilisation across Kenya’s 47 counties as the 2027 General Election draws closer. The movement, rebranded from The Equitable Party, centres its identity on constitutionalism, accountability and people-driven governance. Since its launch on 30 October, it has moved swiftly to convert ambition into structure — announcing county offices, recruiting members and claiming representation in 38 counties. Its roster of allies is growing in stature. Former Meru Governor Kawira Mwangaza, Vihiga Senator Godfrey Osotsi, Mavoko MP Patrick Makau and former Law Society of Kenya President Faith Odhiambo have all associated with the movement, lending it cross-regional credibility. Engagements with opposition figures Rigathi Gachagua and Kalonzo Musyoka have attracted attention, though no formal alliances have been announced. The movement is also looking beyond Kenya’s borders. A diaspora tour running from 21 November to 7 December will take Sifuna through New Jersey, Pennsylvania, Maryland, Washington DC, Texas, Seattle and California, with town hall meetings and community engagements planned throughout. Diaspora support — financial and political — could prove significant heading into a contested election cycle. Sifuna has placed youth squarely at the movement’s centre. During a November engagement in Laikipia, he warned young Kenyans against backing President William Ruto’s re-election, arguing it would foreclose their own path to leadership. The movement is no longer just noise. It is building walls. The post Edwin Sifuna’s Linda Mwananchi Movement expands its influence appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

author: the mt kenya times
title: Challenges university students are facing
description: Kenya’s campus generation is battling poverty, mental health crises and a jobless horizon — and silence is not helping anyone By Kelvin Simiyu Kenya’s university students are struggling — and the pressure is mounting from every direction. Fees remain the heaviest burden. Many students come from families that cannot cover tuition, accommodation and food simultaneously. The Higher Education Loans Board offers a lifeline, but disbursements arrive late and rarely stretch far enough. Students who should be focused on learning are instead consumed by financial anxiety. The emotional toll compounds the financial one. Far from home, under relentless academic pressure and navigating unfamiliar social environments, many students battle loneliness, depression and stress in silence. Without accessible counselling, some turn to alcohol, drugs or destructive peer groups simply to cope. Infrastructure gaps widen the disadvantage. Unreliable internet access and scarce laptops lock out students from digital learning at a time when education increasingly depends on connectivity. Then comes graduation — and the grim arithmetic of a job market that cannot absorb thousands of new graduates annually. Many leave campus qualified but unemployed, their sacrifices yielding uncertainty rather than opportunity. The solutions exist: expanded scholarships, reliable HELB disbursements, affordable hostels, robust counselling services and genuine private-sector investment in youth employment. A student who succeeds does not succeed alone. Neither does one who fails. The post Challenges university students are facing appeared first on The Mt Kenya Times.

title: Sifuna calls Ruto’s State of the Nation a ‘state of imagination’
description: Linda Mwananchi Movement leader Edwin Sifuna boycotts President Ruto’s fourth parliamentary address, accusing him of substituting constitutional obligations for a development catalogue while human rights abuses go unanswered By John Kamau Edwin Sifuna, leader of the Linda Mwananchi Movement and Nairobi Senator, has dismissed President William Ruto’s fourth State of the Nation Address as a “State of Imagination,” accusing the President of violating the constitutional purpose of the annual parliamentary report by substituting genuine governance accountability with a showcase of roads, markets and infrastructure projects. Sifuna, who said he has boycotted the annual address since his election to the Senate, delivered his critique on Wednesday as Ruto spoke before a joint sitting of the National Assembly and the Senate — a platform the opposition leader described as one the President uses to make inflated claims while sidestepping the most pressing questions of democratic governance. With barely eight months remaining before Kenya’s 10 August 2027 General Election, the exchange illustrated with unusual clarity the fault lines along which the coming campaign will be fought. At the heart of Sifuna’s objection is a constitutional argument. Article 132(1)(c) of the Constitution requires the President to report annually to Parliament on the steps taken and progress achieved in realising the national values and principles of governance enshrined in Article 10 — values that include the rule of law, human rights, democracy, equality, human dignity, social justice and public participation. It is a precise and demanding obligation, and one that Sifuna argues Ruto has consistently failed to meet. “The Constitution of Kenya, in Article 132, states that when the President comes to Parliament, he does only two things. You have to tell the country steps taken and progress achieved in the realisation of the values under Article 10,” Sifuna said. “You tell us what steps you have taken as a government to ensure there is respect for human rights, that there is the rule of law, and that there is democracy in this country, as well as what progress has been achieved.” The distinction he draws is not merely procedural. It reflects a fundamentally different understanding of what presidential accountability should look like. For Ruto, Wednesday’s address was an opportunity to present his Bottom-Up Economic Transformation Agenda in its most favourable light — improved exchange rates, reduced inflation, lower commercial lending rates, expanded foreign exchange reserves, 23,000 new classrooms, 100,000 teachers recruited and a northern highway corridor stretching 750 kilometres from Isiolo to Mandera. For Sifuna, none of that answers the question the Constitution actually asks. “You know the values under Article 10: human rights, the rule of law, equality, freedom of citizens and public participation. We are talking about sustainable development — you don’t tell us about roads,” he said, in remarks that distilled the opposition’s broader critique of an administration it accuses of prioritising visible hardware over invisible but essential democratic software. The reference to Albert Ojwang gave Sifuna’s argument its most human and politically charged dimension. Ojwang, a teacher and blogger from Homa Bay, died in police custody in June 2025 — one of hundreds of Kenyans whose deaths in circumstances involving security forces have remained incompletely investigated and sparsely prosecuted. Sifuna invoked Ojwang directly, arguing that the President’s pride in building a market in Homa Bay rang hollow against the unresolved question of accountability for a constituent who died in state custody. “He will go there to tell you, ‘Oh, we built a market over there in Homa Bay,’ while forgetting he killed Albert Ojwang from Homa Bay,” Sifuna said. The Independent Policing Oversight Authority has documented 127 deaths across three major protest periods since 2024. Missing Voices, a rights monitoring alliance, recorded 24 police-related killings in May 2026 alone. Ruto, in his address, acknowledged these events, pledged KSh 2 billion in compensation and called for continued investigations and prosecutions. Critics, including Sifuna, argue that acknowledgement without sustained prosecutorial consequence is insufficient — and that the State of the Nation address is precisely the moment to account for it in constitutional terms. Sifuna used the occasion to offer what amounted to a campaign preview, outlining what he described as his governance priorities should he assume the presidency after August 2027. The pitch was deliberately framed in constitutional language. “When we take the helm next year, when I go to Parliament as the President of this nation, my job will be to explain the steps our government has chosen or taken to ensure there is respect for human rights, there is democracy in our country, there is freedom for citizens and there is the rule of law,” he said. It is a carefully constructed contrast — positioning himself not against specific policies but against what he characterises as a fundamental misunderstanding of presidential responsibility. Whether that contrast resonates with voters whose immediate concerns centre on the cost of maize flour, school fees and matatu fares remains the central political question his movement must answer. The Linda Mwananchi Movement has been accelerating its national infrastructure over recent weeks, establishing county offices across all 47 counties, attracting defecting legislators and embarking on a diaspora tour of the United States. Its political argument is sharpening in parallel: that Kenya’s crisis is not merely economic but constitutional, rooted in an executive that has forgotten what the law actually requires of it. Ruto’s camp will contest that framing vigorously. The President’s address cited tangible improvements across multiple sectors, and his political strategists will argue that voters judge governments on what they can see and touch — classrooms, roads, hospital registrations — rather than on the precise interpretation of Article 132. That argument has carried incumbents through difficult elections before. But with eight months remaining and a cost-of-living crisis that has not fully abated, neither side can afford complacency. title: Ruto’s State of the Nation: Billions promised
description: President William Ruto used his fourth address to Parliament to announce KSh 61.8B in debt settlements, healthcare gains and a major northern road — while firing an unmistakable political shot at Rigathi Gachagua ahead of 2027 By David Kimani President William Ruto delivered his fourth State of the Nation Address to Parliament on Wednesday, announcing the settlement of KSh 61.8 billion in long-outstanding government obligations, pledging police accountability reforms and issuing a pointed, if unnamed, rebuke of former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua’s campaign to consolidate the Mt Kenya region behind his Democracy for the Citizens Party ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election. The address, delivered to a joint sitting of the National Assembly and the Senate in Nairobi, covered ground ranging from university and hospital debts to highway expansion, healthcare registration and examination integrity — but it was the political undercurrent that gave the speech its sharpest edge. With Kenya’s electoral clock ticking toward August 2027, Ruto used the constitutional platform of Parliament to frame the coming contest on his terms: a debate about policy, delivery and evidence, not personality and regional loyalty. “No community should be reduced to a voting bloc. No region should be asked to surrender its judgement to a personality,” he told lawmakers, in remarks whose target, while unnamed, was unmistakable. Gachagua has spent recent weeks describing Mt Kenya as DCP territory, warning residents against incumbent legislators allied to the ruling United Democratic Alliance and declaring a political “transfer window” open until 31 December. On Tuesday, one day before Ruto’s address, Gachagua received three sitting MPs at his Wamunyoro residence — Gatundu South’s Gabriel Kagombe, Nyeri Woman Representative Rahab Mukami and Laikipia West’s Wachira Karani — and declared DCP “the party of the moment and the future.” Ruto’s response was measured but deliberate. He called on all political actors — beginning with his own administration — to submit to a standard of evidence-based accountability. “Those who offer alternatives must explain their proposals. All of us must respect the people’s right to question, scrutinise and choose,” he said, challenging rivals to articulate how they would lower electricity costs, finance infrastructure, expand employment and improve healthcare. It was a calculated pivot: shifting the 2027 conversation from the grievance politics that Gachagua has cultivated toward a terrain where an incumbent with a delivery record believes he holds the advantage. On financial settlements, Ruto announced the approval of KSh 18 billion owed to public and private universities and KSh 16 billion owed to hospitals under the now-defunct National Hospital Insurance Fund. Both payments, he said, were undergoing processing at the National Treasury and would be disbursed within weeks. He also announced the settlement of 28,726 verified pending bills amounting to KSh 27.8 billion, covering claims dating back to 2005. “These payments are undergoing the due process at the National Treasury for payment in the coming weeks,” he said, arguing that the disbursements would restore cash flow to businesses, protect jobs and ease financial pressure across multiple sectors. In education, the President cited the recruitment of 100,000 teachers over four years against a shortage of 116,000 when his administration assumed office, with a further 20,000 to be recruited. He said the government had constructed 23,000 classrooms, was equipping 1,600 laboratories and had increased the annual education budget from KSh 521 billion in 2022/23 to KSh 784 billion currently. Notably, he revealed that for the first time in 65 years, Kenya’s national examination papers had been printed locally — a quiet but symbolically significant assertion of institutional capacity. Some 3.6 million candidates were sitting the KPSEA, KJSEA and KCSE examinations, he added, in conditions described as calm and orderly. Healthcare figures dominated a significant portion of the address. Ruto said 33.7 million Kenyans had registered with the Social Health Authority, compared to approximately eight million under NHIF in 2022. He cited 53,465 patients receiving cancer treatment, 24,468 undergoing dialysis and 89 who had received kidney transplants under the scheme. “Through SHA, cover treatment costs are being financed on behalf of citizens, reducing the amounts that families would otherwise have to raise from either their savings, borrow from relatives, or obtain through sale of their assets,” he said. He acknowledged the troubled transition from NHIF to SHA but maintained that the long-term objective remained the progressive removal of catastrophic medical expenses from household budgets. On infrastructure, Ruto confirmed that plans to dual the Nairobi–Mombasa Highway — approximately 460 kilometres — had reached an advanced stage, with the Kenya National Highways Authority estimating costs at around KSh 300 billion. He said the project would proceed without new taxes or additional public debt, though the proposed toll-road model has drawn scrutiny from the Motorists Association of Kenya, which has called for full public disclosure of the financing structure. Ruto also announced the Northern Kenya Gateway Corridor, a 750-kilometre road linking Isiolo, Wajir and Mandera — a project he acknowledged had attracted widespread mockery when first proposed. “Some have lived their entire lives without a single tarmacked road reaching their communities. Their entire lives,” he said, invoking the equity imperative that has become a recurring theme of his administration. The most consequential passage of the address, however, may prove to be his remarks on police accountability — a subject that has shadowed his presidency since the June 2024 anti-Finance Bill protests. The Independent Policing Oversight Authority has documented 127 deaths across three major protest periods, while Missing Voices recorded 24 police-related killings in May 2026 alone. Ruto acknowledged the pain of those events, confirmed a KSh 2 billion compensation allocation and said KSh 1.2 billion had already been paid to 1,476 verified beneficiaries. He was unequivocal that compensation did not replace criminal accountability. “Investigations must continue, and prosecutions must follow for violations of the law, wherever the evidence warrants,” he said. His pledge to strengthen de-escalation procedures, oversight mechanisms and professional standards within the police service will be measured against a record that rights organisations have consistently found wanting. title: Nairobi health revenue triples to KSh 2.6B as digital reforms and SHA transform county hospitals
description: Governor Johnson Sakaja credits Social Health Authority reimbursements and digital accountability for a revenue surge that is restocking medicine shelves, upgrading diagnostics and funding community health workers across the capital By Jane Njoki Nairobi County has tripled revenue from its public health facilities from KSh 800 million to KSh 2.6 billion following digital reforms and improved reimbursements under the Social Health Authority, Governor Johnson Sakaja announced yesterday, as the county sets its sights on KSh 4 billion in health facility revenue before the end of the current financial year. Sakaja made the disclosure at the Third Annual Nairobi Health Scientific Conference, where he credited the revenue growth to a combination of SHA integration, Facility Improvement Financing, enhanced claims management and strengthened accountability at the facility level. The figures represent one of the most striking illustrations yet of how the transition from the defunct National Hospital Insurance Fund to SHA is reshaping the financial architecture of Kenya’s public health system — at least in the country’s most populous county. The numbers at individual facility level are even more arresting. Riruta Health Centre, which previously generated approximately KSh 100,000 annually, now records around KSh 6 million every month — a transformation so dramatic it strains the imagination of anyone familiar with the chronic underfunding that has long defined Kenya’s lower-tier public health infrastructure. Westlands Health Centre has similarly surged from roughly KSh 200,000 to KSh 6 million monthly, while Pangani Health Centre now generates approximately KSh 1 million each month. These are not marginal improvements — they represent a structural shift in what community-level facilities can afford to do for the patients who walk through their doors. “When we came into office, our county health facilities were generating approximately KSh 800 million annually,” Sakaja told delegates. “These resources help us procure medicines, support healthcare workers and improve our facilities to ensure better service delivery to Nairobi residents.” The additional income, he said, has enabled public hospitals to procure medicines, strengthen diagnostic services, maintain equipment and fund community outreach programmes — the unglamorous but essential work that determines whether a health system actually reaches the people it is meant to serve. SHA registration figures for Nairobi are equally significant. The county has enrolled three million residents under the scheme, representing more than 60 per cent of the city’s population. “SHA has been working well in Nairobi, enabling us to serve more residents through the reimbursement of claims for services provided,” Sakaja said. National Health Cabinet Secretary Aden Duale, who also addressed the conference, placed that figure in a slightly broader context, noting that Nairobi’s three million registrations represent approximately 69 per cent of the county’s population. “This is commendable and demonstrates Nairobi’s commitment to primary health care,” Duale said. Sakaja was careful, however, to frame the revenue growth within a clear philosophical boundary. The reforms, he emphasised, were not designed to commercialise public hospitals or to introduce market logic into facilities whose fundamental purpose is service to those least able to pay. The intent, rather, is to ensure that facilities have the resources they need to deliver care at the standard residents deserve — a distinction that matters enormously in a city where the gap between the healthcare experience of the wealthy and the poor remains one of the starkest expressions of urban inequality. Duale used the occasion to commend Nairobi specifically for two achievements that set it apart from other counties. The first is the Nairobi County Cancer Centre, which he described as the first public cancer facility of its kind in the city — a significant development in a country where cancer treatment has historically been accessible only to those with private insurance or significant personal means. The second is Nairobi’s status as the county with the highest number of Community Health Workers and the only county in Kenya currently paying them stipends. That latter detail is quietly consequential: community health workers are the capillary system of any primary health care model, and the chronic failure to compensate them has long been one of the structural weaknesses undermining community-level healthcare delivery across the country. The county has established 782 Community Health Units supported by 7,820 Community Health Promoters conducting household visits, supporting expectant mothers, promoting immunisation, undertaking disease surveillance and linking families to health services. Sakaja said the county was also strengthening digital community health systems to improve household-level data collection and referrals, and introducing AI-assisted digital X-ray screening for tuberculosis — a disease that continues to exact a heavy toll in Nairobi’s densely populated informal settlements. Health, Wellness and Nutrition CEC Suzanne Silantoi reported that 99 per cent of county health facilities had been digitised and integrated into the SHA system, enabling them to submit claims and receive reimbursements with a speed and reliability that the NHIF era rarely delivered. Chief Officer for Medical Services Maryam Dahir added that emergency response capacity had been strengthened, with residents able to access assistance through the 1508 hotline. Her closing remark carried the weight of a standard that the county’s leadership would do well to remember as election season approaches. “We will be judged not by the discussions we hold, but by the improvements we deliver in service to the people of Nairobi,” Dahir said. The three-day conference, held under the theme One Health in Action: Building Resilient, Climate-Smart and Equitable Health Systems for Universal Health Coverage, brought together healthcare professionals, researchers, policymakers and development partners to examine how urban health systems can be made more resilient, more equitable and more responsive to the compounding pressures of climate change, population growth and emerging disease. For Nairobi’s residents — particularly the millions living in areas where a functioning health centre was, until recently, more aspiration than reality — the revenue figures are welcome. But numbers on a conference slide are not the same as medicines on a shelf, a nurse who answers at night or a referral that actually works. title: Nyeri Catholic Archbishop threatens to sack officials who let politicians into the pulpit
description: between church and state, warning that any official who hands a politician a microphone will be dismissed immediately By Jane Njambi Nyeri Catholic Archbishop Anthony Muheria has threatened to dismiss priests, catechists, coordinators and church secretaries who allow politicians to address congregations, issuing one of the starkest warnings yet from Kenya’s Catholic leadership as political pressure on places of worship intensifies ahead of the 10 August 2027 General Election. Muheria delivered the directive as the Catholic Church escalates its campaign to keep politicians from converting Sunday services into campaign rallies — a practice that reached uncomfortable levels during the 2022 election cycle and shows every sign of repeating itself as Kenya enters another charged electoral season. With barely eight months to polling day, the pews have become some of the most coveted real estate in Kenyan politics, offering candidates direct access to organised, attentive and community-rooted audiences that no roadside rally can replicate. The Archbishop was unambiguous about the consequences for those who facilitate such access. “Whoever allows a leader — anyone among you who allows anybody to speak in the church — will be fired immediately,” he declared. He extended the warning explicitly to administrative staff, making clear that arranging an opportunity for a politician to address worshippers was itself a dismissible offence. “If you are a coordinator, a secretary, and you are the one who arranged this thing, know that once it reaches me, you have lost your job and we will have an election to get another secretary,” he said. The language was deliberate and pointed — the word “election” applied not to the national contest for public office but to the internal process of replacing a church official who had compromised the sanctity of the institution. It was a sharp piece of rhetorical symmetry, and it conveyed Muheria’s message with unmistakable clarity: the Church will govern itself by its own standards, regardless of the political weather outside its doors. His frustration with the 2022 experience was evident. That election period saw politicians engage in heated and at times undignified confrontations inside churches, with congregations pressed into service as audiences for attacks on opponents and displays of political rivalry. Muheria cited those scenes as precisely what the current directive is designed to prevent. “Let us keep politics out of here, so that we can have respect in our churches,” he said. He went further, drawing a sharp and deliberately colourful line between the spaces he considers appropriate for political contest and those he does not. “Let them go to bars, those dens. Let them go there into the fields — there is where they can fight, let them pull each other in the mud. But the church is God’s,” Muheria stated. The image was vivid and intentional: politics, in his framing, belongs to the rough and contested public square, not to the consecrated space where communities gather in a different spirit entirely. Muheria’s directive follows a formal position adopted by the Kenya Conference of Catholic Bishops, which has barred politicians from delivering political addresses in churches across the country. The bishops argued that politicians have no shortage of alternative platforms — television, radio, public barazas, roadside rallies — through which to advance their agendas and seek support. What they do not have, the bishops maintained, is a right to the church’s platform, its congregation or its moral authority. That authority is precisely what makes churches so attractive to Kenyan politicians. In a country where community trust in formal institutions has been eroded by years of broken promises and governance failures, the church retains a credibility that political parties and government agencies have largely forfeited. A politician who can stand before a congregation — or better still, be seen to receive the implicit endorsement of a priest or bishop — gains something that money and advertising cannot easily manufacture. The Catholic Church’s directive is, at its core, a refusal to allow that credibility to be borrowed for electoral purposes. The timing carries additional significance. Kenya’s political landscape is shifting rapidly as the 2027 election approaches. Former Deputy President Rigathi Gachagua is consolidating opposition in the Mt Kenya region through his Democracy for the Citizens Party. The Linda Mwananchi Movement is expanding its national footprint. President William Ruto is defending his record against a cost-of-living narrative that has tested public patience. In that environment, every platform matters — and the Catholic Church, with its reach into rural and urban communities across the country, represents one of the most significant platforms of all. By drawing its boundary now, eight months before polling day, the Church is sending a message that it intends to be a moral voice in the 2027 election rather than a political prop. Whether that boundary holds as campaign pressure mounts will be one of the quieter but consequential tests of institutional integrity in the months ahead. The church, Muheria has made clear, is God’s. The mud is available elsewhere. title: Forex scammer KENYAN PRINCE defrauds a gullible fan Ksh 100,000 to trade for them - Claims he lost the money in two days and shamelessly asks for more
description: Thursday, November 19, 2026 - Controversial forex trader Raymond Omosa, popularly known as Kenyan Prince, has been exposed on social media after a fan accused him of swindling KSh100,000 under the guise of trading on their behalf. The complainant approached Kenyan Prince seeking guidance on forex trading and account management, hoping to make money through his expertise. However, things took a different turn after the fan sent him KSh100,000 to trade on their behalf. According to the complaint, Prince went silent after receiving the money, leaving the fan anxious and wondering whether he had executed the trades as agreed. When the fan followed up to establish whether the money had been invested, Kenyan Prince asked for more money instead of providing a clear account of what had happened to the initial amount. After a lengthy back-and-forth exchange, Raymond admitted that he had lost the entire KSh100,000 in just two days and urged the fan to deposit more money so they could try again. “Fund, we try again,” he reportedly told the disappointed fan. Kenyan Prince has been using hired luxury cars and a carefully curated social media lifestyle to attract gullible victims who are tempted to entrust him with their money. The Kenyan DAILY POST.

title: Popular Kikuyu gospel singer REGINA Wa ANGANIWE’s ex-husband, Bishop BERNARD MUTHOGA, demands to be in their children's lives after the woman he married failed to bear children - Has been absent for 8 years
description: Thursday, November 19, 2026 - A family dispute has erupted after popular Kikuyu gospel singer Regina Wa Anganiwe’s ex-husband, Bishop Bernard Muthoga, expressed a desire to reconnect with their children, whom he has been absent from for the past eight years. Muthoga reportedly walked out of his marriage to Regina and moved on with another woman, leaving the singer to raise their children single-handedly. However, eight years down the line, the bishop is said to be seeking a place in the lives of the children he abandoned after his new marriage failed to give him children. Regina, however, has moved on with her life and taken steps to distance the children from their father's identity. At some point, the gospel singer went as far as changing the children's names, dropping their father's surname and replacing it with her own. Their marriage ended in a highly publicised and contentious divorce around 2018, with the former couple remaining embroiled in several legal disputes since their separation. One of the most bitter disputes emerged following Muthoga's remarriage and centred on the grave of their late daughter, who had died from a brain tumour 12 years earlier. The dispute escalated after Muthoga questioned the child's paternity and threatened to flatten her grave. Regina subsequently obtained a court order in October 2022 allowing her to exhume her daughter's remains and rebury them on private land. Now, with Muthoga reportedly seeking to reconnect with the children after years of absence, the latest development threatens to reopen old wounds in a family whose differences have played out publicly for years. title: WILBRODA’s ex-lover and baby daddy, USTADH KIMATHI, goes on a ranting spree and reveals how she blocked his access to their son after separation - Huyu Mwanamke Ni Kisirani
description: Friday, November 20, 2026 - Former Papa Shirandula actress Wilbroda’s ex-lover and baby daddy, Ustadh Kimathi, has gone on a ranting spree, divulging details of their failed relationship. In a lengthy Facebook post, Kimathi opened up about their separation and accused the celebrated actress of blocking his access to their son following their breakup. He shared his frustrations publicly, revisiting some of the challenges he claims to have faced in trying to maintain a relationship with his child after things fell apart between the two. Read his full post below: There’s this video on TikTok making rounds, and while I have laughed through the parts like I have for the last almost 17 years, the number of forwards compels me to say this: This interview is from about seven years ago, and I remember responding to it at the time with a rather strongly worded letter, through my lawyer. There are, however, a few things I think need to be clarified, even though I know society has a way of sympathizing with the woman in such cases and condemning us (men) unheard. First, I was never married to Wilbroda, contrary to the popular narrative of many years. She moved from her home in Rongai into my house, where we both lived together, and some of her family members moved in. My house lacked nothing and was big enough to accommodate family with two extra DSQs. And I never had issues because I come from a big family myself, until I came to see subsequent interviews years later where she lamented allowing them in, but that’s on her because nobody amongst her siblings wronged or has ever wronged me to that extent. Today, I still consider them family regardless. Before that arrangement, we had not been living together. We would osciallate between my house and hers when she was pregnant with our son. I paid for all the bills and accompanied her to all clinics throughout her journey, despite the fact that “her pregnancy hated” some of the clothes and colognes I wore. (story for another day). When we realized we couldn’t stay together, I just mentioned the reasons, and the answers were very unencouraging. In fact, I had contemplated moving out myself, but I kept on thinking she would struggle considering she didn’t have a good salary. This went on until I returned from an assignment in Tanzania to find my house partially emptied. The last item being undone was the bed in the master bedroom. Anyway, there is a much longer history behind our separation, one that I have consciously chosen not to discuss publicly for close to 17 years now. That silence has neither been an admission of wrongdoing, nor should it be mistaken for an inability to defend myself. I just fear a clash with numbers online. When you fight “big people,” you risk fighting their numbers. Other than that, I have my reasons for keeping certain things private, and they are not trivial; remember I have children, some of whom are adolescents soon to become young adults. But all I want many who have castigated me in my silence to understand is that there are experiences that leave a man with very little appetite for public explanations. Perhaps one day I will elaborate on my side of that story, maybe. But not necessarily to settle scores. I might do it because I know I represent the many men out here who have endured circumstances they never found the courage or an appropriate platform to articulate. Plus, I also cared about the dignity of friends, family, and all of whom this would tamper with. However, it is important to note that immediately after the separation, there were sustained attempts to frustrate my access to my son. Some of those attempts involved her then-boyfriend and the organisation he was associated with at the time, The CRADLE Children’s Foundation. I did not take those matters lightly. I sought legal representation and pursued the appropriate avenues to protect my relationship with my son. The verdict on my relationship and involvement is well known to those who have cared to follow and chronicle it. I don’t do anything for show; I do it to the best of my ability and from my bottomless heart. For the avoidance of doubt, my son has never lacked my support. I have consistently played my part in his upbringing and welfare. The recent disagreement over school fees arose after his mother unilaterally moved him from Mang’u to his current school. I disagreed with the decision and, for reasons I believe were legitimate, declined to finance that particular arrangement. The above disagreement should not be casually rewritten into a story of an absent or financially irresponsible father. If anything, any concerned individual should look at it as a problem they’d love to have in their own family, a situation where either parent can afford their wants. My son has capable parents so this should not worry anybody, and on that front, I think ours are good problems. There is, however, another misconception I have found rather amusing over the years, and it is the impression that I was the financially weaker party in that relationship. The truth is, I have never felt the need to compete over who had more money, but facts matter. I may have come from a difficult childhood, but I never spent my post-college years endlessly looking for my footing financially. I have never earned anything less than a six or seven-figure cheque since leaving college. God has been gracious in ways I will never take for granted. I met my son’s mother while I was working for an international organization that not only paid me well, but also on time. She was in acting which never paid any dignifying wages in this country at the time, unless they just started. Her radio career came along while we were together. Later, I remember advising her to consider the Swahili side of radio when an opening arose and she was faced with the choice to stay or leave the English evening drive show, because I genuinely believed that was where her authentic audience and natural connection with listeners lay. I mention this not to claim credit for anyone’s career, but to put into perspective how independently we were both, with both of us finding our feet professionally. So, I was already working and earning good money before that relationship, and I continued doing so long after it ended. Perhaps the simplest question to ask those who insist on portraying me as financially dependent is this: if I was as incapable as some would have people believe, how did I maintain the same neighbourhood, house, and standard of living for eight straight years after the separation, until I relocated? I was not living off anybody’s generosity. Regarding the allegation of my violent conduct, I am sure there’s no documented report on the same, save for invoking the name of Charles Bukeko (May his soul rest), a man with whom we shared a very cordial relationship and would share loud laughters and lengthy stories in our mother tongue “Olusamia,” whenever we bumped into each other long after all this had happened. The closest we have to debunk this same story is herself saying in subsequent interviews that she was never even “touched,” we simply couldn’t agree on principles that make up a relationship and/or family union. There is also the suggestion that I was physically present when they were moving out or that I subsequently begged for a reconciliation. Neither is true. I have never looked back or pursued a return to that relationship. Those who know me will attest that whenever I have made a physical appearance in circumstances involving my son, it has been shared openly and in solidarity with him, as any responsible father should be. My presence should therefore never be repackaged as evidence of a romantic pursuit because I am yet to even start, especially with him turning into a young adult and needing counsel. Sincerely, not many men would stay quiet for all those years despite interviews all over the place touching on them; I have deliberately remained measured about this entire subject for reasons a sane man will see in my writing so far. I have a family, children, friendships, and important relationships in my present life that deserve respect and peace. They did not create the circumstances of nearly two decades ago, and they should not have to live in the shadow of a dispute I have chosen not to publicise. I am equally conscious that my growing children deserve to mature into their adulthood without being recruited into the grievances of adults they may not agree with even now, but choose silence until the right time. But restraint should not be confused with surrender, and silence should not be interpreted as confirmation of every story told in one’s absence. Sometimes a man chooses not to respond because there are bigger things to protect than his ego. I have been comfortable and remain so, carrying that burden, even when it has meant allowing myself to become the convenient virtual punching bag. And honestly, can we finally allow this chapter to rest? I appreciate that we are living through difficult times, and I understand the pressures of raking social media numbers, propping public relevance and opportunities alive. But must a relationship that ended almost 17 years ago (before it even started) continually be resurrected? I am not the only man here; the world has millions of women and us to boot Surely there is enough life ahead of us for everyone to move on without repeatedly revisiting relationships that belong to another season of our lives. Seasons even you have, only that we have not cared enough to dig in. As I conclude, I mention, like Baks [Pun intended], that I have no intention of entertaining the endless politics of how many women I have dated, how many relationships I have had, or who occupies what position in my life today. I am a grown black, bearded Samia (Luhya) man, and my private life is not a public referendum. I have dated women, as many adults have, I can marry whoever I want, but I have only ever been married once, and I was never married to Wilbroda. So, respectfully, if you have never been married to me, please do not appoint yourself an authority on my marital history. There is a difference between having known someone, having shared a relationship with someone, and having been their spouse. Those distinctions matter, and I would appreciate them being respected. I hope this clarifies the 16 years of silence, ama mnataka Mic Cheque with Chaxy, Mariah, and Mwass ndio hii story iishe? The Kenyan DAILY POST.

description: In today's Daily Fix:As if anyone expected anything different, GTA 6 now has the biggest launch in entertainment history with a staggering $3.79 billion in sales in its first 24 hours. This includes more than 30 million pre-sale copies sold. And keep in mind, the PC version has yet to drop. Although GTA 6's launch dwarfs even the biggest movie releases, it's not a true 1:1 comparison as the game sells for about $80 a copy ($100 if you buy the ultimate edition), and your average movie ticket is nowhere near that expensive. In related news, prior to the launch of GTA 6, gamers spent 14% less this October than last year, despite heavy hitters like Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4 and the Ocarina of Time remake dropping in the same month. This is likely due to the GTA 6 effect, and gamers wanting to save their time and money for that game instead. And finally, Christopher Nolan's The Odyssey film helped boost sales of Ubisoft's Assassin's Creed Odyssey game.
